Thai prime minister meets security chiefs after coordinated attacks in 3 southern provinces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
19:23:02 UTC
04:23:02 KST

Thai prime minister meets security chiefs after coordinated attacks in 3 southern provinces
BANGKOK (AP) — Thailand ’s Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul, already facing a flood crisis in the country’s north, held an urgent meeting on Sunday with high-level security officials in response to coordinated violence overnight in three southern provinces where a small-scale Muslim insurgency is active.
The meeting, held shortly before Anutin flew north to inspect the badly flooded province of Nan, followed 51 incidents on Saturday night in the southernmost provinces of Narathiwat, Pattani and Yala.
The attackers did not engage with military or police forces. Only three civilians were known to have been wounded, and they were reported to be recovering on Sunday.
The violence primarily involved small bombs, arson and other forms of property damage. The highest-profile target was a 7-Eleven convenience store in Pattani. A video circulating on social media appeared to show armed men stalking outside the store while customers and workers fled before it was set on fire.
A bomb that damaged rail tracks in Narathiwat forced the suspension of local and long-haul services. It was not clear when they would be restored due to the uncertain security situation.
As has often been the case with such incidents, no group was immediately publicly blamed or claimed responsibility for the actions.
However, such attacks are generally believed to be carried out by the Barisan Revolusi Nasional Melayu Patani, or BRN. It is the major insurgent group in the south with the organizational means and support to stage such an action. It is also the group with which the Thai government has been holding on-again, off-again peace talks.
The three southernmost provinces are the only ones with Muslim majorities in predominantly Buddhist Thailand and the BRN has said that it is seeking self-rule for them.
Muslim residents have long complained of being treated like second-class citizens in Thailand, and separatist movements have been periodically active for decades.
Insurgent violence escalated sharply in 2004 and was met with heavy-handed crackdowns, further fueling discontent. According to Deep South Watch, a think tank based at the Prince of Songkla University’s campus in Pattani, 7,837 people have died in the violence in the past 22 years.
The last major flare-up came in July, when about 10 attackers opened fire and threw pipe bombs at soldiers at a security checkpoint in Narathiwat. Five paramilitary soldiers were killed and six civilians were wounded, including a 10-year-old boy.
Don Pathan, an independent security analyst, says the BRN carries out attacks largely for leverage as it negotiates with the Thai government.
“From the ground, BRN combatants are turned off by the boasting of military officials and wanted to use the spike in violence to demonstrate their capabilities,” said Pathan. “Many of the targets in these latest incidents were civilians, but BRN combatants were not after body counts. They want to send a stern message to the Thais of what they are capable of doing.”

A US envoy clarifies his comments on Golan Heights that contradicted Trump’s position
BEIRUT (AP) — The U.S. special envoy to Syria and ambassador to Turkey on Sunday walked back his comments from two days ago that Israel “still” occupies the Golan Heights in violation of U.N. resolutions, remarks that went against U.S. President Donald Trump ‘s position on the disputed territory.
Israel captured the Golan Heights from Syria in the 1967 Mideast war and annexed it in 1981. The United Nations and most of the international community consider the territory occupied Syrian land and does not recognize Israel’s annexation of it.
In 2019, Trump recognized Israeli sovereignty over the territory, reversing decades of U.S. policy.
Ambassador Tom Barrack on Friday said that Israel “still” occupies the territory in an interview with Lebanese-Australian entrepreneur Mario Nawfal.
Barrack now says that was a description of the territory’s historical status, “not an endorsement of the United Nations’ position” on the Golan.
“United States policy on the Golan was set by President Trump in 2019 and is unchanged,” he said in a statement to The Associated Press on Sunday.
He said he intended to explain why he does not anticipate annexation in Lebanon, where Israeli forces are occupying parts of the south after the latest Israel-Hezbollah war, and to argue that negotiated agreements, rather than territorial maps, are more durable and that he had cited the Golan as an example that “territory taken by force remains contested for generations.”
In the Friday interview, Barrack had also criticized Israel’s strikes on an airbase in northern Syria earlier last week. Israeli officials said the strikes intended to prevent Turkey from establishing a presence at the base.
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz defended the strikes, saying on X on Sunday that critics who initially called it “unnecessary and politically motivated” changed their position after the government said they were based on “clear intelligence” and at the recommendation of the Israeli army. He added that Israel would not allow Turkey “to establish itself in Syria and threaten Israeli security.”
The strikes last Tuesday have highlighted growing tensions between Israel and Turkey over Ankara’s increased influence in Syria following the fall of Bashar Assad. Turkey and Syria have denied that Turkish forces were due to be deployed at the Abu Duhur base.
Barrack’s comments on the Golan also sparked a backlash in Washington.
Florida Republican Sen. Rick Scott wrote on X that the ambassador appears to have “forgotten” Trump’s recognition of Israeli sovereignty over the territory.
Barrack went further on the defensive on Sunday, responding to criticism of his assessment of ongoing negotiations between Israel and Lebanon over Israeli withdrawal and the disarmament of the militant group.
He had said “there are two people missing from that (negotiating) table – Hezbollah and Iran.” That remark prompted speculation Barrack meant Tehran and Hezbollah should join the U.S.-backed negotiations.
On Sunday, Barrack stressed that the U.S. does not negotiate with Hezbollah, but said he was pointing out that “the weapons in question are supplied and financed by Iran,” which complicates negotiations over their fate.
“I was describing the difficulty of the problem, not proposing a new table,” Barrack told the AP. “Hezbollah is a designated foreign terrorist organization. We do not negotiate with it, and nothing I said suggests otherwise.”
He also defended his remarks questioning who would replace Tehran’s financial support for Shiite communities in southern Lebanon, saying that raising those questions was “not conferring standing on anyone.”

MEXICO CITY (AP) — The embattled governor of Mexico’s Sinaloa state has reversed his decision to return to his post, bowing to an extraordinary backlash from his own ruling party over accusations by U.S. prosecutors he conspired with a powerful cartel to smuggle drugs into the United States.
State lawmakers were expected Sunday to approve Gov. Rubén Rocha Moya’s request for an indefinite leave of absence, about a day and a half after he announced his return by claiming Mexican prosecutors had cleared him of the drug trafficking charges leveled against him by the U.S. Department of Justice in late April.
The rapid reversal demonstrated the authority Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum wields over her Morena party as she walks a fine line between placating U.S. President Donald Trump, who says cartels control Mexico and has repeatedly offered U.S. military help to fight them, and her progressive movement deeply wary of U.S. intervention.
After nearly four months on leave, Rocha Moya announced Friday that he was returning to office, claiming Mexico’s Attorney General’s Office had found “no evidence to support our participation in any criminal conduct.” He declared that he was back “as governor of Sinaloa with my head held high.”
That defiance lasted barely a day, as his return unleashed a torrent of criticism from governors, senators and other prominent figures in Morena, including Sheinbaum.
“No personal interest can ever come before the interests of the people and the nation,” she wrote Saturday in an apparent rebuke of Rocha Moya, without mentioning him by name. “Mexico deserves public servants who understand that positions are temporary, but responsibility to the nation is eternal.”
Morena said its national leadership had no prior knowledge of Rocha Moya’s return, calling it his “personal decision.” The party’s Senate bloc urged respect for the ongoing investigation, while Morena governors declared in a joint statement that “personal or group political projects have no place” when the country’s interests are at stake.
Ricardo Monreal, Morena’s leader in the lower house of Congress, publicly urged Rocha Moya, his longtime ally, to reconsider and remain on leave.
The coordinated response left Rocha Moya isolated. He announced later Saturday that he had asked the state legislature to allow him to step aside indefinitely. “Sinaloa, the nation and the transformation movement come first,” he wrote.
Rocha Moya had been on leave since early May, days after federal prosecutors in New York unsealed a bombshell indictment accusing him and nine other current and former Mexican officials of protecting Sinaloa cartel members in exchange for bribes as they trafficked fentanyl, heroin, cocaine and methamphetamine into the U.S.
The indictment marked the Trump administration’s most significant public action against what it calls official corruption enabling Mexico’s cartels, fueling new tension between the U.S. and Mexican governments. Sheinbaum has denied shielding Rocha Moya but rejected Washington’s request to arrest and extradite the defendants without credible evidence, insisting that any prosecution take place in Mexico.
Rocha Moya, 77, a staunch ally of Sheinbaum’s mentor, former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador, denied wrongdoing and described the charges as a politically motivated attack. He initially stepped aside so he could cooperate with the Mexican investigation without relying on the constitutional immunity attached to his office. Whether taking leave stripped him of that protection — and whether his latest request to step aside indefinitely would do so again — remains disputed among Mexican legal scholars.
After the indictment, the mayor of Culiacán, Sinaloa’s capital, and the state’s deputy attorney general also stepped down from their posts, while two former senior state officials surrendered to U.S. authorities.
Sinaloa has been engulfed for nearly two years in a bloody conflict between rival factions of the cartel that bears the state’s name.

Jared Kushner meets with Democratic leader Jeffries with House control at stake in November
WASHINGTON (AP) — House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries and President Donald Trump’s son-in-law and outside adviser Jared Kushner met privately recently in New York, a signal that the White House is seeking ways to work with Democrats if they wrest majority control from Republicans in the midterm elections.
The meeting, first reported Sunday by The New York Times, touched on issues ranging from housing, immigration to the high costs of living. People in the United States are struggling under inflationary prices that Democrats blame on Republicans, alongside Trump, for failing to get under control.
Kushner suggested that Jeffries, who is in line to become House speaker if Democrats regain power in November, meet with White House chief of staff Susie Wiles as a follow-up.
Jeffries, in a statement Sunday, did not mention the private conversation but said the Republican administration needed to drop the GOP’s “my-way-or-the-highway” approach that “has failed the American people.”
“To stop the madness, we have repeatedly made clear that an extremist approach will not work and will be met with forceful opposition,” the New York congressman said. “The question is whether Republicans will join us.”
The meeting shows the depth of Republican Party angst over losing their congressional majority, particularly the House, and the need to make inroads with the opposing party as the White House seeks to stem any potential political fallout on the president.
If Democrats retake power, the White House can expect an aggressive oversight agenda into what Jeffries has called the “crooks” in the administration, with the threat of impeachment among the many tools at the party’s disposal.
House Speaker Mike Johnson, a close ally of Trump, bristled Sunday when asked about the meeting. He minimized the role that Kushner, who he said “hedges his bets,” plays in the White House.
“I’m telling you what, you better not bet against the House Republicans,” Johnson, R-La., told Fox News Channel’s “The Sunday Briefing.”
“I don’t know what that’s about,” Johnson said. “I know Jared has interests in lots of other things going on. He’s not really directly involved in the admin, at least in the day-to-day in the White House.”
The White House did not respond to a request for comment. A representative for Kushner also did not respond.
Kushner is a familiar Trump emissary to Democrats
Jeffries and Kushner are not strangers.
The New Yorkers allied during the first Trump administration on landmark legislation to allow sentencing flexibility for certain drug offenses as a way to curtail lengthy terms in the federal prison system.
While not necessarily close, the two have maintained a relationship despite the repeated attacks Trump has leveled against Jeffries and the Democratic leader’s responses. In Trump’s second term, Kushner has an oversize role despite having no formal position in the White House. He serves as an outside adviser and envoy, particularly shuttling to foreign diplomatic missions as the U.S. war against Iran drags into its sixth month.
Trump has only met with Jeffries once since the president returned to the White House, taunting the House leader and Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer of New York with red “Make America Great Again” 2028 caps on the desk in front of them in the Oval Office — a nod to Trump’s toying with an unconstitutional third term in office.
After that fall meeting, Trump posted a fake image of Schumer with Jeffries wearing a sombrero with a handlebar mustache in what was widely viewed as a racist trope as he mocked the Democrats before what became the longest federal government shutdown in U.S. history.
Trump has been able to alternately ignore the Congress as he relies on the sheer force of executive power to implement his priorities or to pressure the Republicans in the House and Senate, when needed, to fall in line behind the White House, particularly to confirm controversial Cabinet nominees.
All that is likely to change if Democrats control either chamber, with lawmakers eager for Congress to flex their own power as a coequal branch of government more willing to hold the White House in check.
Republicans and Democrats race for power in midterms
House Republicans are counting on Trump’s popularity among their core voters as they struggle to hold onto majority control, with Johnson believing the GOP will defy history that tends to reward the challengers in midterms and punish the party in power.
The House GOP has a slim majority. Control will likely be won — or lost — in a handful of battleground districts as Democrats put forward candidates in what they hope will be something of a repeat of 2018, when they swept to power riding a wave of voter unrest during Trump’s first term.
While the House is most at risk for Republicans this year, he narrowly split Senate is also increasingly in play. GOP strategists worry about an enthusiasm gap on their side as Democrats appear more eager to head to the polls.
At the same time, Democrats are nominating outsider candidates, some aligned with socialist agendas over establishment backed candidates, in a sign of voter unrest with the status quo.

US President Donald Trump capped celebrations of the US 250th anniversary with a first-of-its-kind auto race through the streets of Washington, closing a summer of sports and spectacle as drivers sped past the capital's iconic landmarks.
IndyCar's Freedom 250 Grand Prix zoomed through the National Mall, past the US Capitol, down historic Pennsylvania Avenue and around the National Archives, in the marquee event on Sunday afternoon.
The race was expected to draw roughly 200,000 spectators, officials said, and tickets were free. Passes to private trackside clubs sold for $5,000.
Trump takes a lap, waves the green flag
Trump's motorcade took an honorary loop around the race course before he waved the green flag to officially start the 250-mile (402-km) race at about 1:18 p.m. ET (1718 GMT). Although the green flag at IndyCar events typically is waved atop a tower at the start/finish line, Trump remained in his presidential box for Sunday's start.
"I don't know if anything will ever top what we're going to be having," Trump said in July as drivers visited the White House to celebrate the start of the race course's construction.
The race is the latest in a series of sporting events Trump has used to celebrate the country and his second term, even as his approval rating has dropped to the lowest point since he returned to the White House in January 2025, and the US is embroiled in a war with Iran.
He opened the summer with a professional mixed martial arts bout on the South Lawn of the White House, then presented the trophy to FIFA World Cup champion Spain a month later.
Earlier in August, he appeared at the “Patriot Games,” a cross between a game show and track meet for high school athletes, televised on sports network ESPN.
For Trump, the events have served to raise his profile, both domestically and globally. The UFC fight card was streamed internationally, and during the World Cup trophy presentation, he lingered at mid-pitch while the Spanish team hoisted the trophy.
IndyCar driver Pato O'Ward, who races for Arrow McLaren, told the Fox News Sunday show he was feeling "pretty surreal" ahead of the race.
"We never thought that we were going to be racing here anytime in 2026," O'Ward said. "Everyone's excited that we're here and, I mean, it's a pretty picturesque backdrop."
Race plans face criticism
The Washington race has faced its share of criticism. The track was originally set to run through the grounds of the US Capitol, but the proposal required lawmakers' approval and stalled in Congress. Advertising is prohibited on Capitol grounds, and the race cars, with their dozens of corporate sponsors, along with trackside billboards, would have run afoul of those regulations.
Trump instead issued an executive order commanding Transportation Department officials to draw up a course that did not require congressional sign-off.
Officials paused air traffic at Washington's Ronald Reagan National Airport for three hours at midday on Sunday to accommodate the IndyCar event's military flyovers, including one featuring a Boeing 747 jet often used as Air Force One, and another including what appeared to be a B-2 stealth bomber.
The city's police closed major thoroughfares downtown due to pedestrian activity and security procedures.
Race officials said the city's roads will not need much refurbishment before or after the race, in which drivers are expected to reach 185 miles per hour (298 km per hour) on the Pennsylvania Avenue straightaway.
The event has dozens of corporate sponsors, including major companies such as Boeing, SpaceX's Starlink, and Delta Air Lines, which will be sponsoring an IndyCar race for the first time, Bud Denker, the Grand Prix's chair and president of Penske Corp., said on Thursday.

Pakistan’s rise as a regional mediator could reshape Middle East diplomacy - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
19:21:05 UTC
04:21:05 KST

Pakistan is increasingly positioning itself as one of the Middle East’s most important diplomatic players.
Over the past week, Islamabad has simultaneously deepened strategic ties with Syria, prepared for high-level talks with Iran, and continued its role as a potential mediator between Tehran and Washington.
In a sense, Pakistan had taken a step back over the last two months. Now it is trying to return to the table. Pakistan is seeking to become an influential actor in shaping the region’s future. This was clear over the last year. The Trump administration has trusted Pakistan and worked with it.
The timing is important. The Middle East remains in transition following the US and Israeli military campaign against Iran that began in late February. While a memorandum of understanding is supposedly in play, tensions continue to grow. Iran is increasing its threat. The US is also talking up new economic pressure.
According to the media site Rudaw, Pakistan’s Army Chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, is expected to travel to Tehran as part of Islamabad’s effort to promote “regional stability.” Iran’s Foreign Ministry said the visit is intended to strengthen cooperation while continuing Pakistan’s “good offices” in promoting peace and security.
The announcement followed a telephone conversation between Munir and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, who discussed developments and diplomatic efforts. There is a lot of generalized language here. However, what is important is that the visit is happening.
Pakistan’s role has evolved over the last several months. Rudaw noted that Islamabad helped mediate between Iran and the United States after the outbreak of fighting earlier this year, contributing to negotiations that produced a memorandum of understanding between Tehran and Washington.
Pakistan has emerged as a mediator between US and Iran
Although tensions remain, Pakistan has emerged as one of the countries capable of maintaining dialogue with both sides.
That role may become even more important as Washington increases economic pressure on Tehran.
US President Donald Trump recently announced what he described as economic warfare against Iran, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent promised tough sanctions. Those measures are expected to further tighten restrictions on Iran’s economy and increase pressure on countries that continue commercial ties with Tehran.
Iran has responded with new threats. Iran feels confident it can outfox the Americans.
According to a second Rudaw report, Mohsen Rezai, head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, warned neighboring countries against cooperating with the new American sanctions campaign.
Rezai stated that if the economic blockade continued, Iran would prevent Gulf oil exports from leaving the region. “If the blockade continues, we will not allow a single drop of Persian Gulf oil to leave via any route,” Rezai said in remarks carried by Iranian state TV.
He also noted that Iran could target American economic interests if pressure continued, while insisting that the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed until Washington changed its policies. Iran is showcasing its continued arrogance.
These comments illustrate how the confrontation between the US and Iran has shifted. Earlier phases centered on military conflict: Missile strikes, drone attacks, and military operations. Now the competition is taking place through sanctions, maritime pressure, and competing trade routes. Each side wants to see who will blink first. Hormuz remains important to that struggle because roughly 20% of global oil shipments previously transited the waterway before the conflict disrupted maritime commerce.
Pakistan FM’s Syria visit highlights expanding regional partnerships
Pakistan is expanding its regional partnerships elsewhere. According to the Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA), Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Hassan al-Shaibani recently concluded the first visit by a Syrian foreign minister to Pakistan in 19 years.
The visit reflects Damascus’s broader effort to rebuild regional relationships following the fall of the Assad regime and to establish what Syrian officials described as a “new Syrian state.”
During meetings with Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar, Army Chief Asim Munir, and other senior officials, the two countries discussed expanding cooperation in politics, security, trade, aviation, and investment. Syria welcomed the recently announced Mecca Agreement for Mutual Defense and praised Pakistan’s role in supporting regional stability.
SANA reported that the two governments also discussed investment forums, restoring direct flights, and coordinating on regional diplomacy, including Pakistan’s efforts to reduce tensions between Iran and the US.
Syrian officials emphasized that Pakistan now sits alongside Saudi Arabia and Turkey as one of Syria’s strategic partners.
Mohammad al-Jaffal, an adviser at Syria’s Foreign Ministry, said relations with Riyadh, Ankara, and Islamabad represent three complementary tracks designed to strengthen Syria’s regional role. This could lead to Syria joining the new alliance of Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan, which would raise eyebrows in Israel, where tensions are growing with Turkey.
Pakistan emerging as a bridge between multiple countries
Taken together, these developments point toward Pakistan becoming a bridge between multiple countries. Islamabad maintains longstanding defense cooperation with Saudi Arabia. It has steadily expanded military and industrial cooperation with Turkey. It is now rebuilding relations with Syria while preserving dialogue with Iran and maintaining working ties with Washington.
For the US, Pakistan’s expanding regional role presents many opportunities. Islamabad’s ability to communicate with Tehran, Damascus, Riyadh, Ankara, and Washington could prove valuable during the next crisis.
Pakistan must be careful, though. It has to show the Trump administration it can achieve results. The administration now wants to see things happen that can help the US wind down this conflict. At the same time, balancing those relationships will become increasingly difficult if conflict between Iran and the US continues to grow.
The coming weeks will provide an early indication of whether Pakistan can successfully maintain its role as a regional mediator while also expanding its strategic initiatives.

Israeli tourism group Aviation Links (Kishrey Teufa) and Greek real estate investment firm Palmo Group announced Sunday a partnership to complete, market and manage an €8.8 million vacation-apartment project on the waterfront in Loutraki, Greece.
The HORIZA LOUTRAKI project will convert an existing eight-story hotel into a complex of 75 vacation apartments, some of which are intended for short-term tourist rentals. Apartment prices will start at €100,000, according to the companies.
Palmo will oversee completion of the project, apartment sales and support for buyers, while Aviation Links will participate in developing and pricing the tourism product and marketing it to vacationers.
Following delivery of the apartments, the project is expected to be operated by a management company jointly owned by the two groups.
Aviation Links plans to use its existing tourism distribution network, including travel agents, companies, employee committees, consumer clubs and direct-sales channels, to market stays at the development.
The partnership creates a model in which apartments are sold to individual investors while the tourism company works to generate demand for them as vacation properties.
“The partnership with Palmo is another step in expanding Aviation Links’ activity in tourism real estate,” said Yehuda Lahav, CPA and controller of Aviation Links Group.
“We bring more than four decades of experience in tourism, deep familiarity with Israeli vacationers in Greece, and marketing and distribution systems that reach broad audiences,” Lahav said. “Palmo brings proven experience in real estate development and investment in Greece, and the combination creates a model connecting the property, the vacation experience and its management afterward.”
From hotel to vacation apartments
Loutraki is a seaside resort town on the Gulf of Corinth, roughly an hour’s drive from Athens. It is known for its beaches, thermal springs, hotels, restaurants and casino, and can be reached directly by road from Athens without a ferry or domestic flight.
The HORIZA LOUTRAKI property sits on a roughly 495-square-meter plot and has approximately 2,400 square meters of built space. The existing hotel comprises a ground floor and seven additional floors.
Plans call for studio and one-bedroom apartments, as well as shared hospitality facilities including a lobby, bar and restaurant, a wellness area and gym, a swimming pool, and a rooftop area with a jacuzzi and seating.
The companies expect the apartments to be handed over and the development to open to guests in summer 2027.
HORIZA LOUTRAKI will be Palmo’s third project in the resort town, following its Forty Five and KARDIA developments.
“The cooperation with Aviation Links allows us to expand the service we provide buyers into the period after the apartment is delivered,” said Peleg Yariv, CEO and founder of Palmo Group.
“Alongside development, construction and support during the purchase process, the apartments will benefit from Aviation Links’ tourism and marketing systems and from the ongoing management of the joint management company.”
Aviation Links expands tourism real estate activity
The deal is part of Aviation Links’ growing push into tourism-related real estate outside Israel.
The publicly traded Israeli tourism group has expanded into property development through subsidiaries operating in Greece, Finland and Cyprus.
Its recent projects include MIFRAS, a development of luxury villas on the Greek island of Paros, and Arctic Panorama Resort & Spa in Finnish Lapland.
The group has also entered the Cyprus property market, including through the Lumina Mare residential development near the Larnaca coastline.
The Loutraki partnership extends that strategy by combining Aviation Links’ core tourism business with Palmo’s real estate development and property-management operations in Greece.

After months apart on reserve duty, married Israeli couples face a new challenge at home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
19:21:00 UTC
04:21:00 KST

After months of reserve duty, Maya imagined her husband Eitan’s return would feel like a special homecoming.
She pictured his warmth, the shared jokes, and the easy rhythm of two people who know each other deeply.
Instead, she found herself surprised by how quiet he was. He was not only not talkative but almost unfamiliar.
Eitan, meanwhile, felt unsettled by how Maya had managed everything alone, all the kids’ schedules, dealing with the finances, and things around the house.
Finally, they were under the same roof, but both felt strangely alone.
The experiences of Maya and Eitan reflect a pattern I have seen often in my clinic emerging across Israel since Oct. 7. Many partners have spent months, and some nearly more than a year, in extended reserve duty periods. Couples are discovering that returning to “normal” life is far more complex than simply coming home.
Israeli research strongly reflects what couples like Maya and Eitan are living through. A 2024 study, published in Archives of Sexual Behavior, of couples during the current war found that wartime stress sharply reduces sexual well-being and emotional closeness.
This isn’t just an academic finding; it’s the emotional reality many partners describe when they sit across from me and try to understand why they are having trouble connecting.
A more recent 2026 Israeli study, led by Kapel Lev Ari, R. et al., in Psychological Trauma found that reunited couples function in “two different emotional systems.” One partner returned shaped by danger and hypervigilance, while the other spent months carrying the full weight of home life alone.
What surprised the researchers – and what I frequently see – is that the partner at home often shows even higher levels of PTSD, depression, anxiety, and stress. Their nervous system has been overloaded with chronic worry and uncertainty. And the at-home partner’s stress level doesn’t end the moment their partner walks through the door.
The study also found something very hopeful. Using techniques of self-compassion protects the partner at home. Those who can look at suffering with kindness rather than harsh self-criticism showed significantly lower PTSD, depression, and anxiety. In other words, how gently we speak to ourselves matters, especially in times of prolonged strain.
The survival brain vs the connected brain
Under prolonged stress, the brain shifts into survival mode: fight, flight, or freeze. This state is protective and necessary, but intimacy needs openness, vulnerability, and slowing down.
Eitan’s nervous system adapted to danger, while Maya’s adapted to carrying everything alone. When they reunited, their bodies were still living in different emotional states. They didn’t realize that reintegration is a process, and that what they were feeling was normal, expected, and temporary.
Common post-reserve duty challenges
The comparison trap
Couples often begin silently scoring who suffered more. The partner who was away may feel misunderstood, while the partner who stayed home may feel invisible.
Resentment can be sparked over small things like washing dishes, bedtime routines, or how quickly one partner “should” be adjusting.
Emotional guarding
Many couples avoid sharing deeper feelings for fear of burdening each other. They stick to logistics like bills, schedules, and errands. This keeps the peace but starves the relationship.
Resentful independence
Extended reserve duty periods push couples into separate emotional worlds. The partner at home becomes highly capable, while the partner who is on reserve duty adapts to functioning independently in a demanding environment.
When they reunite, these adaptations clash. The returning partner may feel unnecessary. And the partner at home may guard the independence that was hard to develop or may feel overwhelmed and shift all responsibility back to the returning partner. This friction isn’t a sign of trouble, but rather is the natural process of the two finding their way back to each other.
The way back: Five therapist-backed strategies
Rebuilding intimacy after long separations isn’t about undoing what happened. It’s about recognizing that reintegration is a process that requires partners to move toward each other, slowly and deliberately.
1. Lower the bar for conversation
Start with 10-minute check-ins. No advice, no problem-solving; rather, just listen. This gentle rhythm helps the nervous system relearn the connection.
2. Prioritize nonsexual touch
Long hugs, holding hands, or sitting close send powerful signals that danger has passed.
3. Acknowledge the two realities
Validation of the other can undo the resentment. Use phrases like “I know it was incredibly hard for you here,” “I know it was frightening and exhausting for you out there.”
4. Schedule micro dates
Short walks or quick coffees help partners reconnect gradually and rebuild emotional availability.
5. Teach self-compassion
Therapists guide people to notice difficult feelings without judgment and respond to themselves with the same kindness they would offer someone they love.
Maya and Eitan’s turning point came not from a dramatic conversation but from a quiet evening on the balcony, sharing tea and 10 minutes of gentle words. It was small, but enough to begin closing the distance.
Rebuilding intimacy isn’t about rushing back to who you were before. It’s about discovering who you are now, and allowing yourselves to step, slowly and compassionately, out of survival mode and back into partnership.■
The writer is a psychotherapist with over 40 years of experience helping individuals and couples navigate stress, trauma, and complex emotional challenges. He works extensively with Israeli couples facing extended reserve duty periods and wartime pressure, with many of his clients being olim. drmikegropper@gmail.com

India’s space price tag comes under scrutiny as Cambridge research flags high launch costs, while the government says key subsidies and savings were overlooked
NEW DELHI: A 2026 University of Cambridge study has found that India’s per-kilogram launch costs are four times higher than America’s and, in fact, the costliest in the world. However, a highly-placed source in the Department of Space told TOI that the study has not factored in India’s subsidies, saving cost in transport and logistic costs and space manoeuvre costs.A peer-reviewed paper published in the respected Elsevier journal Economics Letters by economists Alessio Terzi of the University of Cambridge and Francesco Nicoli of Politecnico di Torino, Turin, points at a novel database covering more than 6,740 rocket launches between 1960 and 2025. The standardised dataset of rocket launches has covered 16 geographical entities, including all the major spacefaring nations: US, Russia, China, India, Europe, and Japan. It includes over 330 different rocket configurations and 4,405 launches.According to the article, at the end of 2025, the cost of launching a satellite from India stood at $13,302 (Rs 12.7 lakh) per kg aboard rockets available in the country, an amount that was more than four times the figure of US, wherein the cost is $3,225 (Rs 3.1 lakh). The study finds the US to be the lowest among all the markets studied. As per the study, India is more expensive than the European Union, Russia, China and Japan.
After India, Europe’s rocket launch cost is the next most expensive at $9,897 (Rs 9.5 lakh) per kg.However, a highly-placed source in the Dept of Space told TOI that the study has not factored in various concessions provided by Isro’s commercial wing NSIL. The Indian space agency gives “satellite customers 30% subsidy on cost of launches”. “Secondly, Indian customers save money in logistics and transport when launched from Sriharikota. Third foreign launchers normally send all satellites from one launcher to the same orbit, which leads to rise in launch cost as satellites piggyback on the primary payload have to be manoeuvred to their respective orbit,” the source said.Moreover, the Department of Space (DoS) and IN-SPACe has rolled out these financial incentives through two parallel frameworks: the Launch Services Price-support Scheme (LSPS) and Price Support Scheme. Both programmes are designed to significantly reduce the entry barriers for Indian non-govt entities. IN-SPACe also provides financial support ranging from 30% to 100% for satellite launches and related space infrastructure under its Rs 800 crore LSPS: up to 50% support for utilising Isro and Department of Space launch facilities; a 30% subsidy on launch costs (capped at $3,000/kg) for small vehicles carrying up to 500 kg; full 100% funding (capped at $13,000/kg for up to four missions) for payloads up to 120 kg.
The Cambridge research also said, “The expense of launching cargo into space will plummet over the next few years, with the cost of reaching orbit forecast to more than halve between now and the end of the decade, and fall around 93% by 2040. The cost of sending a kilogram of payload into low Earth orbit, an average of $3,868 last year, is set to fall more than 58% to just $1,569 by 2030, and could reach as little as 273 US dollars per kilo by 2040, the study suggests.

US envoy walks back his comments on Golan Heights that contradicted Trump's position
The US special envoy to Syria and ambassador to Turkey on Sunday walked back his comments from two days ago that Israel "still" occupies the Golan Heights in violation of UN resolutions, remarks that went against US President Donald Trump 's position on the Syrian territory.
Israel captured the Golan Heights from Syria in the 1967 Mideast war and annexed it in 1981. The United Nations and most of the international community considers the territory occupied Syrian land and does not recognize Israel’s annexation of it.
In 2019, Trump recognized Israeli sovereignty over the territory, reversing decades of US policy.
Ambassador Tom Barrack on Friday said that Israel "still" occupies the territory in an interview with Lebanese-Australian entrepreneur Mario Nawfal.
Barrack now says that was a description of the territory’s historical status, "not an endorsement of the United Nations’ position" on the Golan.
"United States policy on the Golan was set by President Trump in 2019 and is unchanged," he said in a statement to The Associated Press on Sunday.
He said he intended to explain why he does not anticipate annexation in Lebanon, where Israeli forces are occupying parts of the south after the latest Israeli war with Hezbollah, and to argue that negotiated agreements, rather than territorial maps, are more durable and that he had cited the Golan as an example that "territory taken by force remains contested for generations."
In the Friday interview, Barrack had also criticized Israel’s strikes on an airbase in northern Syria earlier last week. Israeli officials said the strikes intended to prevent Turkey from establishing a presence at the base.
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz, defended the strikes, saying on X on Sunday that critics who initially called it "unnecessary and politically motivated" changed their position after the government said they were based on "clear intelligence" and at the recommendation of the Israeli army. He added that Israel would not allow Turkey "to establish itself in Syria and threaten Israeli security."
The strikes last Tuesday have highlighted growing tensions between Israel and Turkey over Ankara’s increased influence in Syria following the fall of Bashar Assad. Turkey and Syria have denied that Turkish forces were due to be deployed at the Abu Duhur base.
Barrack’s comments on the Golan also sparked a backlash in Washington.
Florida Republican Sen. Rick Scott wrote on X that the ambassador appears to have “forgotten” Trump’s recognition of Israeli sovereignty over the territory.
Barrack went further on the defensive on Sunday, responding to criticism of his assessment of ongoing negotiations between Israel and Lebanon over Israeli withdrawal and the disarmament of the militant group.
He had said "there are two people missing from that (negotiating) table – Hezbollah and Iran." That remark prompted speculation Barrack meant Tehran and Hezbollah should join the US-backed negotiations.
On Sunday, Barrack stressed that the US does not negotiate with Hezbollah, but said he was pointing out that "the weapons in question are supplied and financed by Iran," which complicates negotiations over their fate.
"I was describing the difficulty of the problem, not proposing a new table," Barrack told the AP. "Hezbollah is a designated foreign terrorist organization. We do not negotiate with it, and nothing I said suggests otherwise."
He also defended his remarks questioning who would replace Tehran’s financial support for Shiite communities in southern Lebanon, saying that raising those questions was "not conferring standing on anyone."

Former The OC actor on crusade to take down 'stupid' cryptocurrency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
19:18:21 UTC
04:18:21 KST

Ben McKenzie's journey from The OC to calling crypto 'the largest Ponzi scheme in history'
For many millennials, Ben McKenzie is still best known for his role as a troubled teen from the wrong side of the tracks who was adopted by the wealthy Cohen family.
The now 47-year-old actor noted as much in the US Congress, when he appeared before its Senate committee on banking four years ago.
"You can also call me Ryan Atwood from The OC," he quipped.
McKenzie's appearance before the committee highlights the career swerve the Hollywood actor has made since appearing in television shows such as The OC and Gotham.
He is now drawing on his undergraduate studies in economics to publicly criticise one of the highest-profile financial movements of the past decade.
"In my opinion, the cryptocurrency industry represents the largest Ponzi scheme in history," he told the US Senate.
Speaking to ABC News, McKenzie explains how he became a crypto cynic and why he has just put out a documentary openly calling the movement "stupid".
The star and director made the film as a follow to the book on cryptocurrency he wrote with journalist Jacob Silverman.
"I had a lot of impostor syndrome about playing this role of investigative journalist," he tells ABC News about making a feature film.
"That's clearly not my training."
What is cryptocurrency?
Most people know money in the form of currencies such as the Australian dollar or the US greenback.
These are issued by countries and controlled by central authorities like the Reserve Bank of Australia.
Digital or cryptocurrencies propose a different system that is "decentralised" without involvement by states and allowing individual-to-individual transactions.
For proponents such as Kevin O'Leary, who also appeared at the same Congress hearing as McKenzie in 2022, it is a system with "great promise" and "potential".
Loading...
There has also been a lot of money to be made, with the most famous digital currency, Bitcoin, currently worth about $100,000 per "coin" on financial markets.
Yet Bitcoin has also proved incredibly volatile, with huge swings and crashes as governments dictate policy about it or even as Tesla's Elon Musk tweets musings.
McKenzie got interested during COVID-19, when super-low interest rates and fears of currency devaluation were pushing everyday retail investors into Bitcoin.
"The long and short of it is I was really bored over the pandemic," McKenzie says of his foray into crypto.
"Showbiz was shut down. There wasn't much to do. I have a degree in economics.
"A friend of mine came to me, said I should buy crypto.
"But my buddy, I think we all have this friend who we love dearly, but we wouldn't take financial advice from, that's my buddy Dave for me.
"And that led me down the rabbit hole."
McKenzie did see the allure for members of the public, including himself, who felt cynical about "the outsized power that corporations have over our daily lives".
"I think that's true, largely; maybe not exactly in the way that crypto advocates think."
Yet he soon decided deregulating currencies wasn't the solution to post-global-financial-crisis malaise.
"I think that's really a fiction," he says.
"Transferring the trust that is money from the public sphere to the private sphere seems like a really bad idea."
He decided to "short" cryptocurrency, meaning he invested money betting its price would go down.
That happened in 2022 with Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies like Ethereum. McKenzie says the short he made was so lucrative, it half-funded his documentary.
Now available for global viewing, Everyone Is Lying To You For Money delves further into what happened in 2022.
McKenzie even secured an interview with one of the most high-profile faces of the 2022 collapse, FTX's founder and now-imprisoned fraudster Sam Bankman-Fried.
The tit-for-tat with the FTX founder unfolds as McKenzie sips from a mug decorated with the words "fraud investigator".
"I was sipping from my fraud mug as Sam was spouting his crypto baloney," McKenzie recalls.
"What I found with Sam Bankman-Fried is he couldn't answer the basic questions at the beginning.
"It was five, six months before everything went kablooey.
"What I wanted to do with the movie is entertain. It's a 90-minute comedy about how stupid this is."
McKenzie also speaks to FTX investors who lost out when a bank run exposed an $11 billion hole in the exchange's accounts.
"Crypto is really only good for gambling, betting the price of this or that crypto is going to go up or down, and, crime," he said.
It also tracks the actor as he ends up in Congress, giving his impassioned speech into their inquiries into the collapse of FTX.
"You need Ryan Atwood to ask these questions?" he notably said to the senators.
Yet McKenzie's cautionary investigation is now being released globally online as Bitcoin continues to be entrenched in global financial systems.
Just this month, Bitcoin surged again as US President Donald Trump and crypto leaders pushed a last-ditch attempt to regulate the industry, known as the Clarity Act.
Mr Trump himself has notably undergone a dramatic shift from being an outspoken critic to now a supporter, even with his own digital currency, TrumpCoin.
"I'm never going to be able to convince people who believe in cryptocurrency that what they believe is not true," McKenzie says.
"But I didn't make the movie for those people."
For those coming fresh into his financial crusade, McKenzie is also still able to entertain queries about his time as a teenage heart-throb.
Reflecting on the show that launched him, McKenzie had a quick answer when asked who in Ryan Atwood's fictional world would have most likely bought crypto.
"[That] would have been Luke," he quips.
For those who never watched the show, Luke Ward was Marissa Cooper's jock boyfriend. Staying in the theme of the show, McKenzie goes further about who might have issued a digital currency.
"Issued would have been Jimmy Cooper, Marissa's dad," he says.
Mr Cooper was investigated by the US fraud agency in season one for embezzling money from his clients' investment portfolios.

Five years after the chaotic US withdrawal, the Taliban wants Washington back and former US ambassador tells i24NEWS a return is possible
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
19:17:07 UTC
04:17:07 KST

- i24NEWS
- International
- US / Canada
- Could the US return to Afghanistan? Former ambassador to Kabul says yes
Could the US return to Afghanistan? Former ambassador to Kabul says yes
Former US amb. Neumann tells i24NEWS the US could eventually reopen its embassy in Kabul, but any renewed relationship with the Taliban should be built “step by step” and based on concrete actions
Five years after the chaotic US withdrawal from Afghanistan, the Taliban wants Washington back — not with troops, but with diplomats and investment.
And former US ambassador to Afghanistan Ronald E. Neumann says a return is possible.
“Yes, I can imagine that,” Neumann told i24NEWS when asked whether Washington could realistically reopen its embassy in Kabul while the Taliban remains in power.
He said the Taliban would first have to make policy changes, particularly because of the political backlash Washington would face over the organization’s treatment of women.
“But there are reasons to reopen,” Neumann said. “And I can well imagine the United States doing it, but I can’t put any time on that.”
His comments come as the Taliban openly pushes for a new relationship with its former enemy.
In an interview with The New York Times ahead of the fifth anniversary of the Taliban’s return to power this year, acting Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi invited the United States to reopen its embassy, restore a diplomatic presence and invest in Afghanistan.
Muttaqi said the “chapter of war” was over and proposed American investment in Afghanistan’s mineral resources, dams and roads — while ruling out any return of US troops.
For Neumann, the outreach is less surprising than it may appear.
“The Taliban made clear even during the negotiations in Doha that they wanted a political relationship to remain,” he said. “They wanted the military to go.”
Neumann noted that until shortly before the collapse of the US-backed Afghan government in August 2021, Washington had itself expected to maintain an embassy in Kabul.
“There was a discussion about some sort of transition of power in Kabul,” he said. “That fell apart at the last minute when Ghani fled Kabul, the Taliban entered, everybody ran for the airport.”
“But it was always envisioned that the United States might remain,” he added, saying that possibility had been envisioned by the Taliban as well.
US already dealing with Taliban ‘pragmatically’
Formal diplomatic relations remain absent, but Neumann said Washington and the Taliban are already dealing with each other when their interests overlap.
“The United States is already dealing with Taliban pragmatically in certain areas,” he said.
US officials have traveled to Kabul for talks, particularly over Americans held in Afghanistan.
Neumann also pointed to counterterrorism as another area where limited cooperation may already be occurring, particularly against Islamic State, an enemy of both Washington and the Taliban.
But asked whether the Taliban itself has changed since taking power in 2021, Neumann gave a much more complicated answer.
“In some ways the answer is yes, and in other ways it is troublingly no,” he said.
He was particularly critical of the Taliban’s treatment of women, saying it had “gotten worse” and describing its policies as “an almost medieval view of Islam not shared by most Muslim states.”
Five years into Taliban rule, women and girls remain barred from secondary schools and universities and face sweeping restrictions on employment and public life.
Neumann also said questions remain over the Taliban’s relationships with terrorist organizations.
He said the Taliban appears to be controlling Al-Qaeda “as far as we know,” but stressed the uncertainty surrounding that assessment. He also pointed to its failure to control the Pakistani Taliban, or TTP.
“So on the support for terrorism, there is some control, not fully changed, and a lot of questions,” he said.
‘Whenever we turn our back on Afghanistan, we get bitten’
Despite those concerns, Neumann warned that simply ignoring Afghanistan carries risks of its own.
“We’ve stayed out of Afghanistan several times in the past,” he said. “And I would say whenever we turn our back on Afghanistan, we end up getting bitten in some sensitive place.”
Other powers are already filling some of the diplomatic space left by Washington.
Russia became the first country to formally recognize the Taliban government, while China and several regional states have deepened diplomatic and commercial ties without formally recognizing it.
Neumann said it was difficult to determine how much those relationships directly hurt US interests. The larger concern, he argued, is Afghanistan’s potential to fuel instability across Central and South Asia.
“As Afghanistan is a place that is radiating instability with support of the TTP and regional terrorist movements and question marks about Al-Qaeda, that is a serious issue which we are not able to pay much attention to,” he said.
Afghanistan’s minerals: ‘Potentially’ interesting — but years away
Part of the Taliban’s pitch to Washington is economic.
Muttaqi explicitly invited US companies to invest in Afghanistan’s vast mineral resources, an idea that could appear particularly attractive as global competition over critical minerals intensifies.
Neumann said the potential exists — but stressed the word “potentially.”
“It is potentially interesting if you understand that potentially is years away,” he said.
Afghanistan’s mineral resources have been known about for years, he noted, but extracting them requires far more than simply granting mining rights.
“Companies have to invest. That requires a certain amount of security. Companies have to believe the security will last. There has to be a certain amount of rule of law,” Neumann said.
“None of that exists now.”
“It could, in theory, all be created,” he added. “Until it is created, I don’t think this is a serious idea.”
What did America get wrong?
Asked what Washington fundamentally got wrong during its two decades in Afghanistan, Neumann rejected the idea that there was one simple explanation for the collapse.
“After 20 years, you can pick a lot of things,” he said.
And he stressed that the failures were not exclusively American.
Afghan leaders, he argued, ultimately failed to build a state that enough people believed was worth fighting for.
Some Afghan military units did fight effectively even as the country was collapsing, he noted, but “as a whole, there was not the belief that the state was worth fighting for.”
On the American side, Neumann identified one fundamental problem: Washington was never able to convince Afghan political leaders that US protection would eventually disappear.
“As long as Afghan leaders, warlords, others believed the United States would stay and provide a security umbrella, there was no real reason for them to build a cohesive state,” he said.
Instead, he argued, it was often easier for powerful figures to profit from foreign aid while relying on American military protection.
US spending was another major mistake, according to Neumann.
During the earlier, relatively more stable years, he said, too little money was available for reconstruction.
Neumann recalled asking for an additional $600 million in economic support while serving as ambassador and receiving just $43 million because the Iraq war was consuming US resources.
Later, Washington poured billions into Afghanistan — but often faster than the country could absorb it.
“When you put in more money than the country can absorb, it’s like pouring buckets of water into a sink with a limited drain,” he said. “It slops out over the sides because it can’t drain it fast enough.”
When Afghan institutions could not absorb the money, he said, much of it “bleeds off in corruption.”
Neumann also pointed to delays in building sufficiently large Afghan security forces and early US reluctance to become involved when then-president Hamid Karzai struggled against powerful warlords.
The result, he argued, was a series of problems that reinforced one another over two decades.
‘Real actions for real actions’
So what would a different American relationship with Afghanistan look like today?
Neumann said Washington still has interests in the country, including counterterrorism, securing the release of American hostages and, to some extent, how the Taliban treats Afghans.
But he argued that any normalization should proceed very differently from past US negotiations with the group.
“You should only trade real actions for real actions,” Neumann said.
If reopening the US embassy is something the Taliban wants, he said, Washington should identify something concrete it wants in return — and require the Taliban to deliver it at the same time.
“Not by promises, not by hopes that things will be better,” he said. “That has to be step by step because there is no confidence. There’s no reason for either side to have any confidence or trust.”
“If you do things like opening an embassy without getting anything in return, you simply leave the message that the Afghans don’t have to move,” Neumann said.
“They just stay put and the United States will bow and change its position.” That, he argued, was a pattern Washington had fallen into before.
“Our positions weakened over time and theirs didn’t,” Neumann said. “And that’s a pattern that we need to break if we’re gonna have a successful relationship.”

Iranian parliamentary committee approves fees on ships using Strait of Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
19:15:49 UTC
04:15:49 KST

The Iranian parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee has approved a provision in a draft law allowing Tehran to charge ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz.
The official IRNA news agency said on Sunday that the committee continued its review of the proposed “Strategic Action Plan to Ensure the Security and Development of the Strait of Hormuz.”
Committee spokesperson Hassan Qashqavi said members approved Article 3 of the bill after its consideration was postponed at a previous meeting.
The provision allows fees to be charged for navigation and environmental services, fuel supplies in special cases, insurance, security and other services provided in the strait, he said.
Qashqavi said the fees would be collected from vessels belonging to countries permitted to pass through the strait and paid in Iranian rials or another currency designated by Tehran.
He maintained that the draft legislation takes into account the rights of states bordering the Strait of Hormuz.
The text recognises freedom of maritime navigation under international law and regulations while emphasising respect for the security and sovereignty of coastal states and the protection of their rights, he added.
The Strait of Hormuz has been a major sticking point in efforts to end the US-Israeli war on Iran that began in February.
Before the war, there was free passage through the strait, a critical export route for Gulf oil and gas, but Iran now insists on retaining control and charging fees, something the US rejects.
Legislative process
For the proposal to become law in Iran, the relevant parliamentary committee must first debate and approve its provisions.
The committee’s report is then submitted to the full parliament, which votes on the individual provisions and the bill as a whole.
If passed, the legislation is referred to the Guardian Council to determine whether it complies with the Constitution.
Any objections would send the bill back to parliament, while the Expediency Council could intervene if the dispute remains unresolved.
Once approved by the Guardian Council, the legislation is promulgated by the president and enters into force.

French politician Glucksmann launches presidential bid amid fractured left
PARIS, Aug 23 - French centre-left politician Raphael Glucksmann launched a bid for the presidency on Sunday, seeking to challenge firebrand hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon for dominance of France's fractured left ahead of a campaign increasingly shaped by the far right.
Far-right leader Marine Le Pen consistently tops first-round voting intentions, and potential challengers from the political centre and left face an uphill battle to defeat her in a runoff, according to opinion polls.
"Yes, I am a candidate for the presidential election," Glucksmann told French TV channel TF1. "Are we going to hand our country over to the far right? Faced with such a choice, I could not stand aside."
Glucksmann, a pro-European EU lawmaker who led the mainstream left alliance in the 2024 European Parliament election to 14% of the vote, trails Melenchon in opinion polls and a key question is whether he — or other potential centre-left candidates — could unite moderate left-wing forces.
"The left can win the presidential election if it stands firm on its principles," Glucksmann said. "We must stop being afraid of Melenchon."
His candidacy comes as France's political class returns from the summer break and gears up for what is expected to be a highly polarised presidential contest ahead of the vote in April and May 2027.
While being critical of some of President Emmanuel Macron's pro-business policies, Glucksmann has advocated a similar pro-European, pro-Ukraine line, positioning himself as a staunch defender of liberal democracy.
Yet it is not only his politics that have thrust him into the spotlight.
His relationship with Lea Salame, the star presenter of France 2 TV's flagship evening news programme, has become a recurring subject of media attention, with newspapers dubbing them one of France's top "power couples".
Over the summer, pictures of the couple on a beach in Corsica appeared in Paris Match, a celebrity magazine that has been a launchpad for presidential hopefuls over the past decades.
French media report Salame will withdraw from anchoring duties on the public broadcaster during the presidential campaign to avoid any perception of a conflict of interest. REUTERS

'I shouldn't be here': Australian murder suspect speaks from Thai prison for first time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
19:12:46 UTC
04:12:46 KST

Accused murderer Simon Carman says he fought Thai teenager in self-defence
In short:
The Perth man accused of murdering a 17-year-old girl in Thailand after picking her up in Pattaya says he is innocent and acted in self-defence.
Simon Peter Carman, 45, talked to the ABC in his first media interview since his arrest in late June.
What's next?
Pattaya police have concluded their investigation and intend to pass the case to prosecutors today.
Simon Peter Carman, the Australian man charged with murdering Thai teenager Tunchanok Donhomla, has claimed he acted in self-defence to stop her from stabbing him.
The 45-year-old spoke exclusively to the ABC's Foreign Correspondent program in a private visitors' room at Pattaya Remand Prison, where he has been detained for almost two months.
"I'm hoping and praying that I get released," he said.
"I have not done anything wrong. I shouldn't be here … I do not understand what's going on."
Thai police have accused Mr Carman of picking up the 17-year-old along Pattaya's popular Beach Road in the early hours of June 25, then killing her and discarding the body.
In a 30-minute interview, conducted under the close watch of a prison guard, Mr Carman claimed he was innocent and said he did not intend to kill the teenager.
"I feel deeply sad. I obviously wish it never happened, but it was unavoidable," he said.
"All I was trying to do was restrain her from stabbing me."
The ABC is the first foreign news organisation in at least 15 years to receive permission to interview a foreign inmate in a Thai prison. The interview was permitted on the condition that prison officials could review the ABC's footage for security reasons, and that prison conditions were not discussed. The interview was carried out with Mr Carman's consent.
He faces four charges, including murder, concealing a corpse, and abducting a minor for indecent purposes.
If found guilty of murder, he faces the death penalty or life in prison.
"I pled not guilty, and I remain not guilty of all four charges," Mr Carman said.
Mr Carman told the ABC he did not have a lawyer yet and had not received any visitors apart from Australian embassy officials.
Thai police wrapped up their investigation last week and intend to pass the case to prosecutors today.
Tunchanok Donhomla's father, Thongchai Donhomla, said he wanted Mr Carman to receive a life sentence or the death penalty to "serve as a lesson for others".
"I want Simon to receive the harshest punishment because I have lost my child," he told the ABC in an interview last week.
Carman says pair fought over money
Ms Tunchanok, known affectionately by her friends and family as "Cake", was last seen alive on June 25.
CCTV captured her walking hand in hand with Mr Carman into the elevators of his condo building.
Loading...
It later captured Mr Carman dragging a large suitcase out of the building and transporting it on a motorcycle at night.
Two days later, police found Ms Tunchanok's body in the suitcase, which had been dumped along railway tracks near Mr Carman's accommodation.
Mr Carman was arrested at Bangkok's international airport on June 27 while trying to board a flight to Perth, and has been in Thai police custody since.
In the interview with Foreign Correspondent, Mr Carman maintained he had acted in self-defence.
Mr Carman said he first met Ms Tunchanok on the street, where she was accompanied by two friends. He said the 17-year-old then followed him back to his accommodation.
"I honestly do not know why she followed me home," he added.
When the ABC told him there was CCTV showing them entering the building holding hands, Mr Carman said: "I cannot remember that, but if it was hand-in-hand, I believe you."
He said he was not aware Ms Tunchanok was a minor at the time, and believed she was roughly 25 to 35 years old.
Mr Carman said when they got to his room he "gave her 500 baht ($21) … for nothing. And she wanted more money and then she pulled a knife".
He said he repeatedly asked Ms Tunchanok to "put down the knife" during a physical struggle, and that eventually "she went limp".
When asked if he had called anyone, including an ambulance, Mr Carman said he had not because he "didn't trust the police".
Family 'deeply heartbroken' by case
Pattaya Police Colonel Anek Srathongyoo said his investigation team would submit its case file to the Pattaya prosecutor's office today.
Prosecutors will then have until September 18 to indict Mr Carman.
"The autopsy report said that Cake had a brain injury and she suffocated. She had no other injuries," Colonel Anek told the ABC last week.
"We also collected Simon [Carman's] DNA and matched it to DNA found on Cake's body."
Ms Tunchanok's father told the ABC he was "deeply heartbroken" by the case.
"I always told my child to be a good person, never to cheat or harm anyone. But if a bad situation happens, I always told her never to back down to anyone and to fight to the very end," Mr Thongchai said.
"I don't ask for much. I just hope my child gets the justice she deserves."

Every Russian attack on Kyiv costs the city about $12 million. They now come almost twice in week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
19:10:14 UTC
04:10:14 KST

Each Russian attack on Kyiv costs the city budget about $12 million. Russian strikes have already damaged more than four thousand buildings in the capital, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said in answer to a Novyny.LIVE journalist.
Russian forces now strike Kyiv with ballistic and cruise missiles or drones on average almost twice a week. The latest massed attack, on the night of 20 August, killed at least 16 people in Kyiv and the region.
The cumulative damage keeps growing
The toll on the city's housing is vast. More than four thousand buildings in Kyiv have been damaged by Russian strikes, Klitschko continued, with each attack adding to a repair bill the city carries alongside the human losses.
New shelters are planned, but old money went unspent
Kyiv plans to expand its shelter network. By the end of 2026, the city intends to install new mobile shelters, placed first in districts and locations that lack other accessible cover, Klitschko stated.
The plan follows a failure that the mayor acknowledged. Last year, Kyiv allocated $12 million for mobile shelters, but the district administrations did not use the money. It was returned to the city budget.
The capital also still lacks enough professional bomb shelters capable of better protecting people during missile strikes, he added. This gap persists as tens of thousands of Kyiv residents shelter in metro stations through the attacks.
The city is building a backup heating system
Meanwhile, Kyiv is preparing for winter under fire. The city has completed more than 50% of planned work to create a backup heating system, with readiness at some sites already reaching 90%, the Kyiv mayor added.
Russia has struck Ukraine's energy and heating infrastructure each winter of the war. A backup system is Kyiv's insurance that a successful strike on one heat source does not leave districts frozen, part of the same preparation for the heating season that Ukraine's government is racing to complete nationally before the cold.

The EU has sent helicopters and firefighters to Serbia because of large-scale fires

The EU has sent helicopters and firefighters to Serbia because of large-scale fires
Kyiv • UNN
The EU has sent Serbia four helicopters, 124 firefighters and equipment to fight forest fires. The blaze has engulfed the Deliblato Sands and other areas.
On Saturday, the head of the EU mission in Belgrade stated that the European Union Civil Protection Mechanism had sent helicopters and firefighters to assist Serbia in combating a large-scale forest fire in a nature reserve in the northeast of the country, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
Serbia activated the mechanism on Friday after several weeks of battling a forest fire in the Deliblato Sands, a unique site combining sand dunes and forests located approximately 80 km from the capital, Belgrade, as well as other fires in the southwest of the country.
"We are supporting Serbia in protecting lives, livelihoods and the unique natural heritage of the Deliblato Sands," Andreas Beckkerat, head of the EU mission in Belgrade, wrote in his message.
Luka Čaušić, head of Serbia's emergency management department, said that the European assistance included four Black Hawk firefighting helicopters from Romania, Slovakia and the Czech Republic; 55 firefighters and 24 pieces of equipment from Germany; as well as 69 firefighters and 15 pieces of equipment from Romania.
On Saturday, one helicopter from Romania and one from Slovakia joined the firefighting efforts, while the other two from the Czech Republic will be deployed on Sunday, according to a statement from Serbia's Ministry of Internal Affairs.
Romanian firefighters and equipment also arrived in the town of Bela Crkva, located near the fire site. The German team is expected to arrive on August 24, the statement said.
In addition
Serbia is not an EU member, but it has access to emergency assistance from the EU under its Civil Protection Mechanism.
This summer, Belgrade sent a firefighting helicopter and an emergency response team to assist Spain in combating forest fires after repeated fires across Europe depleted the EU's resources.
On Wednesday, a Russian Il-76P firefighting aircraft belonging to the Ministry of Emergency Situations landed in the southern Serbian city of Niš to fight a forest fire that has destroyed thousands of hectares of pine forest since late July.
Čaušić said that the situation had stabilized on Saturday, but strong winds were expected, and the priority was to protect populated areas and human lives.
