Viral 'Cat in the Hat' TikTok trend sparks fun fake videos but also real fear
- Published
"He's so scary!" says 16-year-old Skye, recoiling at the mention of the Cat in the Hat.
Viral images purporting to show a life-sized version of the Dr Seuss character on the streets after dark have sparked fear and confusion among teenagers.
The posts, seen by millions, have convinced some young people that the character is real and that they might encounter it, prompting police forces in Ireland and the UK to issue statements confirming that the images and videos are fake.
"I was having a sleepover," Skye elaborates, "but everyone started watching Cat in the Hat videos. It was 3am. I wanted to go home. When I started walking down my friends' driveway, I got totally freaked out that the Cat in the Hat was going to jump out. I had to call my mum to pick me up."
A quick scroll through TikTok reveals numerous accounts, many of them created in the past few weeks, sharing photos and videos of an elusive black-and-white feline wearing the famous, towering, crooked red-and-white striped hat.
One post showing the original Cat in the Hat costume, accompanied by the caption "Help, what do I do?", has received 14.6m views in just three weeks.
The comments add to the sense of frenzy, with followers asking, "Why is he taxidermied?" Others zoom in on parts of the costume and post conspiracy theories about Mike Myers, who played the character in the 2003 film, being trapped inside.
Another popular account set up this week, posts videos of a real person dressed in a cat in the hat costume, dancing, with captions like "Kent I'm coming. lock your doors." Other users are sharing the videos, adding their own captions and locations across the UK.
Many of the AI generated images have been centred on the Irish counties of Limerick and Wexford, where shaky videos purportedly showed the character wandering through the streets, causing alarm and confusion among residents.
In Wexford, the local Gardaí (police force) quickly dismissed the sightings as fake and confirmed that the images had been generated using artificial intelligence.
That has not stopped the pictures and videos from spreading online - along with unverified claims posted without evidence that the Cat in the Hat has been involved in violent assaults.
"I low-key wanna go meet him…" says 14-year-old Lily, who heard that the Cat in the Hat had arranged a "meet and greet", inviting local TikTok followers to come to the woods in Galashiels, a small town in the Scottish Borders.
Her mother was horrified by the prospect.
"You are not going to meet anyone in the woods in the middle of the night!" she told her.
There is a point at which viral dancing videos and AI-generated clips of the Cat in the Hat become something potentially more sinister, with real-world consequences beyond their impact on teenage imaginations.
In England, South Yorkshire Police has denied social media claims that a 'killer Cat in the Hat' has been spotted. Posts about the alleged sightings have attracted hundreds of thousands of views on TikTok.
There is also a fake Facebook post claiming to be from Yorkshire Police - no force with that name actually exists - and suggesting that the force is taking the rumoured sighting seriously.
In response, a South Yorkshire Police spokesperson said: "If you do see posts online providing policing updates and advice, please check that they are from an official policing account. The cat is not out of the hat on this one… Please don't believe everything you read on social media."
As with so many trends driven by TikTok, comedic reaction and spoofery is what will be appearing right now on many people's For You page.
In recent days, depending largely on what your algorithm serves up, you may be seeing nearly as many people in Cat in the Hat costumes dancing to Beyonce as those stalking the streets. There are several jokey videos depicting police chasing human sized cats, and Scottish drag performer Ellie Diamond has issued a video declaring that she is not the Cat in the Hat killer.
And Irish TikTok star Garron Noone said on one post that it should have been obvious it was a hoax "because even the most soulless, evil, vicious monster" would be "traumatised looking in the window of a Wexford person".
Snapchat filters and images shared in group chats suggest that many teenagers - and those not so young - are simply having harmless fun with the trend.
But some do remain perturbed, including another teenager in the Scottish borders, 16-year-old Ellie, who says: "I was so scared of him when I was little," Ellie confides. "Now it's like he's actually come to life to haunt me."
A post on X that appears to have accelerated the current viral phenomenon appears to have been made on 8 August, by DiscussingFilm, when the pop culture site posted that the original costume was being auctioned off by Propstore.
The post has 10 million views. , externalComments describe it as "nightmare fuel" and "genuinely haunting", suggesting it had been pulled from a 'cursed attic'.
The lot is scheduled to be sold, external on Wednesday as part of an auction of 1,400 pieces of film and TV memorabilia and is predicted to fetch a price of up to $24,000 (£17,500).
Emily, a mother in Scotland, says the trend reminds her of the "Momo Challenge", a notorious internet hoax and digital urban legend. At the time, fact-checkers and authorities found no verified evidence linking the meme to children harming themselves, although the frightening images were still capable of causing distress.
"I'm not worried about my daughters, but there could be people with bad intentions who might take advantage of this trend to manipulate teenagers."
For now, the evidence points not to a real, roaming Cat in the Hat, but to a rapidly evolving online story built from an auctioned film costume, people in costume, AI-generated material and unverified posts.
Whether the claims began as a joke or were deliberately designed to frighten and manipulate, the advice from police is the same: pause before sharing, check the original source and date, look for confirmation from official police accounts, and treat invitations to meet strangers, especially at night or in isolated places, as a serious warning sign.
The rapidly evolving trend terrorising or tantalising teenagers on TikTok across the UK and Ireland is a reminder that online fear can quickly spill into the real world.

Landfill collapse kills at least 30 in Guinea

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
18:34:38 UTC
03:34:38 KST

At least thirty people died in Guinea's capital Conakry on Sunday when a mound of rubbish in a landfill collapsed before dawn onto neighbouring homes following heavy rains, the government has said.
Six others were seriously injured in the 2:00 am (0200 GMT) incident in the Bbessia district's Dar-es-salam neighbourhood on the capital's outskirts, a government statement said.
"Significant material and human resources have been deployed to search for any people who may still be buried, to rescue the victims and to recover the bodies," the government added.
Prime Minister Amadou Oury Bah visited the site of the deadly accident, where excavators take part in a search-and-rescue operation through the collapsed landfill under the gaze of a crowd of onlookers.
Measures have been taken "to ensure medical care for the wounded" and "assistance for those affected by this tragedy", the government statement said.
A ‘tragedy’
Before the official toll's announcement, neighbourhood leader Lancine Sylla had said he feared that many had died in the collapse.
"We have pulled out 18 bodies that were taken to the morgue," he said.
One of Guinea's main opposition figures, former prime minister Cellou Dalein Diallo, who is in exile abroad, called the accident "a tragedy that plunges us into dismay".
"This tragedy is all the more worrying because the closure of the dump had been announced for this Sunday, August 23," he said on Facebook.
"It is now up to the competent authorities to establish, with full transparency, the circumstances that led to this disaster and to draw all the necessary conclusions," he added in the statement posted before the release of the death toll.
In recent days, the government had ordered the eviction of people around the site because of fears of a collapse.
Guinea is led by General Mamadi Doumbouya, who came to power in a coup in 2021 before being elected president in December 2025.

Ukraine war latest: 'Hunting their launch sites' —Zelensky reveals new details about Ukraine's ballistic missile defense
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
18:33:49 UTC
03:33:49 KST

Ukraine war latest: 'Hunting their launch sites' —Zelensky reveals new details about Ukraine's ballistic missile defense
Key developments on Aug. 22-23:
- 'Hunting their launch sites' — Zelensky reveals new details about Ukraine's ballistic missile defense
- Ukraine weighing 'radical' mobilization changes amid recruitment challenges, official says
- Ukrainian drones reportedly strike Wildberries rival, Ozon, in Russia's Orenburg
- Russia planning 'peripheral' mobilization of 300,000 men after elections, Zelensky says
- Ukraine strikes 2 Russian fighters, air defense assets in Krasnodar Krai, drone commander says
Ukraine has launched a new operation targeting Russian ballistic missile launchers near its borders, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Aug. 22, as Kyiv faces a shortage of missiles capable of intercepting ballistic weapons.
Zelensky said that Ukrainian military struck an Iskander ballistic missile launcher near Ukraine's borders on Aug. 22, without providing further details.
The strike was part of a separate operation to hunt down Russian missile systems positioned near Ukraine, which Zelensky described as an alternative tactic amid the dire lack of of anti-ballistic missile interceptors.
The Iskander is Russia's main surface to surface tactical ballistic missile system, with a stated range of around 500 kilometers.
Complemented with North Korean KN-23 ballistic missiles and advanced Zircon cruise missiles, the Iskander has been the workhorse of combined mass attacks again Ukrainian targets in recent months.
When attacking Kyiv and other targets inside Ukraine, Iskanders are launched from mobile erector-launcher systems inside Russian territory, usually in border regions like Bryansk or Kursk oblasts.
With Ukraine's stocks of Patriot ballistic missile interceptor at or near empty, strikes against Iskander launchers have long been proposed as an alternative method of fighting the Iskander threat, but Ukraine has lacked options for quickly detecting and hitting launch sites.
"At one point (the Russians) were planning to launch an attack, but didn’t go through with it. This is no coincidence," Zelensky told journalists.
"In other words, we're working to prevent them from carrying out large-scale missile attacks. These are individual, complex operations, and we're now starting to see the first results."
Zelensky said Russia could potentially produce up to 1,300 ballistic missiles annually and currently has around 600–630 in stock. Moscow could eventually aim to produce around 100 ballistic missiles per month, he said, although it has not yet reached that rate.
Ukraine is also seeking more Patriot interceptors ahead of winter, Zelensky said, revealing that Ukraine had only received 264 missiles for the advanced surface-to-air system this year so far.
The Air Force has requested 360 missiles, up from an initial target of 300. According to the president, Kyiv hopes to secure 5–10% of U.S. stocks, with Ukraine prepared to pay for the missiles.
Zelensky also said Germany had agreed to provide 600 PAC-2 missiles for Patriot systems in 2027–2028, while negotiations with Washington over additional supplies continue.
Longer-term alternatives to the Patriot are also moving ahead, the president said, referring specifically to the Freyja project, a joint effort by European and Ukrainian defense companies to produce a new anti-ballistic missile system.
The project has moved from political discussions to the technical stage, with companies now beginning practical work, Zelensky said.
read also
 Ukraine weighing 'radical' mobilization changes amid recruitment challenges, official says 
Ukraine is preparing changes to its mobilization system, including potential revisions to the country's draft age, secretary of the parliamentary defense committee Roman Kostenko said on Aug. 22.
Kostenko said that financial incentives offered to encourage Ukrainians to sign military contracts have failed to significantly increase recruitment, prompting officials to consider other measures.
"There are already talks and, as far as I know, some things are changing in the draft age," Kostenko said, adding that the Defense Ministry or General Staff would provide further details. He declined to say whether the draft age could be lowered or raised.
The lawmaker noted that Ukraine does not plan to move away from compulsory mobilization in favor of an exclusively voluntary system.
Kostenko also denied reports that authorities are considering eliminating mobilization exemptions for parents with three or more children, saying there are no such legislative initiatives currently under consideration.
No changes are planned regarding the mobilization of women, Kostenko said, adding that military service for women will remain voluntary.
As the fifth year of Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine goes on, mobilization has become among the most contentious domestic issues in the country.
Ukraine's military faces a growing need to replenish fighting units, build reserves, and allow existing soldiers to rotate off the front line. As Ukraine steps up its mobilization efforts, draft offices are often accused of forced conscription without compliance with fundamental civil rights and ill-treatment of conscripts.
Under martial law, Ukrainian men aged 25 to 60 are currently subject to conscription and are forbidden from leaving the country except under a certain number of specific circumstances.
Meanwhile, Russia reportedly plans to mobilize around 300,000 people after State Duma elections in September, but will do so without touching the country's major cities in an effort to minimize backlash from society, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky told journalists on Aug. 23.

Ukrainian drones reportedly strike Wildberries rival, Ozon, in Russia's Orenburg
Ukraine's military reportedly launched a drone attack on the Russian city of Orenburg overnight on Aug. 23, striking an Ozon logistics center, Russian Telegram media channels reported.
Photos and videos posted to social media purport to show smoke rising from the warehouse following a reported strike. Air raid alerts were active in the region ahead of the reported strike.
The attack on Ozon, Russia's second-largest online marketplace and main competitor to Wildberries, marked the second reported strike on the company's facilities. The first direct attack on the company's logistics centers occurred just one night earlier on Aug. 22 in a Ukrainian attack on Samara Oblast.
The Kyiv Independent cannot immediately verify the reports. Ukraine's military has not yet commented on the reported attack.
The full extent of the damage was not immediately clear.
After months of strikes on Wildberries facilities, Ukraine’s military appears to have shifted its focus to Ozon sites across Russia, with Ukrainian officials justifying the attacks on the grounds that the company sells goods to the Russian military.
"Systematic strikes on storage centers for dual-use goods are making it more difficult for the enemy to operate and are negatively impacting the overall economy of Russia," the Defense Ministry said after the Aug. 22 attack.
Orenburg is located in southwestern Russia near the border to Kazakhstan, approximately 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) from the Russia-Ukraine border.
Elsewhere in Russia, a massive blaze erupted at a warehouse in St. Petersburg overnight on Aug. 22, officials reported.
Russia's Emergency Situations Ministry said the first spread to engulf an area of at least 82,000 square metres (approximately 882,000 square feet) in the Kolpino district, southeast of central St. Petersburg.
The fire, located in an industrial part of the city, reportedly burned adjacent to an Ozon logistics center, owned by Russia's second-largest online marketplace and the main competitor to Wildberries.
The cause of the blaze was not immediately clear. Air raid alerts had not been declared in the Leningrad Oblast, nor were explosions heard in the area.

Russia planning 'peripheral' mobilization of 300,000 men after elections, Zelensky says
Russia plans to mobilize around 300,000 people after State Duma elections in September, but will do so without touching the country's major cities in an effort to minimize backlash from society, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky told journalists.
Russia's voluntary recruitment system has increasingly struggled to make up for losses on the battlefield, while diminishing returns in Russian offensives on the front line have fuelled talk of a new wave of mobilization in the country.
Although baring no resemblence to a real democratic process, the Duma Elections are nonetheless seen as a litmus test for support for president Vladimir Putin's regime, and the Kremlin will wait until after to announce a new draft, Zelensky said.
According to Zelensky, the 300,000 mobilized troops will complement existing inflows of recruits into the Russian army, and will either be used to boost Moscow's main offensive effort on the "fortress belt" cities of Donetsk Oblast, or to create new threats in other areas, including Ukraine's northern border.
Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Moscow has only once turned to forced mobilization to fill the ranks of its military: in autumn 2022, when successive Ukrainian counteroffensive successes threatened a broader collapse of Russia's defense lines.
The move triggered an exodus of hundreds of thousands of Russians from the country, with long lines at border crossing points, particularly at the state border with Georgia.
Since then, Putin has famously gone to great lengths to avoid more large-scale forced mobilization, seeing it as a threat to his image as provider of strength and stability to ordinary Russians apathetic to questions of politics and war.
Instead, Moscow has relied on lucrative bonuses offered to those who sign a contract, with responsibility resting largely on regional authorities to meet tough recruitment quotas.
According to Zelensky, Putin plans to minimize perceived political consequences by focusing mobilization efforts away from the large population centers, especially Moscow and St Petersburg.
"They are planning for a kind of 'peripheral mobilization,'" the president said.
"As we understand, it won't happen in the central cities. But I don't think they will succeed in hiding it."

Ukraine strikes 2 Russian fighters, air defense assets in Krasnodar Krai, drone commander says
Ukrainian drones have struck two Russian fighter jets, a large missile-carrying drone, high-value radars, and other air defense assets, Unmanned Systems Forces commander Robert "Magyar" Brovdi said on Aug. 23.
The two jets, a Su-33 and a Mig-29, as well as a large Orion strike drone, were hit at the Vityazevo airfield in Russia's southern region of Krasnodar Krai, Brovdi said.
The Orion is a large Russian unmanned aerial vehicle developed by Russia before the full-scale invasion and similar in class to the Turkish-made Bayraktar TB-2 operated by Ukraine.
On a battlefield dense with enemy air defense assets and interceptor drones on both sides, drones the Orion and TB-2 have been largely rendered useless.
Over 2026, Russia adapted the Orion for a new role: launching the cheap Banderol cruise missile, now regularly used against Ukraine's Black Sea port infrastructure.
All three strikes, videos of which were shared on Brovdi's Telegram channel, were carried out by the 1st Center of the Unmanned Systems Forces, which specializes in long-range strikes.
Other targets included S-400, Pantsir, and Tor air defense systems, as well as eight high-value radars in Krasnodar Krai, Rostov Oblast, and Russian-occupied Crimea.

Pentagon says US casualties in Iran war climb to 774
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
18:31:58 UTC
03:31:58 KST

Yasin Güngör
23 August 2026•Update: 23 August 2026
American military casualties in the war with Iran have reached 774, including 18 fatalities, according to the latest figures from the Pentagon’s casualty reporting system.
The Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS) indicates that 756 service members have sustained injuries since the war commenced on Feb. 28.
The data is now divided into two distinct periods, reflecting a shift in the conflict’s diplomatic and military status.
The first phase, labeled Operation Epic Fury, accounts for 14 deaths and 417 wounded. Among these fatalities, seven were classified as hostile deaths, including those killed in action or who died of wounds. The remaining seven deaths in this category resulted from accidents or undetermined causes, primarily affecting the US Air Force and Navy.
A second category, titled Overseas Operations, tracks losses sustained since July 7, the period after the memorandum of understanding between Washington and Tehran was rendered virtually ineffective and one day before President Donald Trump officially declared the ceasefire "over." This phase has recorded four hostile deaths, all from the US Army, and 341 wounded personnel.
The US Army has borne the heaviest burden of the conflict, with 11 total fatalities and 589 injuries across both reporting segments.

Iraq's 20,000 illiterate electric ministry employees is indicator of larger dysfunction - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
18:29:27 UTC
03:29:27 KST

Iraq is trying to help by enrolling electricity ministry employees in a program to address adult illiteracy after a new report found that “nearly 20,000 Iraqi electricity ministry employees illiterate.”
But the challenge may be larger than the fact that so many are illiterate. The problem is they are working in a key energy infrastructure field in a country that is now at the center of the Iran conflict with the US and Israel. Iraq has suffered greatly from the chaos in the Strait of Hormuz.
In the last weeks, several key Islamic Republic officials journeyed to Iraq to pressure the country. Iran is offering a trade-off. Iraq may be allowed to export more oil via the Strait of Hormuz. However, Baghdad would likely have to shelve a plan to rein in Iranian-backed militias.
What do the 20,000 illiterate electric employees have to do with this? They are a symbol of a system in Iraq that has allowed corruption and infrastructure decay to grow over the last decades. This is in part due to Iranian influence. Iran has tried to control Iraq and make it dependent. Electricity and energy are some of the ways that Iran seeks to make Baghdad dependent.
Iran’s role in trying to harm Iraq’s electric grid is clear. For instance, the one part of Iraq that is partly free from Iranian influence is the autonomous Kurdistan Region. That region was recently able to solve many longstanding electrical problems via new energy investment and the Dana Gas project at the Khor Mor field.
This field helps supply gas to power plants in Erbil and other areas of the Kurdistan Region, accounting for around 75% of the region’s electricity capacity. Kurdistan went from a region where many people relied on generators to a place where there is electricity all day long.
Iran has used its militias to target the Khor Mor field. This has caused a suspension of gas and electricity flow. Now another dispute has arisen. Reports from Rudaw and other media note that Dana Gas and Crescent Petroleum deny claims by the regional government that they supplied natural gas to the rest of Iraq.
Illiterate employees may be 'ghost' employees
The issue is that the illiterate employees of the electricity ministry may be “ghost” employees who don’t even work. It’s not clear how one would have so many illiterate employees in a key sector.
Rudaw says that “nearly 20,000 employees of Iraq’s electricity ministry are illiterate and have been enrolled in a government program to teach them reading and writing, an education ministry official said on Saturday, attributing the high number largely to the hiring of contract workers in recent years.”
“We have launched a joint program with the Iraqi Ministry of Electricity to teach 19,939 employees in Baghdad and other provinces,” Haitham Munther, director of media and communications at the Executive Agency for Literacy Eradication at the Iraqi education ministry, told Rudaw’s Gashaw Khalid.
And why has this happened?
“He attributed the large number of illiterate employees primarily to the widespread recruitment of contract workers in recent years,” Munther said. “In principle, it should be impossible for an employee to be illiterate. However, as you know, the issue of contract workers arose in recent years. Previously, the number of Ministry of Electricity staff was stable between 90,000 and 95,000, but in recent years, more than 100,000 people have been added solely through contracts.”
Illiteracy wider problem throughout the ministry
There are more problems of illiteracy across Iraq’s government. At the Interior Ministry, 11,000 members are learning to read.
“Iraq’s 2024 national census put the country’s illiteracy rate at 15.3%. While senior civil service positions generally require university or technical qualifications, illiteracy among government employees is concentrated largely among lower-ranking personnel, including members of security forces, local police, municipal services, and facility protection forces.”
It should be noted that Iraq’s electricity grid has long been one of the country’s strategic vulnerabilities. Despite possessing some of the world’s largest oil and natural gas reserves, Iraq continues to struggle to provide reliable electricity to its population.
The country’s modern electricity crisis has its roots in decades of conflict. The Iran-Iraq War, the 1991 Gulf War, years of sanctions during the 1990s, the 2003 US-led invasion, and later the war against ISIS have all damaged power plants.
There is also Iraq’s dependence on Iranian energy. Since 2017, Iraq has relied heavily on imports of Iranian natural gas to fuel power plants near Baghdad and Basra, while also importing electricity directly from Iran.
This illustrates how the illiterate employees are only the tip of the iceberg.

IDF begins construction of six new training bases incorporating lessons from Oct. 7
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
18:29:17 UTC
03:29:17 KST

Six training brigade bases will be built for the 7th, 188th, 401st, Kfir, Nahal, and Givati Brigades across Israel, incorporating lessons learned from October 7, a senior Defense Ministry official told Walla on Sunday.
The Defense Ministry views the project as an operational initiative because it directly affects the training and preparation of all IDF Ground Forces combat units for future challenges and extreme scenarios.
“The entire training and instruction environment will change following the establishment of the new training bases, and this will be reflected starting from the basic needs of soldiers, such as the type of beds and hot water in the living quarters, to training classrooms integrated with new technology and simulators,” the senior official explained.
He added, “A rapid access approach for tanks and Namer armored personnel carriers to the training areas has been incorporated in order to streamline the training process.”
According to the official, the 7th Brigade training base in northern Israel, covering 20,000 square meters, including a bus parking area, is in advanced stages of construction and will receive its first group of recruits in August 2028.
Where will the IDF's new training bases be?
The 188th Brigade training base in the Jordan Valley, at the site currently used by soldiers from the haredi Hasmonean Brigade who will move elsewhere, is also under construction and is expected to be delivered in August 2027.
The Kfir Brigade training base in the Jordan Valley is in advanced stages of construction, with its new sections expected to be delivered to the IDF in 2028.
The Nahal Brigade training base near Tel Arad is currently in the planning stage, with construction expected to begin in the coming months as part of a five-year project. The work will be carried out as part of a redevelopment and reconstruction process.
Next to the Shivta training base of the IDF Artillery Corps, the 401st Brigade training base will be established, with construction expected to begin in 2027.
The construction of the Givati Brigade training base, which has faced project delays for more than a decade and a half, is currently in the planning stage and is expected to be completed around 2031 to 2032.
Base planning includes a focus on the IDF's future
According to the senior Defense Ministry engineering official, the planning of all the new training bases includes a focus on future needs. For example, at the armored brigade bases, covered tank maintenance centers will be built adjacent to the living quarters, rather than several kilometers away as they were in the past.
Buses will be able to reach close to the living quarters in order to reduce the time soldiers spend entering and leaving the bases. Similar planning will apply to access routes to dining halls and living quarters, reducing time spent moving between different areas.
New urban warfare training facilities for tanks will also be built. In the medical field, specialist clinics will be established at all of the training bases, including physiotherapy clinics.
Additional emphasis was placed on tank simulators, which will allow training to be more precise and enable soldiers to practice even during periods of extreme heat in the field.
The official explained that the large scale of facilities at each training base will give commanders greater flexibility when planning daily schedules.
Company-level living quarters planned
The official also described the planned company-level living quarters.
“This is a two-story building that includes a kitchenette, a club, bathrooms and showers at the required capacity and not with the overcrowding of the past, with shading, a nearby company area, and nearby fitness facilities,” he said.
The dining hall complex, synagogue, and all other public buildings will be concentrated in a single area close to the company compounds.
“Recruits will not have to walk for hours and hours to the dining hall. Everything will be close to them,” the Defense Ministry official said.
“In the company building, they will have a washing machine, a lounge area, a refrigerator for meals and food and drinks when the dining halls are unavailable, open 24/7 and located inside the living quarters. There is also investment in the sleeping quarters, including outlets for the various mobile devices, shading, and accessible showers inside the building.”
The official also emphasized that thought was given to the location of the new training bases and their surrounding security components based on lessons learned from October 7 and Hamas’s breaches of IDF bases.
The planning includes infrastructure protection, the types of walls and barriers used, protected spaces, perimeter fencing, and measures designed to ensure operational continuity.

North Dakota State has won at a record rate at the lower levels. The Bison are rumbling into the FBS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

18:23:01 UTC
03:23:01 KST

North Dakota State has won at a record rate at the lower levels. The Bison are rumbling into the FBS
FARGO, N.D. (AP) — North Dakota State’s road to the highest level of college football was paved by an unprecedented run of success, with 10 national championships serving as sparkling souvenirs from a two-decade stay in the Championship Subdivision.
That exit sign for the Bowl Subdivision came into view through a rare and bitter taste of failure.
The Bison rumbled last year into the FCS playoffs with the top seed, a first-round bye and an unbeaten record. Then came Dec. 6 and the fateful game against Illinois State. The Redbirds, a conference rival, rallied three times from two-touchdown deficits for a one-point victory at the Fargodome. The 19,000-seat stadium was about half full for the thriller.
“That was the point in time for me when I said, ‘We’ve got to get this done,’” athletic director Matt Larsen recalled. “We were really close already. I remember thinking to myself, ‘If we don’t make this move, this might be the norm.’ I think our fan base is as passionate as they’ve always been, but they wanted a new challenge. This provides that new energy and new competition.”
The latest era for this powerhouse on the prairie starts on Saturday when North Dakota State hosts Jacksonville State in its first game as an FBS program. The Bison then make their Mountain West debut on Sept. 12 at Air Force, marking yet another turn on the sport’s carousel of conference realignment. Sacramento State is also moving up to the FBS this season.
“I always knew it could happen, but I never was really thinking about it,” linebacker Donovan Woolen said. “To play better games against better competition is going to be a lot more fun. To be able to test our abilities and see our fullest potential of what we can do as players and as a team, I think we’re ready for it.”
The Bison built a dominant program decades ago
After winning three national championships (1965, 1968, 1969) in what was then the NCAA’s College Division, the Bison won five more Division II titles (1983, 1985, 1986, 1988 and 1990) after the original lower tier was divided into two. The first big move came in 2004 to the FCS, where attention-grabbing wins over Big Ten and Big 12 opponents laid the groundwork for those record 10 championships over a stunning 14-year span that included four different head coaches.
The Bison went 9-5 against FBS foes, with four of those losses coming by a combined 12 points, and counted Iowa, Iowa State, Kansas, Kansas State and Minnesota — twice — as victims of their stampede. The program’s all-time record in playoff games is 86-20, including a jaw-dropping 51-7 in the FCS tournament.
“There’s been murmurs and all that for probably five years now, but to finally make that jump, it’s pretty cool to see and I’m excited for the guys back at Fargo,” said Seattle Seahawks left guard Grey Zabel, who was a first-round draft pick out of North Dakota State in 2025 and promptly got a Super Bowl ring out of his rookie season. “They’ve got the support staff. They’ve got the coaching staff. They’ve got the community, the fans, the players, the talent. It’s just a matter of putting in the hard work and having the right attitude, effort and mentality.”
Being ready to move up requires a lot more than national titles
Playing in the biggest city in a state without a pro team, the Bison have naturally become a regional draw boasting a proud network of supporters. Tom Blattner, a 1996 alumnus, gave in 2021 with his wife through their foundation a $15 million gift toward the $54 million indoor facility that also allows the soccer, baseball, softball and golf teams to practice in the dead of winter.
Fargo is a growing city of more than 125,000 people with a metropolitan area — including Moorhead, Minnesota — that’s about double that, but a midsize market has its financial limits. The university enrolled close to 12,000 students last fall, including about 9,700 undergraduates, more than only Wyoming and Air Force in the Mountain West.
NDSU’s $5 million reclassification fee to the NCAA and $12.5 million entry fee to the Mountain West were privately funded, so some donors will undoubtedly be tapped out for a while. The football program added 22 scholarships in the move to the FBS, and the increased travel and other competitive upgrades has roughly doubled the operating budget, Larsen said, from 2025 expenses of about $8 million.
As long as the College Football Playoff includes a spot for the Group of Six conferences that comprise the underbelly of the Power Four-driven FBS, the Bison will have a big prize to pursue even if their days of winning national championships with regularity are all but done.
“To be able to compete year in and year out for a conference championship, to me that’s a signifier that we’ve built a competitive program. If you’re doing well in the Mountain West, that means you’re doing well across the Group of Six as well,” Larsen said. “We don’t want to just go. We want to go compete right away.”
The buzz around the football facilities has been palpable this summer, perhaps no stronger than when players began to get their hands on the latest edition of the popular EA Sports video game, College Football, which for the first time includes North Dakota State. Now they can relax at home after practice and pick the Bison to control instead of Alabama or Ohio State.
“To play as yourself in a game, that’s something every little kid wants to do when they grow up,” Woolen said.
NDSU’s traditional rivals probably won’t be a prominent part of its future
North Dakota State was joined on its jump to the FCS by South Dakota State, which beat the Bison in the 2022 national championship game and won it all again in 2023. North Dakota and South Dakota eventually moved up from Division II as well.
The Bison are open to playing regional schools in the future, Larsen said, but that can’t be an annual event with a nonconference schedule that has room for only FCS game. North Dakota State fans seeking matchups with the neighbors to the north and south will probably have to settle for other sports.
Northern Illinois, another one of the three newcomers to Mountain West football this season, could become a rival as the only other Central Time Zone team in the league from a part of the country the Bison try to recruit hard. Wyoming, where current head coach Tim Polasek was recently the offensive coordinator under Craig Bohl, a former North Dakota State head coach, is another candidate to stoke the competitive fire.
For now, Bison fans have some fun road trips to look forward to, with two games in Northern California, one in Las Vegas and one in, yes, Honolulu.
“There’s a lot of excitement around the community for sure,” wide receiver and kick returner Jackson Williams said.
Winning never gets old to coaches or players, but all those blowouts of teams in the bottom half of the top-heavy Missouri Valley Football Conference weren’t doing much for the fan base. Plus, taking home that many trophies in such a short amount of time can create an anticlimactic feeling.
“I think it’s bittersweet, to sum it up, but I do think with where college football is headed there was no other decision to be made,” Polasek said. “We’re excited to be moving up, and the time was right. It’s just an opportunity we couldn’t pass up.”

AP Sports Writers Andrew Destin in Renton, Wash., and Steve Megargee in Green Bay, Wis., contributed to this report.

A fast-moving Nevada wildfire exploded to more than 13,000 acres (5,200 hectares) early on Sunday, pushing from the Sierra foothills toward the center of Reno and forcing nearly 42,000 residents to evacuate as flames threatened neighborhoods and reached the edge of the University of Nevada campus.
The Hawk fire’s “GO NOW” evacuation zone had expanded to the edge of the university campus as strong, gusty winds, low humidity and dry vegetation fueled the blaze, according to Truckee Meadows fire and Rescue in Reno. An additional 45,000 people were in the evacuation warning zone, and encouraged to leave now and be prepared to stay away for several days to clear the roads for first-responders.
“If you have been told to evacuate, please don’t wait!” Hillary Schieve, Reno’s mayor, said in a statement posted on social media on Saturday night. “Structures have already been burned in this fire and your life is more important than a building. Evacuating before the fire arrives also allows our firefighters to focus their efforts on battling the blaze.”
Authorities confirmed three civilians and three first responders had been injured in the fire and several structures have been destroyed.
Governor Joe Lombardo declared a state of emergency in Washoe county and mobilized the Nevada national guard. Two helicopter crews were deployed to support aerial firefighting operations, while 60 troops were assigned to help police safeguard evacuated neighborhoods. However winds were whipping the flames in different directions, complicating the fight.
“Approximately 400 personnel are currently working on the incident, with resources coming together from local, state and federal agencies, including ground crews and air resources,” the Truckee Meadows statement said.
The rapidly expanding fire was surrounded by neighborhoods, and nearly 10,000 homes and businesses in Washoe county were without power on Sunday. Portions of US Route 395, a major north-south highway, were closed because of the fire.
Reno has a population of more than 280,000 residents.
Washoe county emergency officials opened the Reno-Sparks Convention Center to evacuees, but said pets could not be brought there. Small and large animals were instead to be left at two other locations. Casinos in Reno offered discounts on hotel rooms to evacuees.
At least 20 road closures were in effect as of Sunday afternoon.
The University of Nevada’s Reno campus remained just outside the evacuation zone on Sunday morning. The university, which had an enrollment of about 24,000 students in fall 2025, said officials had established an emergency response plan should conditions change. The first day of classes at the university is 24 August. However, students who are new to the university were allowed to move in as early as 13 August.
The Reno-Tahoe international airport also remained outside the evacuation zone, and commercial flights were unaffected on Sunday. The smaller Reno-Stead airport was closed to general aviation traffic because of the Hawk fire but remained open to firefighting aircraft.
Authorities were also closely watching a county detention facility located several blocks from the outer edge of the evacuation warning area.
“We have those inmates in mind and we are making sure that we have plans in place in case we may have to evacuate the facility,” said Darin Balaam, the Washoe county sheriff.
The Hawk fire comes just weeks after three wildfires fueled by dry and windy conditions north of Reno forced more than 13,000 residents from their homes earlier this month, according to the Nevada national guard.

The Nazis came to Kursk for history’s greatest tank victory. They found history’s greatest defense
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
18:14:43 UTC
03:14:43 KST

The Nazis came to Kursk for history’s greatest tank victory. They found history’s greatest defense
By 1943, World War II had turned decisively in the Allies’ favor. At Stalingrad, the Russians destroyed the Wehrmacht’s largest field formation, the Sixth Army. In the Pacific, the Americans and their allies won a hard-fought victory over the Japanese at Guadalcanal. In North Africa, Allied forces trapped the German Afrika Korps and its Italian partners and forced them to surrender. And back in Russia, the Red Army won the decisive Battle of Kursk.
Beating the enemy with a shovel
In the winter of 1942-43, riding the momentum of their triumph at Stalingrad, Soviet forces launched a series of operations across the southern sector of their enormous front. Most met with at least some success. But in March, Field Marshal Erich von Manstein mounted a surprise counteroffensive that drove the Red Army’s battle-weary forces back from Kharkov and Belgorod.
Elsewhere, however, victory at Voronezh allowed the Russians to break through quickly to Kursk, a major transportation hub in central Russia. The result was a bulge in the front known in the West as the Kursk salient and in Russian as the Kurskaya Duga, or Kursk Arc. It projected roughly 150 kilometers westward, measured about 200 kilometers across at its base, and had Kursk at its center. To the north, it was flanked by the German-held Orel salient, which was roughly the same size. To the south, the German line formed a right angle with Belgorod at its corner.
The broad outline of Germany’s plan for the summer campaign of 1943 practically drew itself. After a winter of brutal fighting, the Wehrmacht no longer had enough strength to attack in several directions at once. Kursk, however, offered the best possible target for one concentrated blow. Major highway and rail hubs to the north at Orel and to the south at Belgorod and Kharkov would ease the logistical burden. The attack would have to cover a relatively modest distance – about 100 kilometers from each direction. By comparison, the Germans had advanced as much as 500 kilometers during their drive on Stalingrad in the summer of 1942. Encircling the Soviet armies inside the salient would inflict losses so severe that, for the next several months – perhaps even for the rest of the war – the Russians would be reduced to simply holding the line.
The coming operation was code-named Citadel. German forces would strike along converging axes at the base of the Kursk salient, then surge into the rear of the Soviet armies deployed inside it.
At first, the Germans did not intend to wait long. They planned to launch the offensive in the spring of 1943. Then other considerations intervened. In their memoirs, German generals usually had an elegant way of assigning responsibility for controversial decisions to a dead Führer who could no longer answer back. In reality, however, the man who first called for postponing the attack at Kursk was Walter Model, commander of the German forces north of the salient.
That winter, Model had “suffered a victory” near the town of Rzhev. The Germans had repelled a Soviet offensive there, but their own losses were too heavy to replace quickly. Now Model, who was supposed to attack the Kursk Arc from the north, wanted more time to prepare and as many reinforcements as he could get. Some other generals argued that the operation should be canceled altogether. Yet the Germans had no alternative plan for the summer of 1943. Trying to hold the entire front through passive defense was a dead end. Sooner or later, the Russians would find a weak spot. In war, it is critical to impose your will on the enemy and make him fight where it suits you.
In the end, the plan was simply revised to accommodate Model’s demands. The delay also gave the Germans time to stockpile ammunition and equip their forces with the latest armored vehicles. The most famous were the heavy Tiger tank, the medium Panther, and the Ferdinand tank destroyer. But the new arsenal included several other models as well, including such exotic machines as the Borgward demolition carrier.
Reinforcements poured into two main strike groups. In the north, Model’s Ninth Army had a fairly straightforward plan: smash through the defenses at a single point with a dense mass of tanks, then drive directly on Kursk. In the south, Manstein devised something more elaborate. Here, the Wehrmacht would attack like a trident. SS panzer divisions advancing toward Kursk through Prokhorovka formed the center prong, but their success depended on two flanking formations. One German panzer corps would advance farther west through Oboyan, while another would creep forward to the east, bypassing Belgorod from that direction. Such a three-pronged breakthrough threatened to trap Soviet forces in a series of encirclements before the Germans even reached Kursk, rapidly collapsing the armies south of the city.
The Germans’ problem was that the Soviets had not been sitting still, meekly awaiting their fate. The plan was too obvious, and intelligence reports confirmed what Soviet commanders had already suspected. As early as April, Marshal Georgy Zhukov outlined the enemy’s most likely course of action. Zhukov was no crystal-ball prophet. All it took to arrive at the broad conclusion was a look at the map and a basic understanding of the enemy’s condition.
Curiously, the Russians received independent confirmation of the coming offensive from intelligence agents operating among their own allies. Kim Philby and John Cairncross of the famous Cambridge spy ring sent Moscow a German radio message intercepted by the British that contained the plan for the operation. Some Soviet commanders favored a preemptive strike. Zhukov and Chief of the General Staff Alexander Vasilevsky, however, decided it would be far wiser to absorb and extinguish the force of the German blow, since they already knew where it would fall.
The Red Army spent the remaining time building defenses around Kursk.
Surrendering the initiative to the enemy is normally extremely risky, but in this case the Russians had a reasonably good idea of where the attack would come. Soviet industry, now operating at full capacity, was supplying the troops with enormous quantities of weapons and materiel. There were also enough men under arms to create not only formidable defensive lines, but a safety cushion in the form of massive reserves.
The Steppe Front was deployed across the base of the salient to provide fresh forces and stabilize the situation if the main line collapsed. A common mistake in discussions of the defense of Kursk, however, is to assume that Soviet commanders cared only about digging trenches, laying mines, and taking other measures designed purely to hold their ground. The reality was far more complex.
While troops facing the German armored fists dug into the earth, Soviet armies were preparing offensives of their own near Orel, north of the Kursk Arc, and in the Donbass to the south. At the decisive moment, those attacks were supposed to force the Germans to abandon their own operations and start plugging holes elsewhere. The Soviet offensives were therefore inseparably linked to the defense of Kursk.
The Russians had to hold out until the Germans were fully committed and had burned through men, machines, supplies, and ammunition. Then the Red Army would strike on other sectors. The offensives near Orel and in the Donbass were expected to force the Germans to halt their attacks around Kursk, while the stubborn defense of the salient would wear them down so badly that they could not stop the new Soviet advances.
In early July, the agonizing wait came to an end.
The North: Ponyri Station and Olkhovatka
Konstantin Rokossovsky commanded the front defending the approaches north of Kursk. He received his final warning from the Stavka on July 2. On the night of July 4-5, a clash erupted in no-man’s-land when Soviet scouts ran into a group of German combat engineers clearing lanes through the minefields. Several Germans were killed and one was captured. The prisoner quickly told his interrogators everything he knew. Acting on his account, Rokossovsky immediately ordered his artillery to begin “counterpreparation” – a preemptive strike against the enemy’s gun batteries. Shelling the German positions before the offensive sounded like a good idea, but Soviet intelligence was inaccurate this time, and the barrage inflicted little damage. The decision was, frankly, a failure. Even so, it was with artillery fire in the predawn gloom that one of the largest battles in world history began.
The Germans may have been expected, but their opening blow still carried tremendous weight. They also deployed technically sophisticated assault formations equipped with Tigers and the latest combat-engineering vehicles. Yet advanced equipment alone could not guarantee a breakthrough. On the first day, Model’s forces pierced the Soviet front in only one sector. To their credit, the Germans had conducted careful, effective reconnaissance and achieved their initial success precisely where they had already identified a weak point.
Even there, however, no easy breakthrough followed. The Wehrmacht ran into minefields of staggering size, covered by artillery and sniper fire. Soviet antitank positions were so well concealed that the Germans usually found them only when the Russians opened fire.
The Germans still had one breach, but Rokossovsky had several reserve rifle divisions and an entire tank army with which to plug it. The constant churn of attack and counterattack disrupted the Germans’ momentum. Even successful Wehrmacht assaults developed slowly, allowing Soviet reserves to arrive and block the advancing units.
After the meager gains of the first few days, Model shifted his main effort toward Ponyri, a station on the railroad running from Orel to Kursk. It was hardly a natural fortress, but after months of preparation the Russians had turned it into a small stronghold ringed, inevitably, by minefields. The backbone of the defense, however, was not the mines. Nearly 20 artillery and antitank regiments and brigades were positioned around the station.
It took the Germans a long time to fight their way toward Ponyri. The defenses there could not win the battle by themselves, but they bought time to determine where the enemy intended to break through and to move reserves into place. Before long, the Germans were concentrating forces wildly out of proportion to the importance of this tiny station and had become trapped in a crude frontal slugfest. As a final argument, they sent in two battalions of their newest equipment: Ferdinand and Brummbär self-propelled guns, both armed with heavy weapons and built to withstand intense fire. On paper, they were a formidable proposition. Heavy assault guns were supposed to blast a path for the infantry deep into the Soviet lines.
In practice, the same thing happened as on the first day. After penetrating a short distance, the Germans found only more minefields and a kill zone covered by a sea of artillery of every conceivable type. The mines forced their vehicles to stop, and stationary armor became prey for the guns. The Ferdinands and Brummbärs were certainly well protected, but shells rained down on them, while the infantry could not follow the armored vehicles because the men had no armor of their own. Deprived of support and stranded before the minefields, the Wehrmacht’s steel battering ram was predictably mauled.
Four artillery regiments fired on the two battalions. Attempting to cross the minefield was deadly even for the heavily armored Ferdinands: conventional mines were interspersed with improvised charges made from aerial bombs and heavy shells. Simply escaping the breach became a problem. The remnants of the German assault units managed to withdraw only by abandoning numerous disabled Ferdinands and several Brummbärs on the battlefield. Rokossovsky later made sure to display these hunting trophies to the press, and Soviet soldiers and officers happily posed for photographers among them. Including tanks and support vehicles, some 35 to 40 machines were left behind in a single field.
Something similar unfolded farther west near Olkhovatka, where German attempts to break through resembled a desperate effort to smash a brick wall with their foreheads. They had to batter not only rifle divisions, but an entire tank army fighting on the defensive. In one final effort, the German corps commander at the spearhead grouped all his tanks into a single division, reinforced it with a Tiger battalion, and tried to punch through a narrow sector with a 200-tank horde. The Germans had some reason for optimism: in the summer of 1943, Soviet armor was markedly inferior in quality.
The legacy of 1942 – when everything capable of moving and firing had been thrown into battle – still made itself felt. Soviet formations contained large numbers of light tanks, still being produced according to the principle of “more of them, for less money,” as well as obsolete Lend-Lease vehicles.
As at Ponyri, artillery became the bedrock of the Soviet defense. The fighting continued largely through inertia, shaving several thousand men a day from the German army while its offensive ground to a complete halt. Model also resisted committing all his forces at once. He expected a Soviet attack on Orel and wanted to retain at least some battleworthy reserves. He would not have to wait long.
The South: Oboyan, Prokhorovka, and the Seversky Donets
South of Kursk, where General Nikolai Vatutin was in command, the situation was much worse. Manstein simply had considerably more forces than Model, and he committed them generously from the very beginning, holding nothing back in reserve. As in the north, the southern “trident” sprang into action on July 5.
The Red Army divided its formations into much smaller units than the Wehrmacht did. A Soviet army was roughly equivalent to a German corps – and was sometimes smaller – while a Red Army corps might be no larger than a second-tier German division. It is hardly surprising, then, that the defenses began to buckle when two German corps slammed into the Soviet Sixth Guards Army.
Even so, the Germans did not have an easy time of it. While the Nazis in the north stalled before the minefields, Manstein’s western prong ran into a colossal antitank ditch. The Russians had “improved” a long, deep, swampy ravine by packing it with explosives, creating an obstacle that held up large German forces. After finally struggling across, they were drawn into savage fighting. For the same reason, the Germans could not use their regiment of brand-new Panthers as a battering ram. They also made an uncharacteristic mistake by failing to provide the Panthers with enough infantry and combat engineers. The result was predictable: one mine explosion after another. The number of Panthers actually destroyed was not spectacular, but the number still fit for combat plunged dramatically and remained between 20 and 50 out of an original 200. Most of the tanks sat forlornly in repair depots.
Meanwhile, however, the SS Panzer Corps found a weak point and, in barely a day, smashed through a defensive line that had taken months to prepare. Here, the Germans not only achieved overwhelming numerical and technical superiority, but put it to effective use. Once again, it must be said that they had conducted painstaking, successful reconnaissance and knew where to strike. At the same time, the episode exposed the inescapable weakness of passive defense: the enemy decides where the main battle will be fought, and you may guess wrong about the location – as defenders usually do.
The front did not collapse west of the German breakthrough. As in the north, a tank army stabilized the situation. This time, the Germans ran into the tankers of General Mikhail Katukov. Facing an assault by hundreds of tanks, Katukov showered the advancing Germans with counterattacks, aided by reinforcements sent from the reserves. The left prong slowed. At the same time, Manstein’s right prong also became bogged down. The positions east of Belgorod along the Seversky Donets River were considered a secondary sector, but the Soviet defenders managed to slow the German tanks there, if not stop them altogether. Vatutin could therefore regard the course of the battle on his eastern and western flanks as more or less satisfactory.
The problem was that, at that very moment, the SS was grinding down the Soviet reserves in the center. The enormous, superbly equipped SS corps advanced like a battering ram, and regiments and brigades arriving from the rear shattered against it like glass. For the time being, the Soviets could not stop the SS.
The glass was half empty, but it was also half full. Every day of the offensive cost the Germans roughly 10% of the armored vehicles committed to the attack. Despite local defeats, Katukov’s tankers and the Soviet infantry had hobbled the German left prong. Even the elite Grossdeutschland Division lost most of its equipment. Soviet high command, however, had no clear picture of the enemy’s condition. More importantly, the SS corps – the knife aimed at the heart of the front – was still moving forward. The Stavka therefore made the quick decision to draw on its safety cushion: the forces of the Steppe Front. The Fifth Guards Tank Army was dispatched from there to meet the SS.
Meanwhile, the II SS Panzer Corps lunged far to the northeast and reached Prokhorovka Station, between the Psel and Seversky Donets rivers. The advance had not been easy.
Counterattacks immediately battered the SS flanks, but something still had to be done about the breakthrough itself – especially since the Germans had already captured the Fifth Guards Tank Army’s intended starting positions for its own counterattack. Units of the SS Leibstandarte Division that had reached Prokhorovka took up defensive positions and prepared to widen the breach toward the Psel. Then, on July 12, the Soviet reserves – the Fifth Guards Tank Army – came crashing down on them.
Unfortunately, the counterattack at Prokhorovka was very poorly prepared. The Fifth Guards Tank Army attacked straight from the march and received nowhere near enough artillery support, let alone air cover. In the rush, there was no time for proper reconnaissance, so the Soviet tankers went in almost blind. Worse still, the same haste meant that the Germans were not struck by an entire tank army advancing in a single formation, but by brigades arriving one after another.
It recalled the ill-fated Soviet counterattacks of the summer of 1941, only in an even worse form. Back then, at least, T-34s and KVs could exploit their powerful armor – by the standards of the time – and close with the enemy. Now the attackers were met by shells from heavily armored German tanks and self-propelled guns that Soviet fire could barely penetrate. Over the course of July 12, the Fifth Guards Tank Army suffered devastating losses while only marginally reducing the SS formations’ ability to continue their advance.
The Germans certainly suffered significant damage: 50 to 70 of their tanks were destroyed or disabled, compared with more than 300 Soviet vehicles. But even the Leibstandarte Division, which absorbed the main blow, remained combat-effective. Strange as it may sound, nothing especially disastrous happened to the Germans at Prokhorovka. In practical terms, the Soviets had merely reset the problem to where it had been before.
Yet the forces of Manstein’s right prong, which had been trying to reach Prokhorovka from the other side, were hobbled and failed to break through. The left prong was bogged down as well. The SS now stood alone deep inside the Soviet defenses, without help or support. And elsewhere, the front was beginning to split at the seams…
The Keys to Kursk
On July 12, as armored armies collided head-on at Prokhorovka, the Soviet Western and Bryansk fronts launched their offensive north of Kursk. Their primary objective was to break through toward Orel. The attack immediately succeeded in several sectors. Walter Model received the news almost with relief. From that point on, there was no longer any question of continuing the northern drive on Kursk.
A Soviet breakthrough toward Orel would carry the Russians directly into the rear of the German forces fighting around Kursk. Model’s immediate superior, Field Marshal Günther von Kluge, did not hesitate for a second. On the first day alone, he dispatched three panzer divisions, one infantry division, and several independent assault-gun brigades to counter the threat. The strike force north of Kursk was dismantled with astonishing speed, almost as though the Germans had been waiting for an excuse. Citadel’s northern pincer had been crossed out with a thick Iron Cross. Rokossovsky’s forces could finally catch their breath: they had held for exactly as long as required.
Orel, however, was not the Nazis’ only problem. On July 10, the Allies had begun landing in Sicily at the opposite end of Europe. That same day, German intelligence detected preparations for a major Soviet offensive in the Donbass, which would indeed begin on July 17. Nor was there much comfort to be found south of Kursk itself. The corps on either side of the SS had been hobbled and could offer no help. The SS corps had broken through and repelled the Soviet counterattacks, but it now sat amid a raging sea of Soviet troops. Continuing the advance offered uncertain benefits, while the Germans risked losing an entire series of battles elsewhere in the meantime. Manstein insisted that, with reinforcements and continued pressure by Model on Rokossovsky, his troops could have reached Kursk. In reality, his argument contained far too many “ifs.”
If Manstein received fresh divisions, if they managed to grind down the Soviet reserves, and if Model resumed his attack, Manstein promised that he could reach Kursk – which still would not have encircled the Soviet armies. Meanwhile, as he fought his way toward the city, the last rites could already be read over the German forces in the Donbass and around Orel. No wonder the Führer passed on that kind of good fortune. Army Group South halted its attacks, and German reserves scattered across the front to plug one gap after another. The Leibstandarte Division was sent to Italy and three more divisions to the Donbass. Operation Citadel had failed completely.
Paradoxically, the Germans were not stopped at the battle’s most famous site – the field at Prokhorovka. On the contrary, it was the only place where the Nazis had achieved success by July 12 and retained the ability to continue their advance. That fact in no way diminishes the courage of the men who counterattacked the SS and died in the armored melee. But the Wehrmacht was stopped primarily by skillful, well-timed operations across the entire front, not by what happened in a single sector.
The Russians had, so to speak, gone over to the offensive at the enemy’s expense. Now they had to make intelligent use of the situation.
The moment of truth
Around Orel, the Russians attacked from three directions: east, northeast, and north. The eastern advance proceeded in fits and starts, but it created a crisis in the German defenses and forced the Wehrmacht to commit reserves. More importantly, those German efforts could do no more than contain it. Northwest of Orel, meanwhile, the situation was turning catastrophic for the Wehrmacht. Ivan Bagramyan’s Eleventh Guards Army quickly broke through the front, and Soviet tank corps poured into the breach. The Germans managed to slow the advance, but within days it became clear that Alexander Gorbatov’s Third Army, driving straight toward Orel from the east, and the Eleventh Guards Army approaching from the north threatened to collapse the German defenses throughout the Orel salient. With the Russians committing a tank army on each axis, the German position became critical.
Contrary to his usual stubbornness, Hitler quickly agreed with his generals that Orel had to be abandoned. The Germans took the breakthrough so seriously that the elite Grossdeutschland Panzer Division – 19,000 men, roughly equivalent to two Soviet tank or mechanized corps – marched around the entire Kursk salient and was transferred from south to north. The Germans managed to slow the Soviet offensive considerably. Soviet commanders would later assess their own performance with striking self-criticism, identifying serious flaws in the operation’s organization. Rokossovsky, who was pressing against the salient from the south at the same time, described it as “pushing” the enemy out rather than destroying him. Even so, it was an unmistakable victory: the Germans were forced to evacuate the Orel salient. The Wehrmacht did withdraw in good order to the fortified Hagen Line at the salient’s base, which the Red Army would have to breach in a separate operation.
Events farther south were even more dramatic.
Vatutin needed time to rebuild his strength and restore order to his front after Manstein’s ferocious offensive. The Russians filled that pause with an attack in the Donbass. Fyodor Tolbukhin’s Southern Front broke through the Wehrmacht defenses along the Mius River and began moving west. The Germans were determined not to surrender the Donbass, a major industrial region, and immediately sent several panzer divisions there. The Russians gave battle. Although the fighting near the village of Stepanovka is far less famous than Prokhorovka, the Germans suffered much heavier losses there, battling Soviet rifle and tank units in sun-drenched cornfields. They managed to push Tolbukhin’s strike force back to its starting positions, only to race straight back toward Belgorod and Kharkov without so much as a pause. The Soviet offensive there began on August 3. The Russians quickly captured Belgorod and drove a wedge into the German defenses north of Kharkov. As at Orel, the Germans tried to stabilize the situation by rapidly maneuvering their panzer divisions. The battle south of Kursk became chaotic, with both sides creating local encirclements and the situation shifting abruptly. On August 23, it culminated in the liberation of Kharkov and the formal end of the Battle of Kursk.
One of the greatest successes of the summer campaign was achieved by what was, on paper, the weakest Soviet force. Tolbukhin’s Southern Front had taken a beating in late July when it failed to break into the Donbass. It was the weakest of the fronts advancing west and had the fewest tanks. But now, with the Germans having withdrawn nearly all their mobile reserves toward Orel and Kharkov, Tolbukhin saw his opportunity. The Russians attacked again almost immediately after losing the first battle on the Mius – and won the second in brilliant fashion. Tolbukhin once more smashed through the front, but this time Manstein could not bury him under panzer divisions. The Russians turned sharply south and pinned a group of several German divisions against the Sea of Azov. The Germans fought their way out of encirclement, abandoning their heavy weapons. Having cleared this mass of enemies from his flank, the Soviet commander wheeled north again and emerged behind the German forces in the Donbass. To escape encirclement, they began a rapid, disorderly retreat from the industrial towns of the steppe. The Donbass, almost impregnable only a short time before, was liberated with remarkable speed and an almost matter-of-fact ease. Hitler raged, but there was nothing he could do. By the end of the first week of September, the Wehrmacht had been driven from the Donbass.
In the wake of these battles, Manstein had to retreat all the way to the Dnieper River. The whole of Army Group South rapidly fell back west toward a line considered strong enough to stop the Red Army’s further advance. The Russians paid dearly for their success. The Wehrmacht remained a highly effective fighting force, and Soviet losses in the battles were approximately twice as high as the Germans’. But the Wehrmacht had lost the strategic initiative. Never again would the Nazis be the active side across the front as a whole. The Russians had liberated a territory the size of a small European country. The German line had lost its stability, and for the next several months the Wehrmacht would be forced to retreat westward, constantly scrambling to patch the holes in its formations.
Kursk is often held up as a model defensive operation. But it is essential to remember that the battle was never simply a matter of sitting behind fixed defenses. The successful defense of Kursk went far beyond digging trenches, laying minefields, and preparing kill zones. It required constant offensive action within the defense, and above all, the preparation of an entire cascade of offensives beyond the Kursk Arc itself. By the time the battle around Kursk reached its climax on the SS corps’ sector, Soviet attacks in other directions had rendered the SS effort pointless – even if it succeeded.
On the Eastern Front, Kursk marked the Wehrmacht’s final strategic offensive. Hard and bloody battles still lay ahead, but no one seriously doubted any longer who would win the war. The German high command still hoped to lock the conflict in a clinch and fight its way to an overall stalemate by clinging to the Dnieper line. Within three months, Berlin would be stripped of that illusion as well.

What to Know About the USPS’s Rule for Mail-In Ballots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
18:11:24 UTC
03:11:24 KST

The United States Postal Service (USPS) on Friday issued a 95-page final rule that it plans to implement immediately if the government obtains relief from two existing injunctions. It would require USPS employees to verify that outbound federal ballot mailings comply with new envelope, barcode, and data-reporting requirements before accepting them from election officials.
The rule was designed to comply with President Donald Trump’s executive order from March 31. It directs the Department of Homeland Security, in coordination with the Social Security Administration, to compile and send lists of adult citizens in each state. Separately, it directs USPS to establish state-specific lists of people to whom election officials intend to send mail-in or absentee ballots, along with unique ballot-envelope identifiers.
A pair of court orders blocks the rule from implementing the rule before midterm elections in November.
About the two injunctions blocking Trump’s mail-in voting order
Two injunctions bar USPS from implementing its new rule. They were issued by Massachusetts U.S. District Court Judge Indira Talwani on June 25 and Aug. 11.
What the June Injunction Covers
A coalition of 23 states, along with the District of Columbia, filed a lawsuit on April 3 seeking to block Trump’s executive order, arguing that the President does not have the authority to dictate state voting practices.
In June, the presiding judge granted summary judgment to the plaintiffs, finding two sections of the order unlawful and constitutionally invalid. It barred federal agencies from implementing those sections against plaintiff states and D.C. for elections held on or before Nov. 3. It also blocked USPS from refusing to transmit ballots based on whether voters appeared on the new state-specific lists.
What the August Injunction Covers
Voting-rights groups brought a separate lawsuit against the Trump Administration on April 2, claiming the executive order was unconstitutional, “dangerous,” and could disenfranchise eligible voters. It resulted in the August injunction, which bars USPS from implementing, enforcing, or giving effect to the executive order’s mail-voting provisions for any elections ahead of or on Nov. 3. It also prohibits USPS from completing the specified rulemaking for those elections.
Talwani wrote that the executive order was “causing confusion and threatening both increasing chaos and an erosion of trust in our democracy.” She also concluded that “the executive branch has no authority to regulate elections.”
Critics of the executive order have echoed that concern, saying that the Trump Administration is looking to force federal oversight on elections even though the duty is enshrined to states and Congress in the Constitution.
“Yesterday’s new mail-in voting rule is an attempt to weaponize USPS as part of the Trump administration’s efforts to take over elections,” Michael McNulty, the senior policy director for government-reform nonprofit Issue One, said in a statement Saturday.
McNulty argues that the rule would shift postal workers “from neutral transporters of a state-led process to a federal gatekeeper of states’ outbound mail ballots.”
However, the USPS has asserted in the final rule that the requirements “do not amount to election administration, nor do they usurp state resources.”
“Rather, they regulate the use of the mail to improve operational efficiency and support the faithful execution of federal law,” it says within the rule.
Voting-rights groups challenge the USPS mail-in ballot rule
A coalition of voting-rights organizations has filed an emergency motion asking the federal district court to enforce its Aug. 11 injunction against USPS. The plaintiffs argue that issuing an immediately effective final rule, intended for possible use in November, violated the injunction.
USPS acknowledged that it would not implement the final rule for the 2026 election unless the government obtains relief from both injunctions. However, the coalition argued that USPS issued the rule in violation of the Aug. 11 injunction, without seeking a stay or filing an appeal.
It also said that USPS could have given the rule an effective date that falls after the 2026 midterms without violating the injunction, while the “immediate” effective date could sow “chaos” and “confusion” ahead of November.
“Enforcement of the court’s preliminary injunction is necessary to hold this administration accountable for its unlawful action and make clear that voters can confidently cast their mail ballot free from federal interference this November,” said a statement on behalf of the plaintiffs, which includes the League of Women Voters, Association of Americans Resident Overseas, and the U.S. Vote Foundation.
Postmaster General David Steiner defended the rule when it was proposed in June, saying at a Senate hearing that he “would think that states would want the information to ensure that the ballots that they think they’re sending out are the ballots that are actually getting sent out.”
TIME has reached out to USPS for comment.
In late July, the Trump Administration asked the Supreme Court to stay the June 25 injunction while its appeal proceeds. After Talwani issued the Aug. 11 injunction, the Administration urged the justices to address that second order as well through the pending proceeding—an approach the plaintiff states opposed.
But unless the Aug. 11 injunction is separately stayed or lifted, or the Supreme Court expressly addresses it, it continues to bar USPS from implementing its new rule for the midterm elections.
