PM Tarique Rahman’s trip stalled: What it means for Bangladesh-India ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
14:17:18 UTC
23:17:18 KST

PM Tarique Rahman’s trip stalled: What it means for Bangladesh-India ties
New Delhi and Dhaka have not been able to move past the contentious question of Sheikh Hasina, the ousted Bangladeshi leader now living in exile in India.
New Delhi, India – Bangladesh’s Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s first trip to India has been put on hold, highlighting the strained ties between the two South Asian neighbours since the July 2024 student-led uprising that forced Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina to flee the country.
Since coming to power in February, Rahman – the son of Hasina’s archrival, the late Khaleda Zia – has aimed to improve ties with India. But a press conference conducted by Hasina, who lives in India in exile, has riled Bangladesh.
Dhaka says that the August 5 press conference has “vitiated” the atmosphere, adding that “a propitious environment needs to be created for the visit” of Prime Minister Rahman.
For now, Rahman’s trip looks uncertain, as Bangladesh’s Foreign Ministry said officials from both countries have been engaged in talks for “several weeks” to work out a possible solution.
Here is everything you need to know about the latest diplomatic turbulence between the South Asian neighbours.
What’s up with Rahman’s India visit?
New Delhi had extended an invitation to Rahman for a stand-alone visit to India this month, ahead of next month’s scheduled BRICS summit. BRICS is a grouping of major emerging economies, currently chaired by India.
Since Rahman took office, there have been several exchanges between top ministers and diplomats from both sides. India appointed Dinesh Trivedi, a former minister and member of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), as its envoy to Dhaka in a rare political appointment to the key post.
Last Tuesday, Trivedi appealed to Rahman’s government, arguing that the Indian mission is not asking Dhaka “to forget the past”, in an apparent reference to Hasina’s exile in India. “Keep the past and sort out the differences of the past. But move on. Don’t get stagnant,” he added.
At a reception hosted by the Indian High Commission in Dhaka, Trivedi said that Modi wanted Rahman’s visit to be “memorable”.
But those plans for a visit were already derailed after Dhaka took offence to Hasina virtually addressing a presser at the Foreign Correspondents’ Club in New Delhi on August 5, marking two years of her ouster.
India clarified that it had nothing to do with the event, but to no avail.
What have both countries said?
Both capitals have been tight-lipped about Rahman’s visit. “I have nothing to say right now,” said India’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal, responding to a question about Rahman’s visit.
Speaking at an event on Saturday, India’s Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar said India and Bangladesh’s bilateral ties must meet the “test of mutual interest”.
“It has to work for them, it has to work for us,” he said.
“There has to be a reasonable degree of my recognising and respecting what is their interest, just as I expect them also to do so,” Jaishankar said.
Rahman’s foreign affairs adviser, Humayun Kabir, told a Bangladeshi news agency that there is “no rush” in Dhaka to facilitate the prime minister’s visit to India.
Kabir added that Dhaka is still ascertaining what kind of relationship India wants with the newly elected government in Bangladesh.
“The neighbouring country must properly understand the reality of Bangladesh’s July Mass Uprising, which took place through the sacrifices of more than 1,500 people,” he said, referring to India sitting on the request for Hasina’s extradition.
Earlier this month, New Delhi had said that it was considering Hasina’s extradition request based on the established procedure. Both countries have an extradition treaty, but with an exception for political cases.
What are the points of tension?
Bangladesh has made Hasina’s extradition a major issue. Hasina’s government was seen as especially close to India, and New Delhi’s backing of her authoritarian rule also angered Bangladeshis.
Dhaka has been seeking the extradition of Hasina, who was handed a death sentence in absentia in November 2025. Some analysts have accused New Delhi of using it as a diplomatic bargaining chip.
Bangladesh has expressed its displeasure with India for hosting Hasina and sees Hasina’s political speeches as an interference in its internal affairs. During the August 5 presser, Hasina said she would return to Bangladesh.
“We have requested Indian authorities to expeditiously act on our request to extradite Sheikh Hasina and other fugitive criminals,” the Bangladesh Foreign Ministry said in an X post on August 16.
“We reiterate that we will continue to pursue our ‘Bangladesh First’ policy to promote friendly bilateral relations with other countries, including our neighbours, on the basis of sovereign equality, national dignity, non-interference in each other’s internal affairs and mutual benefit.”
For New Delhi, Dhaka inching closer to Pakistan after decades of strained ties is a major diplomatic setback. India played a major role in the formation of Bangladesh from Pakistan in 1971.
Shakil Ahmed, an assistant professor of government and politics at Dhaka’s Jahangirnagar University, noted that domestic politics tends to influence foreign policy at times.
“Relations between India and Bangladesh are constrained by their domestic politics, especially in Dhaka,” he said.
“People in Bangladesh want that any relation with India should be based on self-respect and mutual interests,” he said, adding that Rahman’s government has been diversifying its friendships with foreign countries, including the US, China, and Pakistan.
“New Delhi saw Bangladesh as one of India’s foreign policy followers,” Ahmed said, noting that that is not the case anymore. “Hasina gave India a blank cheque in foreign relations, which is not happening anymore.”
India’s Hindu nationalist government’s push to fence the 4,096km-long (2,545-mile) border with Bangladesh has also strained ties. Anti-Bangladesh rhetoric by ruling party officials has further antagonised Dhaka.
India has been deporting what it calls undocumented Bangladeshi immigrants across its borders. Dhaka has accused New Delhi of pushing people extrajudicially into Bangladesh without diplomatic verification.
What’s ahead for India-Bangladesh ties?
Sanjay Bhardwaj, a professor of South Asian studies at the Jawaharlal Nehru University in Delhi, told Al Jazeera that Bangladesh’s Prime Minister Rahman is playing to the gallery by stalling his maiden India visit.
Hasina’s case is one of political persecution, said Bhardwaj, as her own government chased Rahman – who lived for the last 17 years in London, the United Kingdom, including all of Hasina’s years in power – with several criminal cases.
“India has been positive to cultivate and have a developmental partnership with Bangladesh, with no reluctance to develop the economic participation,” he added. “But Rahman is interested in politics and not thinking about the development of Bangladesh.”
Hasina’s extradition is a contentious issue, he said, adding that both capitals must move beyond this to maintain a productive bilateral relationship.
Sreeradha Datta, a professor specialising in South Asian studies at India’s OP Jindal Global University, said that both countries need to talk, since “there is no alternative”.
As neighbours, “they do not have a choice to disengage”, she said, adding that merely the passage of time will not repair the relations.
India is concerned about the Mecca defence pact, Datta told Al Jazeera, “But how can one have any control when there is no dialogue and engagement?”
“The initial warmth diluted in nationalistic noise on both sides,” Datta said, referring to initial interactions, including an Indian delegation led by Jaishankar visiting Dhaka last year for the funeral of Rahman’s mother, Khaleda Zia.
Datta argued that New Delhi needs to come to terms with a new reality that the government of Bangladesh may not share the same warmth as the one under Hasina did. “But that doesn’t matter,” she said. “These are neighbours, and a relationship based on objectives or interests is what will take it forward.”

Ilkhanid-era stone inscription discovered in central Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Ilkhanid-era stone inscription discovered in central Iran
TEHRAN – A stone inscription dating to the Ilkhanid period has been discovered during restoration work at the eastern entrance of the Jameh Mosque in Nimvar, a historic city in central Iran.
The white travertine stone measures approximately 85 by 34 centimeters and is 10 centimeters thick. It bears eight lines of carved writing, ISNA reported on Sunday.
Preliminary examinations suggest that the inscription may be a stone endowment deed, a local official said, adding that a definitive assessment of its content and exact nature will require further specialist studies by epigraphists and researchers.
The date recorded on the inscription is 764 AH, corresponding to 742 in the Iranian calendar, placing the artifact in the Ilkhanid period, the official said.
The inscription could provide researchers with further information about Nimvar's historical, cultural, religious and architectural development, the official added.
Nimvar is a city in Mahallat county of Markazi province. It is regarded as one of Iran's ancient settlements, with historical links to the Parthian and Sasanian periods. In antiquity, the city was also an important center of Zoroastrianism.

Hamedan Day: Herbal medicine festival opens near Avicenna’s tomb
TEHRAN – A herbal medicine festival and sales exhibition, named after Avicenna, opened next to the renowned Persian polymath’s tomb in Hamadan on Sunday, coinciding with Hamadan Day and commemorations honoring the celebrated scholar.
The event, titled the “First Festival and Exhibition of Herbal Medicines and Herbal Products of the Millennium Sage,” will run through August 28, according to Mohsen Masoum-Alizadeh, director general of Hamadan’s Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts Department.
Speaking at the opening ceremony, Masoum-Alizadeh said the event provides an opportunity to showcase Hamadan province’s capacities, expertise and products in the field of medicinal plants.

Visitors will also be introduced to the properties and applications of medicinal plants, while specialized sessions are scheduled with university professors, researchers, experts and professionals working in herbal medicine and traditional medicine.
Masoum-Alizadeh said the development of health tourism is among Hamadan’s key tourism priorities, adding that promoting the province’s medicinal plants, traditional medicine and indigenous knowledge could help strengthen the sector and create new economic and tourism opportunities.
The festival is being held adjacent to the tomb of Avicenna, whose influential works in medicine shaped medical scholarship for centuries and remain closely associated with Hamadan’s cultural identity.

Ukraine’s ousted defense minister confirms M&M’s operation planning and discloses real story behind its name
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
14:12:50 UTC
23:12:50 KST

Former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov has confirmed that Kyiv had planned an operation against targets in Moscow. Recently, The Atlantic reported that at the beginning of 2026, Kyiv had planned Operation M&M’s, which involved using AI-powered drones against Moscow's airports to paralyze them.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned at the time that if any of the drones struck a civilian aircraft, Ukraine’s actions could be perceived as an act of piracy. Nevertheless, work on implementing the plan began.
Sources in the Office of the President have declined to confirm the organization of the operation in comments to journalists. However, former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who initiated the operation and whose departure from office led to the plan being shelved, did confirm it.
Why M&M’s?
In an interview with 24 Channel, Fedorov declined to explain the idea behind the operation, adding that it could still be implemented in the future.
But he provided details on the operation’s codename, saying journalists had misinterpreted it, as the plan had nothing to do with deploying a large number of cheap drones.
“That is a mistake. At a meeting where we were discussing fully autonomous deep-strike drones, I was handing out M&M’s to everyone. It was my birthday, and someone gave me a box of M&M’s. I shared them with everyone and said that we would call this autonomous-drone project M&M’s," Fedorov said.
What does the former minister plan to do next?
During the interview, Fedorov said he wants to create a venture fund to attract Western capital for investment in Ukrainian startups and developers.
“I have several priorities. One is cheap missiles, because I am convinced that they are the future of warfare involving artificial intelligence. These are inexpensive missiles that could be used to deter strikes and further escalation," he explained.
Another priority for him is the robotization of the front line and the deployment of sensors.
"We need to think about how to remove infantry from the front line. We need to robotize the front line as much as possible so that people do not have to spend months in dugouts under drone attacks," he said.
Opposition to the system
Fedorov also announced that he planned to travel to the US the following week, not to seek President Donald Trump’s support after calls for Ukraine to hold elections.
When asked whether he planned to meet Elon Musk there and continue their cooperation in some form, the former minister replied, “We’ll see.”
He said he did not yet know whether he would run for president or parliament, or, if so, which political team he would join, adding that everything would become clear only after it was possible to prepare for a vote.
The former minister also said that he was currently in opposition—not to any particular politician, but to the system.
“We are not talking about one person, or two people, or just some top officials. We are talking about hundreds of people who have simply become accustomed over the years to making money from the state budget,” he said.

A powerful storm swept through the Baltic countries: there are casualties, and the streets of three capitals are flooded
Kyiv • UNN
Cyclone “Priska” hit the Baltic region, Poland, and Belarus, causing two deaths and widespread destruction. More than 550,000 households were left without electricity.
A powerful cyclone, "Prisca," passed over Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia, as well as Poland and Belarus, on August 22 and 23: wind gusts exceeded 30 meters per second. One person died in northeastern Lithuania after being struck by a tree; a second person was killed under the rubble of a building in Jelgava, Latvia. Many residents were injured by fallen trees, reports UNN, citing DW.
Details
The publication notes that 14 people sought medical assistance in Latvia, with doctors reporting serious injuries. Most people were injured by falling trees and branches, including those that fell onto cars. Some were trapped in their vehicles. Riga Airport warned of possible flight delays.
The storm caused disruptions to the power supply. According to local media reports, more than 250,000 households in Latvia were left without electricity, as were more than 150,000 in Lithuania and almost 3,500 in Estonia. In Poland, more than 145,000 households were without power, while in Belarus, outages were recorded in more than 650 settlements. In addition, many mobile operator customers in Latvia experienced problems with communications.
"This is undoubtedly the strongest storm we have recorded this summer," the dpa news agency quotes a representative of the Lithuanian Meteorological Service as saying. Latvia’s Leta news agency described what happened as "the most destructive storm to hit the country since 2005."
Heavy rains also caused flooding in several regions, resulting in disruptions to road traffic, rail services, and maritime transport. As of the daytime on August 23, a moderate wind warning remains in effect in the region.

‘We’ll Be a Banana Republic’ – Unless…
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
14:06:00 UTC
23:06:00 KST

Just before my teenage father was taken from Ukraine to work as forced labor in Germany, his father told him not to come back until Ukraine was free. That was September 1942. My father didn’t expect it would take half a century. And along the way, he lost hope that Ukraine would ever be free in his lifetime.
When I first arrived in Ukraine, shortly after the Soviet Union collapsed, it was a mythical land to me. I knew the language, culture, history – and the people somewhat. But reality there was like a weathered billboard – its advertisement faded, peeling and tattered in the wind – suddenly coming to life.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
I was traveling with one of my closest friends, the artist Roman Hrab, also the child of Ukrainians displaced during World War II who eventually settled in the New York area. Roman had been studying and teaching at a university in Pécs, Hungary, at the time. I’d been visiting friends throughout Europe. Roman and I met up in Budapest. Our plan was to take a train to the border and walk across it into that mythical land of Ukraine we’d heard so much about. Once there, we would improvise through the bucolic Carpathians toward Lviv. The final destination in our epic roots pilgrimage would be the capital, Kyiv.
But borders, especially the ones in Eastern Europe, were much more impervious at that time. The Berlin Wall had only recently fallen, and the Iron Curtain’s cultural divide was still stark.
Ukraine’s Independence Shaping Our Collective Future
The Záhony-Chop border crossing had a queue of cars that went on for miles on both sides. We got to within a few hundred meters when border guards told us we couldn’t cross over on foot – which seemed absurd. Before we even had a chance to protest, a friendly local invited us into his car to cross through the controls with him. He was an ethnic Hungarian who lived in Ukraine, just across the border, and spoke to us in Russian or Hungarian, which Roman spoke.
When he found out we were American and spoke Ukrainian, he was impressed and invited us to stay with his family overnight. The following day, they took us along with them to a lakeside barbecue, then dropped us off in the evening at a train station that seemed to double as a Roma camp.
We took the overnight train straight to Lviv. So much for our Carpathian improv ambitions. Instead, we visited some of my family in the countryside outside Lviv.
Poets in Kyiv
Around the time of independence, I met Ihor Rymaruk, a well-known Ukrainian poet, while he was visiting New York. He had been invited by the Shevchenko Scientific Society to speak and recite his works. I’d been translating diaspora poets from Ukrainian into English, and through my connection with the New York Group I was introduced to Rymaruk. I told him I was planning a trip to Ukraine during the summer and he suggested I come as a guest translator to bask in Kyiv’s fervent literary revival.
When Roman and I got to the capital, we met Rymaruk at the offices of Dnipro Publishers, where he was the director, just down the street from St. Sophia. He immediately introduced us to some of the most active poets of the early 1990s: Mykhailo Hryhoriv, Viktor Kordun, Vasyl Herasymiuk, Volodymyr Tsybulko and others. He set us up with an apartment in the Podil neighborhood, which belonged to a journalist friend of his. He even took me to the Writer’s Union and signed me up.
                                                                                                                                                                         
One of my first surprises in Kyiv was the fact that no one (apart from intellectuals and women selling produce at the market) spoke Ukrainian. Everyone understood me when I asked for something in Ukrainian, but they responded in Russian, as if taking for granted that I understood.
Unfortunately, I didn’t, and I had to learn quickly if I was to feel comfortable in the city. At the time, I was reading Dostoevsky’s “Demons” in English translation, and the apartment where we were staying happened to include the original Russian text in its excellent library. So I read the book in English, marking memorable passages, then reread them in Russian, which is close enough to Ukrainian that I could figure out the meaning.
Later, Roman and I befriended a group of actors from the Koleso theater on Adriivsky Uzviz, who were performing a Jean Anouilh play, and they would help me with Russian pronunciation and grammar.
There were virtually no proper restaurants in the city, apart from inside the major hotels – only a few cafeteria-style eateries or places where you could get butterbrot sandwiches and vodka by the gram: usually 100 grams per glass, but with the poets, it was more often 250.
We spent long hours sitting in restaurants or outdoor bars, talking and drinking (I’d recently given up alcohol, so Roman would need to compensate for my awkward abstemiousness). The conversations were often surreal. One of them stood out in memory. We were sitting in a hotel restaurant: me, Roman, Rymaruk, Hryhoriv, and their sidekick Vasyl, who was always the brunt of jokes because he adored Pushkin. “Oh, you and your beloved Pushkin,” they’d quip. Or “Go tell it to Alexander Sergeyevich [Pushkin].” Vasyl also revered William Faulkner, and he loved pronouncing the name – heavy on the silent “l” – with extreme solemnity.
Vasyl’s boyish devotion to his poet friends was a comical contrast to Hryhoriv’s severe bearing and monumental gray mustache evoking exile and poetic suppression. Born in 1947, Hryhoriv had been active with the so-called Kyiv School of Poets in the late 1960s, and the KGB had forced him out of the University of Kyiv. He eventually left Ukraine for Latvia and returned after independence. He struggled to get the popular notoriety that Rymaruk had – though among the other poets he was highly esteemed by nearly all. Maybe his temperament had something to do with it. At times we’d be walking down a street together and he’d suddenly disappear. “Oh, Mykhailo does that. He likes to just vanish.”
                                                                                                                                                                         
Rymaruk, for his part, was also an odd character with his long straight, almost waxen, hair framing that affable goateed face, and those trademark eyeglasses as thick as the vodka bottle bases that tended to accumulate whenever he and his friends got together. At times he seemed withdrawn to the point of autism. But then he’d regale you with a flourish of insight.
At lunch one day, the waitress came to serve us. She spoke Russian, as did everyone else in the city. The poets categorically refused to speak Russian. They ordered in Ukrainian. This particularly haughty waitress rolled her eyes at them and their “peasant tongue.”
“You see that reaction?” Rymaruk said. “That’s what we’re facing. De jure independence or not, unless we manage to get rid of that ‘Little Russian’ mentality, Ukraine will be doomed to the status of vassal. We’ll be a banana republic.”
At the end of lunch, Roman and I insisted on paying the bill. Rubles were no longer in effect, and Ukraine had no proper currency yet. They used “coupons” that looked like Monopoly money. Everything was ridiculously cheap for anyone with Western currency. You could treat a dozen people in a hotel restaurant for the price of a Big Mac in Times Square.
Invariably, Vasyl, whose innate romanticism would be amplified by the alcohol, would wind up weeping. “It’s just so shameful that I’m not able to pay the bill. I have no money.”
And the others, who treated him like their ingenuous disciple, would say something like: “Now, now, Vasylko, no need to get all emotional. You’ll never have money. Just stop advertising for Pushkin and we’ll take care of you.”
“But I love Pushkin! And I’m ashamed of that too!”
“Stick to Faulkner.”
“Ah, Faulk-ner! Now there was a genius!”
                                                                                                                                                                         
In hindsight
Over the years – especially since the Maidan Revolution, followed by the Donbas War that broke out in 2014, and now the full-scale fight raging in the East and Kyiv getting pummeled regularly by ballistic missiles and drones – I’ve given a lot of thought to what those poets said about Ukraine back then.
Rymaruk died in 2008, hit by a car while walking down a Lviv street. Hryhoriv died in 2016; Kordun in 2005. I have no idea what happened to Vasyl the sidekick. Only Herasymiuk and Tsybulko are left of the ones I’d met in those early days of independence.
But they all felt the same way: Independence had fallen into the laps of Ukrainians virtually out of the sky. Only a small portion of the population had actively sought it in the lead-up to the Soviet Union’s collapse. Those poets all felt that independence would still need to be earned. And since they were poets, their starting point was language – which was more than a mere vehicle for communication. For them it was the spiritual foundation of a still inchoate nation.
Then and now
Before my father died, he managed to return to a free (or at least freer) Ukraine and see his remaining family. The first visit was euphoric. The second was a bittersweet confrontation with reality and how much work it would take for his people to crawl out from under the Soviet legacy.
Even for him, who had left as a teenager, Ukraine had become a mythical land.
Yet one of the unexpected positive aspects of Soviet Ukraine I encountered in that summer of 1992 was the dearth of advertising. In the capitalist West, we’ve been inundated with advertising for generations – billboards, radio, TV, and now social media, all aggressively trying to cajole and convince us to, as the great American stand-up philosopher George Carlin said, “buy more shit we don’t need with money we don’t have.”
In Ukraine, though, there was a limited range of consumer goods to be had then. And the high-end Western imports were only available in special stores for people with foreign currency, dollar shops that could have advertised with the tagline: “Keep your coupons to yourself… We need greenbacks here.”
Today Kyiv is chock full of excellent restaurants and cafes. Even in the middle of the war, the food scene is exceptional by any international standard. You can easily find just about anything you can get elsewhere in the West – except maybe Russian caviar, which is now scarce.
The advertising today, however, is unmistakably Ukrainian with its martial messaging: “We don’t promise romance. Drones are coming.” Or: “The 3rd Corps is love.”
I have mixed feelings about Ukraine becoming overly “Western.” But one aspect of the current reality, at least from the point of view of the poets I’d met who are no longer with us, is edifying: Ukraine is now in the midst of a poetic renaissance. The language is reviving, blossoming after successive efforts over the centuries to suppress it.
In Kyiv, on the street, about half the conversations are in Ukrainian, and much of the rest is a sort of Russian-Ukrainian mix called Surzhyk. The youth, above all, are giving the language fresh life – spiced by struggle and passion stoked in a war few would have imagined 35 years ago.
Although I believe my poet friends understood long before independence that – given the weight of Pushkin’s legacy and Russia’s inherent Putinesque ambition – there was no other alternative.

Eleven bodies recovered after boat carrying migrants sinks off Tunisia
TUNIS, Aug 23 - Eleven bodies have been recovered by Tunisia's coastguard after a boat carrying Tunisian migrants sank at the weekend en route to Italy, with three others still unaccounted for, the National Guard said on Sunday.
Coastguard, military and civil protection teams, backed by two helicopters, continued to search for the missing.
The boat, which set off early on Thursday with 15 mostly young people on board, sank off the Tunisian coast, and so far only one person was rescued alive, the head of a migrant rights group said on Saturday.
The man who survived said he had been adrift at sea for 48 hours before being rescued by a commercial vessel.
Among those on board were seven members of the same family and a man with his pregnant wife, the head of the Tunisian Observatory for Human Rights told Reuters.
All of the migrants were from the Ben Guerdane area in southeastern Tunisia, and dozens of young people gathered late on Saturday in the town near the Libyan border to demand that search operations be accelerated.
Police fired teargas to disperse the protesters.
The central Mediterranean route from the North African coast is one of the world's deadliest migration routes, used by migrants from Africa and the Middle East seeking to reach Europe, often in overcrowded or unseaworthy boats.
Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and dozens of other human rights and humanitarian groups said in a statement last month that a migration agreement between Tunisia and the European Union had fuelled and normalised serious abuses against migrants and asylum seekers in Tunisia.
The groups called on the EU to suspend funding for migration and border-control activities involving Tunisian security forces. REUTERS

‘I love it. It’s hope’: the mysterious self-willed wildflower meadow that seeded itself
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
14:00:34 UTC
23:00:34 KST

Tucked away on a country lane, a small field bursts with yellow and pink flowers. Quail and whitethroats call from the thick hedges and the plants, including common centaury, yellow rattle and marsh and common spotted orchids, bounce with hoverflies and butterflies.
More than 150 plant species have been recorded on Sayer’s Old Meadow, in north Norfolk, England, which is remarkable when there was just one – oilseed rape – growing there 21 years ago.
This transformation has happened without sowing any commercial wildflower mixes or making any other expensive interventions such as deep ploughing or top-soil removal, often undertaken when arable land is “restored” to nature-rich meadow. Instead, the four-acre field was simply cut for hay once every summer, with an abundance of wildflowers naturally – and rather mysteriously – finding their way into the field.
These findings, published in a scientific paper in Restoration Ecology, could transform the approach to recreating flower-rich meadows. Conservationists and landowners are pushing to revive old meadows because 98% in England and Wales have been destroyed over the last century.
“Everyone is planting and seeding wildflowers, but sometimes we’re not patient enough,” said Carl Sayer, a professor of limnology and freshwater ecology at University College London and lead author of the paper. “You don’t always have to reach for that expensive commercial wildflower seed mix. We’ve forgotten that nature has known what to do for quite a long while.”
The fact that Sayer shares his surname with the meadow is no coincidence: it is owned by his father, farmer Derek Sayer, 86, and has been part of a tiny traditional farm for generations. The land was ploughed and fertilised and sprayed with pesticides as was conventional in postwar farming, but Derek Sayer stopped cultivating it in 2005 because the small field was always “hit and miss” at producing good yields.
Springs feeding the Glaven chalk stream rise in the meadow and parts of the field were always boggy. The land was “abandoned” for five years and became a forest of thistles before Carl Sayer began studying its growing diversity, beginning an annual hay-cut in 2011.
Fifteen years on, thistles and other arable annual weeds have almost completely disappeared – without any human intervention – to be replaced with a flower-rich perennial sward, which is growing more biodiverse every year.
For Sayer’s father, watching farmland run wild with “weeds” was challenging but he gradually became more interested in his son’s experiment. “He started off saying: ‘What are you doing, Carl? What a load of rubbish.’ Now he’s like: ‘How many orchids are there this year?’” said Sayer.
When Derek Sayer arrived to look at the field during the Guardian’s tour, he still cast a fierce countryman’s gaze over it, checking for “weeds” such as ragwort. “It looked a bit strange at first but I quite like it now,” he said.
Each August, a neighbouring farmer cuts and removes the hay, which he feeds to his cattle, grateful for the biodiverse hay crop. “Much more diversity is a tonic to cattle because it’s full of medicinals,” said Carl Sayer. “The monoculture of a rye-grass field may not give them everything they need. The old farmers had it right.”
Cutting it each year prevents the meadow becoming an oak woodland. The sward is full of baby oaks and sallow, and a patch of the field which hasn’t been cut regularly is now filled with hummocks of sallow as high as a house: still wildlife-rich habitat but not as rare or much-needed as flower-rich meadows.
Removing the grass growth each year with the hay-cut also reduces the nutrients, enabling more delicate wildflowers to flourish. Several years ago, yellow rattle found its way into the meadow. This is known as “the meadow maker” because it parasitises grass and creates space for other wildflowers, although Sayer said the meadow was thriving without it.
“Everyone will tell you this approach [not sowing wildflowers] doesn’t work unless you’re close to a seed source. But no one has done a long-term study like this,” he said.
The surrounding land is intensively farmed and the nearest populations of some of the rare flowers now found in the meadow are at least 3 miles (4.8km) away. One possibility is that seeds have been brought in on the hooves or coats of wild deer that roam the countryside.
“Everyone’s accused me of bringing it in on my upturned trousers but I don’t wear upturned trousers,” joked Sayer, who was wearing shorts.
Sayer’s Old Meadow looks noticeably different from what some conservationists disparagingly call generic “McMeadows” created from popular wildflower mixes which are dominated by white oxeye daisies and purple knapweed. The advantage of “self-willed” meadows is that they are filled with locally-appropriate plants which are likely to be more genetically diverse than those found in commercial seed mixes. This type of meadow creation was also much cheaper, said Sayer.
Since last year, barn owls have taken up residence in a field-edge nest box and hunt over the field. The Sayers allow local people to walk in it and an informal path now runs down one side. “Everyone in the village loves it, people walk through it and respect it. It’s working to make people happy as well,” said Sayer. “It’s the thing I’m most proud of in my life. I love it. It’s hope – we can recover things. We just need to do less in the recovery process.”

An AI ‘debt bomb’ crisis? No. This isn’t Enron 2.0 | Gene Marks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
14:00:34 UTC
23:00:34 KST

Some experts are warning of a looming “debt bomb” crisis because big datacenter builders such as Meta, Oracle, xAI and CoreWeave are not only raising billions to construct these facilities but are also not recognizing these long-term debt obligations on their balance sheets.
Should we be concerned? No. I know because I’ve seen this movie before.
It works like this: Meta wants to build a datacenter to accommodate its growing AI and cloud computing needs. It forms a separate entity that’s not consolidated in its financials, which builds the datacenter. To fund this, the entity raises money from investors, banks and other financial firms (including some from Meta) that own the majority of the entity. There is a contract by which Meta has exclusive and full use of the datacenter once built. This way Meta gets its datacenter but most of the debt incurred to build it is not shown as a liability on its books.
The worry comes from the enormous sums of money being plowed into these entities. The Financial Times reported in December 2025 that tech companies had shifted more than $120bn of AI datacenter spending off their balance sheets through special-purpose vehicles and similar financing structures. Goldman Sachs estimates that hyperscalers could spend $5.3tn on AI and datacenters through 2030 and expects private markets to play an increasingly important role in financing that buildout.
Skeptics are worried that these tech guys are pulling the wool over the public’s eyes and not properly disclosing the long-term impact of all this debt. They point to Enron, the energy firm that spectacularly failed in 2001, causing tens of billions of dollars of losses to its shareholders and contributing to a historic market meltdown.
Fine. Scrutinize them. Read the footnotes. Argue about consolidation. But don’t call them Enron. Enron caused the Enron crash. It’s highly unlikely that fraud at that level is being perpetuated now by these companies.
When I first started out in accounting back in the mid-1980s, my biggest client was a publicly held biotechnology firm called Centocor, which, at the time, was developing drugs using a technology based on monoclonal-antibody treatment for various purposes including sepsis. To raise money, Centocor also did off-balance-sheet financing. The company formed limited partnerships in which it held a minority interest but the entity issued debt and took in investments from limited partners in order to fund the development of various drugs, which Centocor then had the exclusive right to use.
In the 1980s and early 1990s, hundreds of millions of dollars were plowed into these partnerships. This was common practice in the biotechnology during that time.
Did some of the drugs fail in clinical testing? Yes. But did this cause a stock market panic? No. Like with today’s datacenters, the risks were spread. During that time – before the Internet, SEC disclosures and 24/7 media scrutiny – the public little knew of these vehicles. The good news is that the accounting has evolved, although the economic idea has stayed the same – no debt was shown on Centocor’s balance sheet. Ultimately, this financing vehicle became more expensive and less popular because it was easier and more affordable to raise money other ways.
The off-balance-sheet financing strategies today that are being used by big tech firms have different risks than what the biotech companies were doing when I was younger. Today, the disclosures required by companies doing this are significant. The scrutiny is intense. The investing public is smarter. Today’s risks are different and arguably more recoverable.
In the 90s Centocor, Genentech, Amgen, Biogen and other companies like them were raising millions in partnerships that were developing products with a high probability of failure during clinical testing.
Today’s investors are financing land, buildings, electrical infrastructure and computing equipment. A datacenter can disappoint financially, but it doesn’t disappear because a clinical trial fails. It’s why Jeff Bezos calls AI an “industrial bubble”. Industrial bubbles leave things behind. Railways. Fiber-optic cable. Factories. And this time, datacenters.
If this is a glut, it’s a strange one: developers increased North American capacity by 36% last year and vacancy still fell to a record 1.4%. According to CBRE’s North America Data Center Trends H2 2025 report, demand is outpacing supply in nearly every major market. Unlike the drug companies hoping for success, there’s a legitimate market need today for datacenters. AI isn’t going away. Microsoft estimates that only 17.8% of the world’s working-age population currently uses generative AI. If that’s anywhere near correct, we’re still much closer to the beginning of adoption than the end.
Some of these investments will fail. Some lenders will lose money. Some datacenters will be worth less than their owners paid for them. But that’s exactly why these financing structures exist: to spread enormous capital requirements and risk among investors willing to take it. The obligations are disclosed, the assets are real and demand for computing capacity remains strong. That’s why I’m not losing sleep over big tech’s off-balance-sheet debt. I see financial engineering, yes. I don’t see a debt bomb.

Your backyard could hold a rare earth fortune – and this orange lichen is the clue
Chinese scientists discover link between lichen growth and potentially untapped rare-earth-bearing carbonates and mineral deposits
Next time you spot a vivid orange-yellow crust spreading across a rock in your garden, on a country wall or along a hiking trail, take a closer look – you might be standing on a fortune.
Chinese scientists have spent decades trying to identify biological indicators that could help locate mineral deposits.
“This is the second time Chinese scientists have discovered a similar indicator – the first was copper grass in the 1950s – and both are original scientific discoveries in mineral exploration,” said Professor Li Yang of Peking University and the Chinese Academy of Sciences on August 17.
The study, titled “Lichen as a Potential Exploration Tool for Rare Earth Element – Enriched Carbonatites”, was published in the peer-reviewed journal Economic Geology on July 27.

Survival of the wittiest: How humor and cleverness shaped human evolution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
14:00:05 UTC
23:00:05 KST

A new theoretical paper suggests that human cognitive and linguistic evolution was driven by early humans’ ability to be clever and humorous, an idea dubbed the “survival of the wittiest.” The analysis argues that the earliest stages of grammar provided a platform for verbal competition and sexual selection, gradually replacing physical violence with verbal agility. The research was published in PNAS Nexus.
For decades, discussions of human evolution have revolved around two dominant ideas. The first is Charles Darwin’s original concept of the survival of the fittest, which is often narrowly interpreted as physical strength or health. The second is the more recent hypothesis of the survival of the friendliest. This newer idea proposes that humans evolved primarily through selection for prosocial behavior and cooperation, which allowed early humans to form alliances and outcompete other groups.
Wayne State University linguist Ljiljana Progovac authored the new paper to offer an alternative viewpoint. Progovac argues that physical fitness and friendliness fail to capture the unique role that language played in human development. Being physically strong or socially cooperative are traits shared with many other animals, including bonobos and other primates. These traits alone do not explain the rapid and unique expansion of human cognition.
According to Progovac, focusing entirely on friendliness misses the competitive nature of human interaction. Evolution involves both cooperation and ruthless competition. To fully understand how our ancestors evolved into modern humans, researchers must account for the biological advantage of eloquence, imagination, and the ability to outwit rivals. This perspective centers on sexual selection, where traits that make an individual attractive to mates are passed down through successive generations.
To build this argument, Progovac analyzed linguistic structures that represent the earliest stages of grammar. Language leaves no physical bones behind, so researchers must rely on a process called reverse engineering. By peeling back the complex layers of modern syntax, linguists can reconstruct the most foundational building blocks of language. These foundational structures are referred to as living fossils.
In modern languages, these fossils appear as simple two-word combinations consisting of one verb and one noun. Examples in English include words like “killjoy,” “crybaby,” “pickpocket,” and “scatterbrain.” These basic compounds do not rely on complex grammatical rules. They lack the structural layers required to distinguish between subjects and objects or to establish tense.
These simple word pairs are remarkably consistent across entirely different language families. Progovac notes that similar verb-noun compounds exist in languages ranging from Serbian to Berber to Twi. Historically, these basic constructions have been used to create highly vivid, metaphorical nicknames. Often, these nicknames are derogatory or humorous, describing a person based on a prominent action or physical trait.
Progovac proposes that as early humans developed these two-word abilities, a new form of social competition emerged. Individuals who could quickly invent clever, insulting, or amusing names had a distinct social advantage. They could demean rivals and impress potential mates without resorting to physical combat. This quick-wittedness represented an enormous cognitive leap, showing that early language was not just for sharing information but for social maneuvering.
The biological benefits of this verbal agility are still visible in human populations today. In many traditional oral societies across the globe, the most eloquent speakers hold the highest social status. Individuals who can manipulate words effectively gain access to political power and better reproductive success. The ability to charm a mate through humor and metaphorical language proved to be highly adaptive over time.
The paper also reviews experimental evidence from neuroimaging to support this evolutionary timeline. In a prior functional magnetic resonance imaging experiment, researchers tracked brain activity while participants read ancient verb-noun combinations compared to more modern, complex words. The older compounds evoked a more visceral reaction in the brain than modern words.
The experimenters found that processing the older, fossil-like compounds activated the right side of the fusiform gyrus in the brain. This specific brain region is directly involved in face perception and face recognition. Finding that the same brain area handles both face recognition and basic verb-noun processing supports the idea that the earliest grammar was closely tied to naming individuals and attaching linguistic labels to faces.
A related brain imaging experiment looked at how the brain processes simple sentences compared to hierarchical, modern sentences. The simpler sentences resulted in less activity in the Broca’s area and the basal ganglia. The basal ganglia are deep brain structures involved in motor control and learning.
Over the course of human evolution, the connections between the Broca’s area and the basal ganglia became much denser. The gradual mastery of more complex language likely drove the physical evolution of these brain networks. This aligns with genetic changes unique to humans and Neanderthals, including variations in the FOXP2 gene, which is associated with speech and language development.
By replacing physical fighting with verbal dueling, quick-wittedness played a direct role in reducing physical aggression among early humans. Humor and laughter act as natural stress antagonists, lowering cortisol levels in the body. This biological response connects the survival of the wittiest with the concept of human self-domestication. Over time, societies selected for individuals who could use words to defuse tension or assert dominance, leading to a species that prizes cognitive contests over lethal battles.
While this perspective offers a robust framework for understanding language origins, measuring the evolutionary impact of humor and wit relies heavily on reconstructing the past. Researchers must reverse-engineer modern languages and rely on brain imaging proxies, which cannot definitively prove how ancient ancestors behaved in their daily lives. Brain scans of modern humans only provide an approximation of ancient cognitive processes.
Future studies could test this hypothesis by examining how individual variations in cognitive conditions process these fossil grammars. By observing how brains with different neurological setups handle early grammatical structures, scientists can better map the exact neural pathways that allowed language to flourish.
The study, “Survival of the wittiest (not friendliest): The art and science behind human linguistic and cognitive evolution,” was authored by Ljiljana Progovac.

Burnham stays away from No 10 North wedding after bride’s plea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
13:56:40 UTC
22:56:40 KST

Andy Burnham fulfilled a bride’s wishes by not turning up for her wedding after she asked him not to spoil her big day as she got married at the building housing No 10 North.
Sarah Burwin had pleaded on TikTok in July for Burnham not to work from the building in Manchester that day, which hosts the government’s northern headquarters and the city’s register office.
Burwin had said she feared the security detail Burnham requires would ruin wedding photographs outside the venue when she got married on Friday.
She told the prime minister he would be welcome at her wedding, but told him to give his security detail “an hour off”. She later joked he could DJ the afterparty.
Burnham did not turn up, but did send a video message to her and her new husband Fred. “Thank you so much for the invite. But sadly, I’m honouring your initial request for me to stay out of the way, as I’m filming this as I’m about to leave No 10 North for the day,” Burnham said.
He added: “I couldn’t let the day go by without sending you both a message. I hope you have the best day celebrating, and thank you for being such a good sport about No 10 North suddenly being a big part of your big day. The DJ set will have to wait for another time, but I hope you play some good tunes on my behalf, big Manchester bangers.”
Burwin could be seen replying: “Oh my God. What a lad. I love him!”

HAIKOU, China (AP) — China said on Sunday it was postponing its planned ambitious Chang’e-7 lunar mission, which was set to carry out explorations including searching for water ice on the moon.
The Chang’e-7 spacecraft was originally set to lift off in the coming days from the Wenchang Space Launch Site on China’s southern Hainan island.
The mission does not meet the launch conditions, said the China Manned Space Agency in a brief statement, and “cannot take place during the planned window this year.”
The decision was made following a “comprehensive assessment,” the agency added, and was based on the principles of “prudence, reliability and absolute mission success.” It did not further elaborate on the reasons behind the decision.
Preparations have been carried out at the Wenchang launch site for the Chang’e-7 mission over the past weeks, the seventh in the Chang’e moon exploration program. It aimed at making breakthroughs in key technologies, the official Xinhua news agency previously reported.
It was set to explore permanently shadowed craters on the moon and conduct environmental and resource surveys of the lunar south pole, the Xinhua report said, citing the space agency.
Chang’e refers to a Chinese moon goddess. The Chang’e-6 probe returned to Earth in 2024 with rock and soil samples from the far side of the moon in a world first.

Over 8.2 million voters cast ballots in Kazakhstan's first election under new Constitution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
13:49:52 UTC
22:49:52 KST

Elena Teslova
23 August 2026•Update: 23 August 2026
Turnout in Kazakhstan’s first elections to the new unicameral parliament, the Kurultai, reached 65.37% by 4 pm local time (1100 GMT) on Sunday, surpassing the turnout recorded in the last parliamentary elections in 2023, the Central Election Commission said.
CEC member Assel Zhanabilova said 8,240,336 (8.2 million) voters cast their ballots, representing 65.37% of those registered to vote.
Turnout varied significantly across the country, she noted.
Almaty, the country's largest city, recorded the lowest rate at 36.65%, while the highest turnout was reported in the Kyzylorda region at 81.38%.
In the capital Astana, 46.38% of registered voters cast ballots, according to CEC data.
Turnout in the 2023 elections to Kazakhstan’s lower house, the Mazhilis, was 54.21%.
The Aug. 23 vote is the first parliamentary election held under the new Constitution, adopted in a referendum earlier this year.
The new document abolished the previous bicameral parliament and replaced it with a 145-member unicameral Kurultai.
All 145 seats are being contested through party lists, with voters choosing among seven registered political parties.
There is no minimum turnout threshold for parliamentary elections, meaning the vote is considered valid regardless of the number of voters who participate.

Pilot, 23, lands crippled plane in ocean off Florida | Watch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
13:47:14 UTC
22:47:14 KST

An extraordinary scene unfolded off the coast of South Florida over the weekend when a 23-year-old pilot facing a cascade of mechanical failures calmly landed her light aircraft in the ocean in front of stunned beachgoers.
Faith Tenkley had taken off Saturday morning in her family’s plane from Page Field in Fort Myers and was flying to the Bahamas, where she was due to pick up her parents. The emergency began when she was about 15 miles from Boca Raton. First, the aircraft’s landing gear broke. Then the right engine failed.
Tenkley received clearance to make an emergency landing at the local airport, but she was concerned about the large amount of fuel still on board. A belly landing on a hard runway, she feared, could trigger a fire or explosion. Instead, she turned toward the Atlantic Ocean. After maneuvering past buildings along the shoreline and avoiding paddleboarders in the water, Tenkley carried out a controlled water landing several miles east of the airport.
The aircraft came down smoothly, and Tenkley was able to get herself out unharmed. About a minute later, a local lifeguard reached her, followed by a fire-rescue boat. The aircraft, a twin-engine Piper PA-30 propeller plane, gradually sank over the following hours until only its tail remained visible above the water.
Tenkley has held a pilot’s license for four years and has been flying since graduating from high school. Witnesses on shore described the landing as surreal. “I was there when it happened,” Maria Marquez told WPBF. “One moment I’m spraying sunscreen on my child, and the next I look up and think, ‘Is that supposed to happen?’”
Michael and Alexis Arizzi were also nearby on a boat with their young son Sebastian and were among the first to alert the Coast Guard. “We were the first boat to see the plane land off the beach that morning and respond,” Alexis told WPBF. “The plane made a slow descent and landed gently in the water.”

Rock art: Tiny Sasanian bird motif discovered in southern Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
13:42:07 UTC
22:42:07 KST

Rock art: Tiny Sasanian bird motif discovered in southern Iran
TEHRAN – Archaeologist Abolhasan Atabaki has reported the discovery of what he describes as the smallest known bird motif from the Sasanian period, measuring just 3 by 2 centimeters and engraved on the rocks of the Marvdasht Plain in Fars province, southern Iran.
The tiny image was executed using a pecked or incised technique and is located beside a Middle Persian (Pahlavi) inscription dating to the late Sasanian period. According to Atabaki, the bird appears to be related to the concepts expressed in the inscription, particularly the idea of the soul’s salvation, Jamaran news website reported.
Atabaki said birds in ancient Iranian culture were often associated with auspiciousness, the carrying of messages, the ascent of the soul, and the connection between the earthly and celestial realms.
“This visual tradition did not disappear after the fall of the Sasanian Empire,” he said, adding that it continued, with changes, during the Islamic period and reached a high point in Persian miniature painting.
Birds perched on branches became recurring elements in the art of various Persian miniature schools, particularly during the Ilkhanid, Timurid and Safavid periods. Atabaki said such birds were not merely decorative motifs but also contributed to the poetic and spiritual atmosphere of paintings.
He said the roots of this visual tradition could be traced to Sasanian art, in which animals and plants were arranged according to symbolic and geometric principles.
The bird’s ability to fly between earth and sky also made it a fitting symbol of the relationship between the material and spiritual worlds, Atabaki explained. A bird perched on a branch could reinforce this symbolism, with the tree or branch representing life, growth and continuity, while the bird evoked the celestial realm.
In that regard, historian Najmeh Ebrahimi said the motif could also be interpreted in relation to death and beliefs about the soul.
“In Iranian traditions, death was not regarded as the end of existence, but as a transition of the soul from the material world to the spiritual realm,” she said. The bird perched on a branch, positioned between earth and sky, could therefore be understood as a metaphor for the soul’s passage and the connection between earthly and afterlife existence.
Ebrahimi said examination of the engraving showed that the bird had been rendered in a highly linear manner, using narrow and shallow grooves cut into the rock. The artist appears to have defined the small image mainly through its outlines with a pointed tool.
The nearby Pahlavi inscription, with its references to salvation and the fate of the soul, provides a basis for a possible symbolic interpretation of the bird, she added.
According to Ebrahimi, birds in Iranian religious and epic traditions often carried meanings beyond their natural existence and were sometimes regarded as intermediaries between the material and spiritual worlds or as bearers of divine messages. Some birds in the Avesta and Middle Persian texts were also associated with concepts including divine glory, guidance, protection and the spiritual realm.
The location of the engraving and inscription further adds to their significance. The Marvdasht Plain remained an important political and religious landscape of Iran from the first millennium BC through the Sasanian period. Its proximity to major archaeological sites such as Persepolis, Naqsh-e Rostam and Naqsh-e Rajab suggests that the area continued to form part of an important ritual and cultural landscape during the Sasanian era.
Ebrahimi added that the combination of a religious inscription with a symbolic natural motif on the rock was consistent with traditions in which natural elements were used to convey religious concepts.
She described the small engraving, together with the Pahlavi inscription, as a rare example of the interaction between image and text in late Sasanian art. She also noted that full publication and study of the find, including a complete reading of the inscription and comparison with similar examples, could contribute to a better understanding of the role of bird symbolism and religious concepts in Sasanian art and culture.

UK's proposed ban on Israeli settlement trade would breach int'l legal obligations, lawyers warn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
13:40:46 UTC
22:40:46 KST

UK Lawyers for Israel has warned the UK government that a proposed ban on trade with Israeli businesses in east Jerusalem and the West Bank would breach several of Britain’s international legal obligations.
Former trade minister Chris Bryant argued that the UK has a legal obligation not to “aid or assist” the Israeli settlements, saying that he is actively considering bans on the import and export of goods and services.
UKLFI has sent a briefing paper to Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and Legal Adviser to the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office Sally Langrish challenging this legal analysis.
In the paper, UKLFI argued that there is no international law obligation requiring the UK to impose a general ban on private businesses from trading with Israeli businesses operating in the West Bank.
In fact, UKLFI warned that imposing the proposed bans could place the UK in breach of several international agreements.
Outright import or export ban explicitly violates UK-Israel Trade agreement
For example, the UK-Israel Trade and Partnership Agreement prohibits quantitative restrictions on imports and exports. UKLFI wrote that an outright import or export ban would be the clearest possible form of such a restriction and would therefore be prima facie inconsistent with the agreement.
UKLFI also noted that the proposed ban would breach the UK’s obligations under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) and the General Agreement on Trade in Services (GATS), as well as the Protocol on Ireland/Northern Ireland to the Brexit withdrawal agreement.
Additionally, the paper said that if the UK government sought to introduce a ban in response to alleged Israeli conduct, it would first be required under the agreement to refer the issue to the UK-Israel Joint Council and seek a mutually acceptable solution.
“A unilateral ban introduced without following that procedure would breach the TPA irrespective of the underlying merits of the policy,” UKLFI said.
Furthermore, it put forward the argument that a ban on trade could “harm the very Palestinian population it is supposedly intended to assist.”
Thousands of Palestinians are employed by Israeli businesses in areas of settlement in the West Bank, earning often twice the salaries paid by Palestinian employers.
UKLFI said that damaging these businesses would “jeopardize the livelihoods of many Palestinians, undermine the Palestinian economy, and further hinder a two-state solution.”
British companies could be caught between British and American laws
Finally, UKLFI warned that companies operating in Britain could find themselves caught between conflicting British and American laws.
US federal and state anti-boycott legislation can penalize participation in boycotts of businesses in territories governed by Israel. UKLFI said this could discourage US companies from investing or operating in Britain if compliance with the law exposed them to sanctions in the United States.
“Statements made on behalf of the UK government appear to be the opposite of the correct position,” Jonathan Turner, CEO of UKLFI, said.
“There is no international legal obligation requiring the UK to impose a blanket ban on trade with Israeli businesses in east Jerusalem [and] Judea and Samaria. On the contrary, our analysis shows that imposing such a ban could itself put the UK in breach of several binding international obligations, including the UK-Israel Trade and Partnership Agreement, the GATT, the GATS and, if the ban extends to Northern Ireland, the Protocol on Ireland/Northern Ireland to the Brexit Agreement,” he said.
“We urge the government to reconsider this proposal in the light of the points made in our paper.”

Long-term investment in youth best solution to address demographic change
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
13:40:15 UTC
22:40:15 KST

Long-term investment in youth best solution to address demographic change
TEHRAN – The United Nations Fund for Population Activities (UNFPA), in collaboration with the ministries of health and labour, commemorated World Population Day focusing on what young people want for their lives — and what stands between them and the families and futures they hope to build.
By reading Iran’s population momentum through the lens of what young people themselves say they want, the commemoration reaffirmed a shared conviction: that responding to demographic change means long-term investment in young people, and cross-sector policies spanning education, employment security, housing, reproductive health services, and social protection — the conditions that help young people contribute to societies that are innovative, resilient, and economically robust, UNPFA website announced in a press release on August 16.
Anchoring much of the day’s discussion was UNFPA’s flagship report, Lives, Choices and Futures, which presents the findings of the 2025–2026 Demographic Futures Survey — one of the most geographically diverse bodies of evidence yet assembled on how young adults think about relationships, parenthood, and the future. Drawing on the voices of more than 108,000 people aged 18 to 39 across 73 countries, the report gave participants a global mirror in which to examine Iran’s own debates.
Among the findings that shaped the discussion:
 
 More than two-thirds of respondents want to marry or live with a partner.
 
 A two-child family is the most commonly reported ideal family size in five of seven regional groupings.
 
 Economic and housing constraints are the most common obstacles to forming partnerships for both men and women.
 
 Financial security is the top consideration for entering a partnership (81 percent) and for parenthood (88 percent).
 
 Stable employment (87 percent) and emotional readiness (85 percent) rank high among the preconditions young people set for becoming parents.
 
 Two-thirds feel somewhat or very positive about the future — even amid worries about conflict, economic insecurity, and inequality.
Bringing together university deans and academics, civil society organizations, and representatives of governmental bodies at the Tehran Ghalb Hotel by the Ministry of Health and Medical Education, the gathering set out to move the demographic discourse beyond numbers and targets — toward the hopes, choices, and constraints of a generation deciding whether, when, and how to form families in an uncertain world.
The event opened with remarks by Dr. Alireza Raisi, Deputy Minister of Health, who called for a change in how policymakers approach population structure. “Population does not grow through policymaking based on fear, coercion, or ‘the stick and the club’ — and even if it did, it would bring no benefit. What young people need is hope, trust, and confidence in the future: a job, a home, economic security, and a future they can predict. Our task as policymakers is not to place blame on people, but to remove the obstacles in front of the young.”
Dr. Raisi added that no population policy can succeed without attention to women who, he said, should never be forced to choose between employment and family and even if we increase the population that ageing is an inevitable structural shift due to increased life expectancy resulting from advances in health and welfare system for which the country must prepare, from the design of its cities to its health and welfare systems. He also mentioned the importance and availability of data for evidence-based policy and effective programming.
Two panels, one question
The program featured two expert panels drawing together specialists from universities, ministries, and international organizations.
The first expert panel examined Demographic changes and policies in Iran and around the world, testing national trends against global experience and comparing how different countries have responded. The second panel turned to youth marriage, childbearing, and population resilience.
Mr. Keita Ohashi, UNFPA Representative in Iran, praised Iran’s strong human capital while pointing to the gaps that remain in the labour market:
“Iran has remarkable human capital — high levels of knowledge and literacy — and that is a tremendous asset. But gaps remain: too many women, and too many young people who are not in employment, education or training, have yet to find their place in the labour market, and they deserve our attention. We should not see motherhood and entering the workforce as competing choices; rather, support for working mothers — and for women more broadly — must grow, so that women can join the labour market without having to postpone motherhood.”
Mr. Majd Hosseinpour from the Ministry of Cooperative, Labour and Social Welfare opened the second panel, emphasizing the very low economic participation rate of women, approximately 4 million out of the 25 million economically active, and the need for economic entities to adapt themselves and their policies.
Presenting to the second panel, Amir-Hossein Vaezi, Head of the Centre for Strategic Studies and Research at the Ministry of Sport and Youth, drew on three waves of the National Survey of Iranian Youth Values and Attitudes (2013, 2020 and 2024):
“Panel survey evidence shows that young Iranians still place a high value on family, marriage and childbearing — but the way they realize these aspirations has undergone an ‘attitudinal transition.’ Today, young people weigh their decisions in terms of economic security, prospects for the future, quality of life, mutual trust and whether they can balance their family and social roles. Rebuilding population resilience does not mean a mechanical return to old patterns; it means building lasting capacity for family formation by listening to young people’s voices and turning research evidence into practical policy.”
UNFPA Iran reiterated its commitment to working alongside national partners based on national priorities so that every young person can realize their hopes and aspirations — today, and for the future.

Sydney Marathon mishap: Munich's Allianz Arena appears on finisher medal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
13:39:00 UTC
22:39:00 KST

More than 40,000 people are expected for the Sydney Marathon, but just before the start the finisher's medal causes a stir: it appears to show Munich's Allianz Arena instead of a Sydney stadium.
In Sydney, final preparations are under way for next weekend's marathon. As the runners get ready for the race, it is the finisher medal that is unexpectedly attracting international attention. The reason: between the landmarks of the Australian metropolis, what appears to be a German football stadium has ended up on the medal.
The medal's design is actually meant to reflect the marathon course. "Those who look closely will discover the story of the course in the details," the organisers wrote on their official social media account.
But it is precisely in these details that the mistake lies, as the medal apparently shows Munich's Allianz Arena rather than the Allianz Stadium in Sydney, which the 42.2-kilometre marathon route passes. Social media mockery was not long in coming, with some users tagging FC Bayern in the post.
The organiser has since admitted the mix-up. "A little too much international flair has crept onto the back of the finisher medal, in the form of an incorrect depiction of the stadium," a spokesperson for the Sydney Marathon said. "We won't shy away from it – it was a regrettable mistake, even if it has certainly given everyone something to talk about this weekend."
In Munich, the mix-up was taken with good humour. "Oh wow, that wasn't on our bingo card at all!" wrote the official Instagram account of the Allianz Arena.
More than 40,000 participants expected
More than 40,000 runners are expected to take part in the marathon next weekend. The flawed medals will not be exchanged before then.
"One week before the event, this is the medal our runners will receive," the Sydney Marathon spokesperson explained. "It is a beautiful medal, and now it is just that little bit more unique."
Since 2024, the Sydney Marathon has been part of the Abbott World Marathon Majors series as its seventh race. That puts the Australian metropolis alongside Berlin, London, Boston, Chicago, New York and Tokyo.

“Support and reconstruction of Ukraine are also important for European security,” Støre said in the announcement. “Therefore, the government proposes to continue emergency support in the amount of 85 billion kroner next year.”
The proposed financial aid falls under the Nansen Support Programme for Ukraine, which allocates funds for both civil and military purposes.

In May, Norway pledged an additional 2.8 billion NOK ($302 million) to NATO’s Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative, a mechanism designed to coordinate and speed up the delivery of urgent military equipment by pooling allied resources.

The establishment of modern schools has marked a new chapter in Iran’s education system, a development that plays an important role in reducing illiteracy and creating the conditions necessary for the country’s growth and development, Simaei-Sarraf concluded.
The third national event on future schools was held in February, honoring eight top ideas from more than 200 received by the event’s secretariat.
More than 200 ideas were submitted to the secretariat, said Hamidreza Khanmohammadi, the director of the Organization for Development, Renovation, and Equipping Schools, adding that 174 were evaluated and, ultimately, eight were selected.
The space designed and built as a school should be multifaceted, flexible, and equipped with diverse learning environments, with an eye on the future, IRNA quoted Khanmohammadi as saying.
Schools should be a place where students practice living and prepare for a spiritual life, accompanied by progress, he stressed.
The third national event on future schools highlighted the use of modern technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI) and blended learning in fostering thinking skills and creativity, as well as collaboration among the future generation of students.
Future school and the public education system (the role of teacher and student in future schools, modern teaching and learning approaches, schools and students with specific needs); Future school, a center for education and development of community (schools as social institution for the development of the neighbourhood, school’s interaction with cultural, social, and urban institutions); Future school and physical environment (designing green schools, utilizing renewable energies and modern construction technologies); and Future school, equipment, educational technologies (modern educational tools and technologies, AI-based learning platforms, digital infrastructures) were the four key topics of the event.
Technology and knowledge-based companies, consulting engineers, universities and research centers, science and technology parks, professors and students, and researchers in technical, engineering, humanities, art, and psychology fields were among the main target audiences of the event.

Boosting digital literacy will prepare students for future job markets, help them develop their critical thinking, and become familiar with emerging technologies; it will also foster creativity and innovation among students.

Rising U.S. Treasury yields intensify pressure on European bond markets
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
21:37:19 CST
22:37:19 KST

BELGRADE, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- Long-term U.S. Treasury yields have climbed to near 20-year highs in recent days, exerting sustained pressure on European bond markets. Although intervention by the U.S. Treasury Department eased selling pressure on U.S. debt for a time, European bonds have remained broadly strained.
On Aug. 21, the yield on the 30-year U.S. Treasury bond, one of the targets of the Treasury's buyback operations, rose to 5.27 percent. Earlier in the week, it had briefly reached 5.34 percent, its highest level since 2007. Yields on major European government bonds rose in tandem. As of Aug. 21, Germany's 10-year yield hovered around 3.25 percent, close to a 15-year high; France's 10-year yield broke above 4.13 percent, the highest since 2008; and Italy's 10-year yield climbed to 4.08 percent.
Several European market institutions believe that volatility in the U.S. Treasury market could continue to affect European financial markets. Britain's Aberdeen Investments said the U.S. Treasury's intervention was a clear signal that the U.S. government is willing to hold down long-term Treasury yields, but noted that such support does not extend to Britain or other European countries, leaving European bonds to weaken to a limited degree.
Guy Miller, chief market strategist at Zurich Insurance Group, said the direction of U.S. Treasury yields is crucial not only for bond markets but also for other financial assets in markets such as Europe, adding that any further upward breakout could undermine market confidence.
Rising U.S. Treasury yields have already affected the asset allocation of European investors. Denmark's Saxo Bank said Treasury yields remain the primary cross-market risk, with high yields and inflation concerns continuing to pressure European technology and financial stocks. Dutch bank ING said European asset managers are insufficiently hedged against the currency risk of their U.S. holdings, and that sharp swings in the Treasury market could further amplify the risks facing European investors.
As for the outlook, Mark Dowding, chief investment officer for fixed income at BlueBay Asset Management, warned that if U.S. economic growth slows and concerns over the sustainability of U.S. government debt intensify, European financial markets could see a sharper correction. ■

Putin Wants to Draft 300K New Troops, Zelensky Says
