Single adults in early midlife often prefer cohabitation over marriage, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
10:00:59 UTC
19:00:59 KST

A recent study reveals that unmarried adults in their thirties and forties hold highly diverse goals for future relationships, with cohabitation being more popular than marriage. The findings indicate that previous life events shape what people want for their future, challenging the idea of a universal relationship path. The research was published in the journal Family Transitions.
In the United States, roughly one in three adults between the ages of 30 and 49 live without a spouse or partner. As people delay milestones like first marriages and first births, a growing share of the population remains single into midlife. Currently, about one in five adults in their early forties have never married, and almost one in six women in their late forties do not have children.
Sociologists Susan L. Brown, Wendy D. Manning, and Karen Benjamin Guzzo of Bowling Green State University and the University of North Carolina-Chapel Hill initiated the study to understand the long-term relationship and parenting goals of this expanding demographic. Past research on family planning has heavily focused on teenagers and young adults, who often express a desire to marry and have children.
Alternatively, researchers have studied older adults, who are frequently uninterested in reentering a formal union. Adults in early midlife occupy a unique transitional space because many have already experienced milestones like marriage, living with a partner, or having children.
The research team applied a sociological framework known as the life course perspective. This concept suggests that prior life events establish a foundation that guides an individual’s subsequent choices. For example, a person who has already navigated a divorce might view the prospect of a new marriage differently than someone who has never wed. A related concept highlights how family relationships influence personal decisions, such as single parents weighing their own desires for a romantic partner against the potential impact on their children.
To explore these dynamics, the researchers analyzed data from the 2023 Singlehood in America survey. The dataset included 799 single adults between the ages of 30 and 50. In this context, single was defined as individuals who were neither married nor currently living with a romantic partner. The participants were drawn from a large, nationally representative online panel.
The sample featured roughly equal numbers of men and women with diverse educational backgrounds, income levels, and racial identities. Participants answered questions about whether they wanted to marry, live with a partner without marrying, remain unpartnered, or if they were unsure about their future relationship plans. They also indicated whether they wanted to have a child or additional children in the future.
The researchers used statistical models to evaluate how a person’s prior relationship history and parental status related to their future preferences. These models accounted for demographic factors like age, education, income, homeownership, and sexual identity. The analysis revealed a wide spectrum of relationship goals among single adults in early midlife.
Cohabitation emerged as the most desired relationship format, favored by roughly 38 percent of men and 29 percent of women. Marriage was less popular, desired by only 18 percent of men and 23 percent of women. At the same time, roughly a quarter of both men and women expressed no desire to live with or marry a partner in the future, and many others reported feeling unsure.
The researchers found that past experiences with cohabitation were associated with a desire to live with a partner again. People who had previously lived with a romantic partner were more likely to want to marry or cohabit in the future compared to those who had never lived with a partner. The researchers expected that individuals who had been married previously might be less eager to marry again. The results showed that prior marital experience had no negative association with a desire to marry.
Formerly married men were simply more likely to express uncertainty about their future relationship goals than men who had never married. The team also anticipated that having children might act as a deterrent to forming new residential unions. Being a parent had no measurable association with an individual’s desire to marry or live with a partner.
Current life circumstances also played a role in future planning. Women who had a college degree were much more likely to want to marry or cohabit than women with less formal education. Conversely, women who owned a home were more likely to express a firm lack of interest in forming a new residential union. For both men and women, those who had ended a live-in relationship within the past five years were more eager to cohabit in the future compared to those who had been single for six years or more.
The researchers then evaluated the participants’ desires to have children. Most single adults in early midlife did not want to have a child or additional children. Only about 20 percent of women and 17 percent of men expressed a desire to expand their families. This low percentage is likely due to the fact that approximately 80 percent of the study participants were already parents.
For women, earlier experiences with marriage, cohabitation, or parenthood were entirely unrelated to their future fertility desires. A woman’s desire to have a child was not tied to whether she was already a mother or whether she had been married. Women with higher incomes were slightly less likely to want a child in the future.
For men, the patterns were slightly different. Fathers were much less likely to want additional children compared to men without children. Men who had previously lived with a romantic partner were more likely to want a child in the future.
Age also influenced male preferences, with men in their early thirties being substantially more likely to want a child than men approaching age 50. Men with a college education were more likely to want a child, while men who owned their own homes were less likely to want to expand their families.
Because the survey data was collected at a single point in time, the research cannot determine whether these preferences will lead to actual marriages, cohabiting relationships, or births. The analysis only captures an association between past experiences and current desires. The survey also limited relationship preferences to living together or getting married.
This omits the possibility that some individuals might prefer long-term committed relationships where partners live in separate households. The dataset provided a snapshot of relationship history, but it did not capture the duration, quality, or specific timing of past marriages and cohabiting relationships. Future investigations could benefit from tracking individuals over time to see if their relationship goals shift as they age or if they meet a compatible partner. Researchers could also explore how unmeasured factors, such as the strength of a person’s friendships, might shape exactly what early midlife adults want from a future partner.
The study, “The Future Family Desires of Single Early Midlife Adults,” was authored by Susan L. Brown, Wendy D. Manning, and Karen Benjamin Guzzo.

Artemis II crew to receive top US space medal for historic lunar journey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
10:00:30 UTC
19:00:30 KST

The crew of the historic Artemis II lunar flyby mission have earned the US’s top space medal, officials have announced.
Cmdr Reid Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover, and mission specialists Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen are set to receive the Congressional Space Medal of Honor on 28 August, the US space agency Nasa said.
Nasa’s website indicates that only 30 astronauts have gained the honor – among them Neil Armstrong, the first person to walk on the moon, and John Glenn, who was the first American to orbit Earth and then served four terms in the US Senate.
Wiseman, Glover, Koch and Hansen were selected for the medal, despite its name, by Donald Trump after the Nasa administrator, Jared Isaacman, recommended them to the president.
The Artemis II crew broke Apollo 13’s record for farthest distance traveled from Earth during their 10-day mission, which began on 1 April. They reached 252,756 miles (406,771km) as they swung above the lunar surface, surpassing the 1970 record of 248,655 miles as part of US plans to again land on the moon – then eventually reach Mars.
Furthermore, Hansen – who is from Canada – became the first non-US citizen to fly to the moon.
“This was not easy,” Wiseman said to reporters after the Artemis II mission safely ended with a textbook splashdown in the Pacific Ocean. “Before you launch, it feels like it’s the greatest dream on Earth. And when you’re out there, you just want to get back to your families and your friends. It’s a special thing to be a human, and it’s a special thing to be on planet Earth.”
The medal ceremony scheduled for Wiseman and his colleagues at the Johnson Space Center in Houston comes four months after Trump hosted the Artemis II crew at the White House. The occasion was marked in part by the president, who turned 80 in June, telling the astronauts: “I would have had no trouble making it – I’m physically very, very good.”
Nasa listed an 11am start time for the ceremony, with a video live stream of the event available at www.nasa.gov/live.
Trump has sought to embrace the Artemis II crew’s achievements despite his administration’s proposal to cut Nasa’s budget by 23%, including a 46% reduction for space science initiatives, for the 2027 fiscal year beginning on 1 October. A House commerce, justice and science subcommittee led by Trump’s Republican party responded by advancing its own Nasa budget proposal that would maintain the science projects the president has been aiming to eliminate.
Beside Armstrong and Glenn, previous Congressional Space Medal of Honor recipients include astronauts who were killed in the Apollo I fire as well as the explosions of the Challenger and Columbia space shuttles.
Douglas Hurley and Robert Behnken were the last astronauts to have been chosen for the medal before the Artemis II crew. Hurley and Behnken in 2020 became the first to launch into orbit on a commercial spacecraft, and they accepted the medal in 2023 during Joe Biden’s presidency.

Finland tried to end homelessness. What can we learn from its runaway success – and recent failures?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
10:00:30 UTC
19:00:30 KST

At 3.30am, Vello Senkel awoke to a knock on his door. Standing on his doorstep were his neighbours with an urgent request: “Do you have salt? We want to boil macaroni.” He acquiesced, but it turned out that salt wasn’t the only ingredient they were missing: “And do you also have macaroni?” His warm face, framed by jaw-length white hair, is at once charmed and outraged as he recounts the interaction while smoking a cigarette outside his apartment building the following morning.
Senkel, whose nickname is Velho (Finnish for wizard), is known for his proficiency in the kitchen. In his apartment, where he lives alongside 77 other formerly homeless people in a Helsinki suburb, he shows me his fully stocked freezer. From his neatly organised fridge he pulls out the jars of pickled cabbage and shrimp salad he has prepared to take to a friend’s house for lunch later.
When Senkel, 67, moved here three and a half years ago, he had been living on the streets of the Finnish capital for 10 days after being evicted from his home. Before that there had been a diagnosis of borderline personality disorder, and a devastating loss. His partner, whose photo is framed on his bookshelf, died after two years in a coma that started when her heart failed in her sleep.
After getting a place here, little by little, he started to build a new life. As well as cooking, he likes to play a bit of guitar every day. He brings his bass into the kitchen and becomes emotional as he plays along to an Estonian power ballad (he is originally from Estonia).
Having this apartment, he says, has “changed everything”. The housing unit, attractively set around a courtyard in converted student accommodation, follows the “Housing First” principle that has made Finland a world leader when it comes to tackling homelessness. The model focuses on housing as a fundamental human right rather than a reward. Temporary accommodation is seen not as a solution, but something to be avoided. All support is centred on ensuring that people have permanent homes, with everything else following from that – treatment, healthcare, employment. In the long run, advocates say, it is cheaper for the state for people to be permanently housed, taking pressure off other public services.
Another key component of Housing First for Senkel is the 24-hour staff support. Without it, his home would have been a “black hole” of loneliness. He feels understood by the staff here, he says. He has an agreement with the management that if they don’t see him for 72 hours they will get in touch.
In a communal living room-dining area, porridge and coffee are served every morning and there is a weekly community meeting to discuss any issues. Residents can volunteer to do small tasks such as cleaning shared spaces or picking up litter in return for a small fee that is transferred directly into their bank accounts. “You are precious,” a notice on the pinboard says. “We listen and support and together with you we build the life that is true to you. Your pathway, our shared journey.”
Marko Lahtela, who manages the unit where Senkel lives, says their tenants come to them from a range of homeless situations: some come directly from the street; others may have been evicted from their apartment or had problems paying rent. While housing is essential, it is by no means an instant fix. Many have substance-abuse issues or other long-term problems, which means building trust is vital. It is “more of a marathon than a sprint”, he says. There is no limit on how long you can live here. Some haven’t left since it opened in 2022; others move on to more independent forms of accommodation after just six months.
Tenants range in age from early 20s to 60s, but the most common demographic is men who are about 40. There are two apartments for married couples, but the rest are single-person homes. Usually people cover the rent, which starts at about €850 (£728) a month, using benefits or, for those who have one, a pension. The unit, which is run by the health and social care provider Rinnekodit, has lots of success stories, but the system is not perfect. Lahtela says there is not enough in place to stop people running into rental debt, which after two months can result in eviction – and for some, a return to the streets.
Since 2008, when the Housing First principle was introduced as the foundation of all homelessness policies in Finland, the country has achieved remarkable results. Between 2012 and 2023, homelessness rose across Europe, but in Finland, the number of homeless people dropped by more than half, from about 8,000 to about 3,400. Homelessness statistics are notoriously difficult to measure, but for context, the number of people experiencing homelessness in Spain rose by about a quarter between 2012 and 2022. In December, the charity Shelter reported that homelessness in England had risen 8% in the past year to a total of 382,618 – including a record number in temporary accommodation – and that rough sleeping had increased by 20% in just a year. Finland’s success has drawn attention from politicians from around the world – including Britain’s new prime minister, Andy Burnham. In his first speech as PM, Burnham pledged to end rough sleeping in England, and he recently launched a £442m campaign to “get everyone in for Christmas”.
But is Finland still the model? Not long ago, the goal of the former Social Democrat prime minister Sanna Marin’s government to end homelessness by 2027 was seen as within reach, but in the last three years sweeping cuts to social services, healthcare and benefits by Finland’s rightwing government have seen the country’s success story go into reverse. The latest national survey, from last November, found that the number of homeless people had gone up for a second year in a row, to 4,579 people, a 20% rise on the previous year. Key factors cited by the government’s own report include rising housing and living costs, cuts to benefits and more cases of substance abuse and mental health problems. Homelessness has especially increased among women, under-25s and people with non-Finnish backgrounds.
As people come through the doors for breakfast at the cosy former restaurant premises of Vailla vakinaista asuntoa ry (No Fixed Abode), an NGO founded by homeless people 40 years ago, it is striking how young many of them are. After picking up food, donated by a local conference centre, and coffee, people sit down at long tables under low hanging lights. There’s a TV on in the background.
Sitting down for breakfast, Jari Häkkinen, 57, says finding a place to live is not a problem, but finding one that will be covered by his benefits is. He is determined to keep the pensioners apartment he has found, but it is €14 over his monthly limit. “I’m fighting to get that €14 a month no matter what,” says the former construction worker.
Another visitor, who asked to be named only as Leila, joins the conversation. She has been homeless for nearly 12 years and currently lives under a nearby bridge. “They are saying [Finland is a] happy country. It is not true,” she says, referring to its reputation as the world’s happiest country. “This is the reality you see.”
No Fixed Abode serves breakfast, lunch and coffee throughout the day, and in the winter, when temperatures in Helsinki can sink to -30C, they run a night cafe where a small number of people can keep safe and warm. Visitors can also pick up new clothes and speak to peer workers for support and advice. At the moment they have about 100 visitors a day, and in the colder months the number doubles.
There is no “one size, one idea, one model, one type of support service”, says Erja Morottaja, No Fixed Abode’s head of communications. “Some people might need quite light support. And then some people need quite heavy support.”
Suski Kankaanmäki, 44, is now employed there as a peer worker, but she first came as a homeless visitor after she was evicted in 2015. For six months she spent the nights on trains and in railway stations in and around Helsinki – taking the last train to somewhere, sleeping in the station then returning to the city for morning. She then spent the best part of a year in “hidden homelessness” – cooking, cleaning and dog-walking for a friend in return for a place to sleep. It was better than sleeping outside, she says, but there was an uncomfortable power imbalance.
During that time she managed to successfully apply for an apartment, but it quickly became a “drug using centre”. Having grown up in 11 different children’s institutions, it took her time to work out how to build a stable life. She got help from social workers with managing her finances but it wasn’t until a major health scare in 2021 that her life completely turned around. The feeling of not being safe is still there, says Kankaanmäki, and she never stops being on alert, but she is positive about the future and is training to be a nurse. She wants to work at a Housing First unit.
Based on what she has seen here, Kankaanmäki is pretty certain that homelessness numbers will rise further. NGOs are being gutted and new groups, such as working people on low incomes, are becoming at risk of losing their homes. There are not enough shelter places, she says, so people are sleeping in shopping centres, stations, public toilets and Helsinki airport.
Last year, homelessness in Helsinki, which has the largest homeless population of anywhere in Finland, rose by 25% – to 979 people. The increased strain is being felt at the city-run Hietaniemenkatu service centre, one of three places offering emergency short-term accommodation – intended to be for one night, although many stay longer. Staff say they are seeing more women, particularly elderly women, and more people with jobs than before. There is a sense that the country’s most vulnerable have been left to fend for themselves. “We all came to the conclusion that it is because of the current government,” says social worker Viveca, who cannot give her last name for security reasons. “There are cuts to everything. The only place they didn’t cut from is the rich.”
Its 52 emergency housing places, with multiple beds to a room, are free of charge but in high demand. From there, residents can apply for one of its 52 temporary housing places, which are individual rooms but come with a fee of up to €14.60 a day. There is a day centre with showers, washing machines and a sauna, and access to health and housing support. There is something of a revolving-door phenomenon at the centre, however, staff say, where people keep coming back because they do not have the life skills to maintain a permanent apartment alone once they have one.
Despite the recent dip in progress on reducing homelessness, there is still much for other countries to learn from Finland. Arguably, the recent problems make it an even better case study for Burnham and others.
Burnham visited Y-Säätiö (Y-Foundation), which played a central role in the creation and implementation of Housing First, in 2019. Since then, Y-Foundation, which owns more than 19,000 homes in Finland, making it the country’s largest nonprofit landlord, has twice been to the UK to support Burnham’s Manchester homelessness programme, which was inspired by the Finnish model.
Juha Kahila, Y-Foundation’s head of international affairs, is enthusiastic about what has already been achieved. For people who have been homeless, dedicated housing units with 24-hour on-site support are not the only option. The vast majority of formerly homeless people in Finland live in “scattered housing”, he says: affordable housing among different demographic groups. During a walk around Jätkäsaari, a newly developed area of Helsinki in a former container port, he is proud of how students, elderly and low income people live alongside prime real estate and green space. Often the affordable housing looks nicer than the most expensive properties.
There are about 400,000 affordable homes in Finland (in a population of 5.6 million), constituting about 30% of the overall housing stock. When he talks about affordable housing – a term often misappropriated by property developers – he is referring to the real construction costs of a property with no profit for anyone. “We have understood that the need has to be the first thing,” he says. “It is not about the quantity of the affordable homes but how you target them that makes a big difference.”
Comfort and cosiness are often cast aside as a luxury, but they are actually a key part of Finland’s successes in bringing down homelessness. If an apartment isn’t cosy, you won’t feel safe there, says Kahila, as he shows me around a building where a third of the apartments are reserved for low-income musicians. And if you don’t feel like it’s yours then it becomes a roof over your head rather than a home.
“Home is something you want to decorate, you want to spend time there. When you close the door you can … ” he pauses to take a deep breath in and out. “You can be whoever you want. It’s your safe place.”

Trump laying groundwork to impose national emergency by sowing election distrust
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
10:00:29 UTC
19:00:29 KST

A series of moves by Donald Trump’s administration to sow doubt in the integrity of US elections has intensified concern among voting experts – and sparked hope among election deniers – that it could declare a national emergency.
The White House and US federal agencies have released a string of documents this summer – including disputed analyses of alleged voting by noncitzens and historical intelligence memos – stoking expectations that the US president could move to exert greater control over November’s US midterm elections.
Trump used a primetime television address in July to claim – again – that US elections were vulnerable to foreign manipulation, and repeat the lie that the 2020 presidential election, which he lost to Joe Biden, was stolen.
Trump’s speech prompted Steve Bannon, his former political strategist, to predict the US president will declare a state of emergency on national security grounds to “protect” elections.
“Take your No 2 pencil out,” Bannon, a rightwing commentator, said on his War Room video podcast on 29 July. “It’s coming. It’s coming. Just block the last week of August out. It’s coming.”
While Trump and his allies could try to use a national emergency declaration to delegitimize results of November’s results, experts say such a declaration would not supersede the constitutional restrictions on executive power on election administration. No president has ever attempted to invoke an emergency to assert control over voting.
Asked earlier this month by Wayne Allyn Root, a rightwing broadcaster, if he would “declare a national security emergency for elections”, Trump notably did not shoot down the idea.
“Let me just say, stranger things have happened, OK?” the president told Real America’s Voice, a rightwing cable channel. “I’ll leave it at that.”
The administration is “trying to lay the groundwork to declare some sort of emergency to nationalize elections”, said Aria Branch, a partner at the Elias Law Group, who led a lawsuit blocking Trump’s previous executive orders on election administration. “I think the president is looking for any opportunity to do that.”
‘We need to be prepared for everything’
“I mean, listen, I think it is quite obvious that the man is losing his grip in reality, so I think we need to be prepared for everything,” said Santiago Mayer, president of Voters of Tomorrow, a gen Z-led voter advocacy organization. “We have spent a long time thinking and preparing for any eventuality and anything that he might attempt. I think our focus at the end of the day is to turn out enough voters where, no matter what he pulls, it won’t succeed.”
Democratic members of US congress have been wargaming strategies to respond to executive provocations in recent months, considering scenarios such as AI-generated disinformation videos and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents being dispatched to polls. Progressive organizations in the democracy space have also been preparing for something to happen before the election.
The presence of Tulsi Gabbard, Trump’s former director of national intelligence, at an FBI raid in Fulton county, Georgia, raised questions earlier this year. Gabbard later testified before Congress that she had been leading an investigation into claims of foreign interference in US elections. Gabbard’s team was involved in the seizure and examination of voting equipment in Puerto Rico, and spent months scrutinizing potential vulnerabilities in voting machines and the possibility of foreign interference.
When Gabbard resigned on 30 June, Trump named his longstanding ally Bill Pulte as her acting replacement, a widely criticized move by members of both parties, who pointed to Pulte’s lack of intelligence experience. While Jay Clayton later took up the post permanently, Pulte is said to have pushed the election interference narrative in a less-visible role.
“This is why Pulte is so important,” Bannon said in July. “So, ah, Jay has got to – Clayton – has big shoes to fill. Every day we’re going to be dogging him on, like, where’s the next release on this.”
On the night of Trump’s July address, Bannon texted CNN: “We need a National Security Emergency about the midterm elections immediately – this is a powerful predicate for that.”
Ty Cobb, a former White House attorney, now a sharp Trump critic, warned of the same while speaking to PBS following the president’s July TV address. “Well, I think tonight’s speech is intended to add the predicate that he needs to declare an emergency at or about the time of the elections,” he said.
ICE agents at polls is “a virtual certainty”, said Cobb, who questioned whether National Guard officers would also be presented. “Anything to intimidate minority voters, particularly immigrant voters, and also I think anything that allows them to try to seize voting machines, as Trump wanted to do in 2020, but [then-attorney general] Bill Barr explained to him there was just no basis for it.”
‘Noncitizen voting … is just not a widespread problem’
After Trump’s TV address, a White House “Government Transparency Task Force” – composed of members of the office of the director of national intelligence, the National Security Agency, the Central Intelligence Agency and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) – began releasing declassified “election integrity” documents on the White House website.
The first tranche included declassified intelligence memos which described electronic voting machine vulnerabilities, foreign access to state voter registration data and foreign digital manipulation strategies. Much of the material was already known to the public and amounted to a US intelligence assessment that found no evidence Beijing altered the 2020 vote, which Trump lost.
A week later, Trump and his allies quickly seized on an announcement from Mikie Sherrill, the New Jersey governor, that 6,600 non-citizens had registered to vote because of a software error. While fewer than 400 of them voted, the disclosure was used to escalate false claims that there are scores of noncitizens on the voter rolls.
On 31 July, DHS released a public notice arguing that New Jersey’s administrative errors demonstrated a need for standardized federal oversight.
The taskforce also declassified documents in a Michigan case where the FBI investigated suspected fraudulent voter registrations by a get-out-the-vote organization, in which no criminal charges were filed, and investigative material related to a data scrape of voter information in Maricopa county, Arizona.
The pace of releases has been accelerating.
On Monday, the taskforce declassified and released investigative files related to an investigation into Chinese intelligence, which disclosed how disgraced former Democratic US representative Eric Swalwell had told FBI agents how he had “occasionally hooked up” with Christine Fang, a Chinese national allegedly engaged in a political influence campaign.
On Tuesday, the US Census Bureau released a brief claiming it had identified 24,000 noncitizens voting in the 2020 election in a preliminary match of 128m records. It did not reveal its methodology and was sharply criticized by democracy advocates.
“This alleged analysis based on census data fails the laugh test,” said David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation and Research. “The administration does not provide a sufficient explanation of how it arrived at these numbers – and for good reason.”
Branch, of Elias Law Group, suggested the Trump administration is “searching for” the legal basis for an executive order. “I think they believe there may be one. I think such a document just doesn’t exist, because the fact is our elections are secure,” she said. “Noncitizen voting in our elections is just not a widespread problem … All of the fear and narrative around that issue is just completely unfounded, and it’s really just to stoke fear and lay the groundwork for future action.”
In July, DHS also released an analysis arguing that 278,000 noncitizens are registered to vote in federal elections. It did not reveal its methodology for identifying the noncitizens, either, or disclose how confident its officials were in their assessment. The tool it used to flag noncitizens on voter rolls is known to be inaccurate.
‘The founders recognized the risk of centralizing power’
Asked about the possibility of an executive order declaring a national emergency on elections, the White House did not rule it out, refusing to comment on hypotheticals.
“Extreme liberal Democrats are keeping Americans from having full confidence in their elections by refusing to vote for the Save America Act,” said Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, referring to legislation that would enforce a crackdown on voting. “The American people overwhelmingly support this commonsense legislation that ensures Americans, and Americans only, decide our elections. President Trump is absolutely right: we fix this now, or we lose our country.”
The Save America Act would require states to submit their voter rolls to federal inspection, effectively give DHS the power to de-register anyone it deemed ineligible to vote. The act would also sharply curtail mail-in voting – a practice Trump repeatedly criticized, but has reportedly done himself as recently as in this week’s Florida Republican primary – and require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote and a narrow set of photo IDs to cast a ballot.
“I mean, we’ve been closely monitoring what the administration is saying,” said Branch, who sees the rhetoric itself as an act of intimidation.
“The constitution is extremely clear on this, and the founders recognized the risk of centralizing power over elections in the executive branch,” she added. “Very helpful, in terms of litigation to push back on these types of efforts.”

Is Russia preparing an offensive against the Kyiv region: Zelenskyy named the conditions and a possible direction
Kyiv • UNN
Russia may try to advance into the Chernihiv and Kyiv regions to create a buffer zone. At present, there is no strike force near the border.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated on August 23 that, in the future, Russia may attempt to launch an offensive from Bryansk Oblast in the Chernihiv–Kyiv direction, in particular to create a so-called "buffer zone." At the same time, there is currently no troop grouping near Ukraine's northern border necessary for such an operation, reports UNN.
Details
According to Zelenskyy, the Kremlin's further plans may depend on the situation in eastern Ukraine and the launch of a new wave of mobilization in the Russian Federation.
If he has the success there that he is counting on, then he may redistribute forces to another direction. For example, to create a "buffer zone." There could also be an operation in the Chernihiv–Kyiv regions
Zelenskyy noted that this concerns a possible offensive from Russian territory, specifically Bryansk Oblast. At the same time, Ukraine currently does not see the number of personnel necessary there to conduct a large-scale offensive operation, although it is detecting Russian military equipment near the border.
The president also stated that after the elections to the State Duma of the Russian Federation, the Russian authorities may carry out an additional mobilization of around 300,000 people. In the view of the Ukrainian leadership, most of this manpower could primarily be sent to eastern Ukraine, where Russia seeks to intensify its offensive actions.
Context
Ukrainian authorities have been reporting for several months on Russia's possible plans to intensify combat operations in northern Ukraine.
In May, Zelenskyy chaired a meeting of the Staff of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief dedicated to possible scenarios of Russian offensive operations in the Chernihiv–Kyiv direction. At the time, the president said that Ukrainian intelligence was analyzing several options for the enemy's actions, including from the territory of Bryansk Oblast and Belarus.
At the end of June, the then Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, Oleksandr Syrskyi, stated that the most likely scenario could be a Russian offensive from Bryansk Oblast specifically toward Chernihiv Oblast, rather than directly toward Kyiv. According to him, one of Russia's objectives could be to seize part of the border territory and force Ukraine to redeploy reserves there from other sections of the front.
At the same time, in August, Ukrainian intelligence and the State Border Guard Service reported that they had not detected the formation of a Russian strike force near the northern border.
Vadym Skibitskyi, Deputy Chief of the Main Intelligence Directorate of the Ministry of Defense, noted that, to create such a force, Russia would first need to carry out an additional mobilization. According to an assessment by Ukrainian intelligence, if it is conducted in the autumn of 2026, preparing a sufficient number of troops for a large-scale operation could take several months.
The State Border Guard Service also emphasized that it is not currently observing a buildup of Russian forces either near the border with Bryansk Oblast or on the territory of Belarus. At the same time, Ukraine continues to strengthen the defenses of its northern regions, fortifications, and border protection system.
Reminder
At the beginning of August, State Border Guard Service spokesperson Andrii Demchenko reported that the enemy was planning an invasion in Chernihiv Oblast in order to divert the Armed Forces of Ukraine.

How the deadliest Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak can be stopped
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
10:00:20 UTC
19:00:20 KST

How the deadliest Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak can be stopped
The priorities are clear: reach every affected area, protect frontline workers, and turn commitments into action.
Each time we travel to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), we first go to listen.
In Bunia, we have met dozens of community representatives: survivors, women, young people, local organisations, health workers and leaders from affected areas. Their message is direct: involve us. We know our communities. We know where families seek care, how information moves and why trust is breaking down. Give us the means to help drive the response. They are right.
Ebola spreads through communities and communities hold the knowledge required to stop it. They can identify illness early, alert health teams, help identify and trace contacts, challenge dangerous rumours and support families through access to treatment and safe, dignified burials. The response always moves faster when communities lead alongside national authorities and health workers.
One hundred days ago, the government of the DRC declared the country’s 17th Ebola outbreak, following confirmation of the Bundibugyo virus. WHO subsequently declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern, followed by Africa CDC’s declaration of a Public Health Emergency of Continental Security.
The scale of the emergency is immense. As of August 21, the DRC has reported 5,290 confirmed cases and 2,516 deaths across 56 health zones. This is now the second-largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded and it is moving faster than any previous one. It is being fuelled by insecurity caused by decades of armed conflict that have undermined law, order and social services, and displaced more than a million people.
At the centre of the response are the people who show up every day. Health workers care for patients. Laboratory teams identify the virus. Contact tracers follow its path. Community health workers build trust where fear and misinformation have taken hold. Burial teams help families honour their loved ones safely and with dignity.
They are working under extraordinary pressure, often in insecure and hard-to-reach areas. Some have contracted Ebola in the line of duty.
Their service must be met with action: safety, protective equipment, training, sufficient medical supplies, timely payment, psychosocial support and access to rapid diagnosis and high-quality supportive care if they fall ill. The safety of frontline workers is central to stopping transmission.
The response has made progress. Under the leadership of national authorities, Congolese responders, WHO, Africa CDC and partners have expanded surveillance, deployed laboratories, supported treatment centres, reinforced infection prevention and delivered essential supplies.
Neighbouring Uganda has interrupted locally acquired transmission of the virus. Several health zones in northern Ituri and South Kivu provinces in the DRC have also interrupted transmission. These experiences prove that the outbreak can be stopped more quickly when rapid detection, decisive national leadership and close cooperation with communities break the chains of transmission.
But the continued emergency in the rest of Ituri province and five other provinces demands urgently scaled-up action.
To turn the corner, surveillance teams are being expanded and equipped to detect cases early and rapidly identify contacts. Safe clinical care and infection prevention measures are being increased wherever people seek treatment.
More risk communication and community engagement teams are being deployed to reach out to communities to empower them to participate in the response and address barriers to care. More safe and dignified burial teams are working to prevent transmission associated with deaths. Special efforts are being made to reach vulnerable populations and communities in insecure and hard-to-reach areas.
But despite all these efforts, more is needed. We need to scale our response by two to three times current capacities, across all the response pillars.
Health facilities also require urgent protection from infection. As of August 20, 158 health workers have been infected and 45 have died. Every facility in an affected or high-risk area needs trained staff, protective equipment, clean water, sanitation and functioning infection-prevention systems.
National and local teams need predictable funding for surveillance, laboratories, treatment, logistics, infection prevention and community engagement. Frontline workers must be paid on time. Local organisations need direct support to work consistently with communities. Supplies must arrive before stocks run out.
Delayed financing costs lives. Fragmented financing leaves gaps. Ebola exploits both. On the ground, we at WHO and Africa CDC have established tight integration among health and relief organisations working with the government. Donors therefore need to support and enhance that integration, rather than back siloed and disconnected efforts.
Cross-border coordination also must remain strong. People move within and between countries to trade, work, study, seek care and support their families. Borders must serve as bridges for coordinated public health action. This does not require closing borders or imposing blanket travel and trade restrictions. Such measures can disrupt response operations and livelihoods without stopping transmission. The priority is coordinated surveillance, rapid information-sharing and prepared health services along movement routes.
The first 100 days have made the priorities clear.
Find every case. Follow every contact. Break every chain of transmission, protect every health and frontline worker, save lives and ensure that no community is left behind. Bring testing and treatment closer to every affected community. Bolster cross-border coordination. Scale up international support. Turn every pledge into action.
WHO and Africa CDC will continue working with the DRC, neighbouring countries, communities and partners to deliver on these priorities. Our responsibility is to bring the full strength of international and continental cooperation behind the nationally-led response.
Uganda and areas in DRC have shown how the course of the outbreak can be turned, through rapid detection, decisive action and close cooperation with communities. But these measures must be delivered at scale. Success depends on sustained national leadership, continental solidarity and international support. We must rise to this challenge, together.
The views expressed in this article are the authors’ own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Why Chinese media says US historians are giving ‘ammunition’ to separatists
As ethnic issues grow ever more sensitive, Beijing is alleging the New Qing History movement seeks to fracture the nation
China has stepped up its offensive against a US-born school of thought on China’s last imperial dynasty, accusing it of providing “theoretical ammunition” for attempts to divide the country.
An article published by the state-run China Ethnic News last Monday warned that New Qing History was “seriously eroding the historical foundations of the community for the Chinese nation in the real world” and should be “forcefully refuted”.
That marked the latest broadside in a two-year campaign by the outlet to attack the loosely defined scholarly movement, which began to take shape in the late 1980s.
Rather than being an organised movement with a unified doctrine, New Qing History refers to a broad revisionist approach to understanding how the Manchu-led Qing managed both China’s Han majority and the many other ethnic groups under their rule.
Scholars taking this approach have drawn on Manchu-language sources to question the long-held assumption that “Sinicisation” – the idea that conquerors of China and even neighbouring peoples were transformed by Chinese culture, often portrayed as a spontaneous and largely one-way process – was the only explanation.

Why More Medical Testing Doesn’t Always Make Us Healthier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
10:00:03 UTC
19:00:03 KST

Today, if you wish, you can go get a staggering amount of granular data about your health without your doctor’s involvement. All on your own, you can get an MRI of your entire body, a CT of your coronary calcium, an ultrasound of your blood vessels, and maybe someday an immersion ultrasound in a spa.
Direct-to-consumer medical imaging tests are a huge and growing business worth billions of dollars. Over 100,000 Americans are already customers. But do these test results actually make us healthier?
As a radiologist, a doctor specialized in the alchemy of turning information into health, I translate data hidden in images into words that motivate behavior to promote healthier, longer lives. Because it is central to what we do, radiologists have grappled for decades with the question of whether and how information improves health. It turns out to be surprisingly complicated.
In order to make a difference in someone’s health, the test must accurately predict or diagnose a condition, resulting in a change in mindset and behavior, and that change in mindset and behavior must produce a better outcome than not doing the test.
For example, whole-body MRI of the general public, a test not recommended by any medical guideline, medical society, or payer, creates information by taking a picture of your body. That information is accurate for some diseases but not others. It might change your mind by finding something you didn’t know about, like a small mass in your kidney or thyroid gland, which then might change what you or your doctor does. For example, your doctor might order another test to better understand if the mass is important or perform surgery to take it out.
This seems logical. But the reason whole-body MRI of the general public isn’t recommended while other screening tests are is because in the absence of evidence, it is believed to be unlikely to produce a better outcome than doing nothing at all.
Many people think, as I once did, that early diagnosis always improves health. That logic is especially intuitive for an early diagnosis of cancer. But in many cases, that intuition, however understandable, can be wrong. Finding something with a diagnostic test might not help, despite creating an illusion that it does.
For both examples I gave—small thyroid masses, small kidney masses—it has been well documented that aggressive efforts to treat them, despite many being cancer, does not help most people. Isn’t that strange? Yet despite ourselves, we keep finding and removing them.
That’s the tricky thing with diagnostic tests. It’s terrifically hard to unsee something. For those who receive no benefit from treatment, only secondary harm results: surgical pain and complications, the anxiety of a scary diagnosis, and financial burden.
There are numerous non-intuitive examples like this in which only in retrospect do we realize patients have been harmed because a diagnostic test and its downstream actions were promoted to millions before confirming things worked as intended. This is why scientists and medical professionals are so obsessive about evidence and statistics. It’s really hard to know if something is hurting or helping if we rely on common sense.
The likelihood of benefit and the likelihood of harm matter tremendously. For example, if whole-body MRI is performed on a high-risk patient with a cancer-causing genetic syndrome, it is much more likely to create health benefits than if it were to be performed in the general population. This is one of the paradoxical things about diagnostic tests. It’s not just about test accuracy. Equally important is the people being tested, because baseline risk strongly influences the benefits.
Harm is often caused not by the test itself, but from actions taken to manage the information of unknown significance it produces. It is in this way that a seemingly harmless test can hurt people. We do tests to find things, and when we find things, we commonly act, even when we shouldn’t, because we aren’t rational decision-makers.
Direct-to-consumer testing will change how medicine is practiced. It empowers us to make personal decisions about our health and generates novel, complex information that will unlock scientific breakthroughs.
When buying one of these tests, we should pay attention to what the company is claiming. Is their test a curiosity, an entertainment product, a research tool, or clinical care? The lines are often intentionally blurry.
The need for scientific support, informed disclosure, and regulatory compliance increases as the test moves from curiosity toward clinical care. If the test has only been shown to provide information or to make a diagnosis, or has only been shown to improve health in patients with specific risk factors different from our own, we should be skeptical. As they say, buyer beware.
Many companies encourage us to assume their test improves our health. In such cases, the information we are buying may help us, hurt us, or be a placebo and do nothing at all.

Barabak: Ripple or blue wave? This race will test Democratic strength in November
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Ripple or blue wave? This race will test Democratic strength in November
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- The contest in Nevada’s 2nd Congressional District should be a shoo-in for Republicans.
- But a problematic candidate, inflation and Trump’s unpopularity give Democrats not-far-fetched hopes for a massive upset.
The high desert is not typically a place you look for a wave. But in the vast expanse between the Sierra Nevada and Utah border, a not-exactly-wide-open race for Congress is testing whether a blue wave, should one come November, is ankle-high or something more akin to a political tsunami.
Nevada’s 2nd District has been represented by just four lawmakers since its creation more than 40 years ago. All those representatives have been Republicans.
November’s contest should be another shoo-in for the GOP and its nominee, David Flippo. The district, which takes in northern Nevada, is overwhelmingly white and rural, which makes it solidly conservative. In 2024, Donald Trump beat Kamala Harris by a decisive 56% to 42%; only Washoe County, home to Reno, kept things that close. Trump won other portions of the district by 50 percentage points or more.
But inflation, Trump’s sagging approval rating and other factors — northern resentment toward southern Nevada, where Flippo lived until fairly recently, the refusal of the incumbent to support his party’s nominee — offer Democrats the not-entirely-far-fetched hope of a major upset.
Barabak: This Las Vegas Republican had high hopes for Trump. But a ‘Trump slump’ made life worse
Aaron Mahan, who’s spent decades as a server on and off the Strip, says inflation and Trump’s pugnacious immigration and foreign policies have chased tourists away. He’s feeling it in his wallet.
“It will be an interesting summer and fall,” Mark Amodei, who has represented the district for 15 years, wrote on social media after the June primary. “But I believe it’s fair to say that CD-2, for the first time in its history, isn’t a Republican guarantee.”
That’s just about the kindest thing the congressman has had to say about his would-be successor.
All of which make the sprawling district in Nevada’s rough and rocky Great Basin an improbable political bellwether. A win on such forbidding terrain would almost certainly mean a nationwide Democratic gain of 30 or more seats in November; they need to flip just three to take control of the House.
Flippo, 63, a 25-year Air Force veteran and Trump stalwart, arrived in the district from Las Vegas. He ran for Congress there in 2024, losing in the Republican primary. He was preparing for a second try in the Democratic-leaning 4th District when Amodei unexpectedly announced his retirement in February. So Flippo hightailed it north to run in the far more hospitable 2nd District.
He took on the favored candidate of Amodei and others in the GOP establishment, James Settelmeyer, a former minority leader of the state Senate. Backed by a constellation of MAGA celebrities, Flippo waged a fiercely negative campaign, accusing “Tampon Jim” of voting to put menstrual products in boys’ bathrooms and coddling undocumented immigrants, among other distortions. With Trump’s endorsement, Flippo handily defeated Settelmeyer and 11 other primary opponents.
“”Absolutely scurrilous campaign against ... one of the nicest guys around,” Amodei said afterward, on the program “Nevada Newsmakers.” “The voters are never wrong. But guess what? Mark Amodei’s not endorsing [Flippo.] I wish him all the best. No way. No, thank you.”
Apart from his exceedingly short-term residency in the district, questions have also been raised about Flippo’s opaque finances. He has lent his campaign more than $1.6 million and failed to provide the personal disclosure information required of federal candidates. There is also no record of Flippo filing the required statement during his 2024 campaign, according to the Washington news outlet NOTUS.
In addition, it reported that Flippo was fired from a job in the financial services industry after his company accused him of violating policies and regulations.
So, a carpetbagger with a sketchy history.
Flippo’s main opponent is Teresa Benitez-Thompson, 48, a longtime Reno resident, former member of the state Assembly and a relatively moderate Democrat. Those credentials also buoy Democratic hopes. The party’s congressional campaign committee has, for the first time in decades, added Nevada’s 2nd District to its target list, though it remains to be seen how much time and money national Democrats commit to the race.
To prevail, Benitez-Thompson would have to defy political gravity, which is to say overcome the reflexive partisanship that has typified politics in this age of deep voter polarization.
In the last two midterm elections, according to the Pew Research Center, more than 90% of Republican and Republican-leaning voters supported GOP candidates for the House. In other words, the kind of crossover voters that Benitez-Thompson needs to win have become rare indeed.
““Trump is a huge liability for Republicans; there is no question that the GOP is going to have huge turnout problems, meaning that in a lot of races, Democrats are going to greatly exceed expectations,” the veteran election handicapper Charlie Cook wrote in a recent midterm analysis. “But converting Republican voters to actually back a Democrat — even for a day — is so much harder now.”
Jon Ralston, one of Nevada’s leading political savants, agreed.
The former Senate majority leader tried multiple times to have Jon Ralston fired before finally succeeding. Reid then turned to the veteran journalist to write his biography.
“Some of those rural Nevada voters would rather commit hara-kiri than vote for a Democrat,” Ralston said. (No, Japan’s ancient suicide ritual is not particularly associated with honor or custom in the cow counties, as Nevada’s lightly populated stretches are known. But you get the point.)
“I don’t think it’s impossible,” Ralston, founder and chief executive of the Nevada Independent news site, said of a Democratic upset. “But I remain skeptical.”
Here’s the thing, though, about wave elections — and, to be clear, your friendly political columnist is offering no predictions ahead of November. Like a massive ocean swell, which can bear all kinds of flotsam and jetsam ashore, a political wave that is big enough, broad enough and strong enough can carry all manner of unlikely candidates to victory.
Even in the bone-dry desert.

Unknown

-    Click here to listen to this article

- Democratic leaders, election officials and civic groups are preparing responses to potential Trump efforts to intimidate voters, seize ballots or deny the outcome of November’s midterms.
- Much of the work is being done quietly to avoid revealing too much of the strategy to the Trump administration or stoking unnecessary fear among voters.
Big-city mayors are giving poll workers panic buttons in case election skeptics question their work. County and state officials are gaming out responses to immigration raids near voting centers.
Lawyers for Democratic states and civic groups are pre-writing legal challenges to ballot seizures. And Democratic aides in Washington are preparing members of Congress to push back in the court of public opinion against any baseless claims of voter fraud in competitive districts.
Across California and the nation, civic organizations, voting rights advocates and Democratic leaders are preparing for a raft of potential actions by the Trump administration to interfere in, subvert or deny November’s midterm vote.
President Trump, an election denier for years, has without evidence described the U.S. election system as badly corrupted by fraud and dangerously vulnerable to both domestic and foreign interference.
He has said he would do “anything necessary” to have “honest elections,” and has tried since returning to office to unilaterally rewrite the rules for voting nationwide and wrest control of elections from the states through executive orders and other administrative measures.
Now, he has declined to rule out additional and unprecedented steps to force his will on the November election, including through emergency declarations and military deployments, and in February suggested Republicans should simply take over voting in blue states.
Election experts say there is no evidence of widespread voter fraud in American elections, despite Trump’s allies searching for years.
Much of the work to resist any Trump interference or power grab is being done quietly to avoid revealing too much of the strategy to the Trump administration or stoking unnecessary fear among voters.
It is designed to match what Trump’s opponents see as his three-part “interference playbook” — to “deceive” voters before the election, “disrupt” the vote itself and “deny” any unfavorable results after, said Justin Vail of Protect Democracy, a prominent litigant against the administration.
“The threats are real,” Vail said, “but the preparation is larger and more coordinated than ever before.”
A convicted election denier went to prison. Now, she might help run elections in a California county
Shasta County registrar of voters Clint Curtis said he wants to hire Tina Peters, the former Colorado county clerk convicted of charges related to election tampering.
The scenarios being planned for include the president deploying troops or immigration agents to polling sites to intimidate voters, fomenting unrest as a pretext to declare a national emergency, claiming fraud in the ballot counts of key congressional races or commanding the U.S. Postal Service to intervene in mail ballot delivery.
All told, the efforts amount to an unprecedented exercise to ensure the nation’s elections are safe from its own federal government.
They also reflect a deterioration in trust between states and counties overseeing elections, voting rights and pro-democracy advocates and a federal administration that has denigrated their work and tried to take control of voting away from states.
As public frustration with the economy mounts and Trump’s approval rating sinks, Democrats have become hopeful their party will retake power in Congress. Trump, meanwhile, has suggested that alleged election integrity problems will be the culprit if Republicans lose.
In California, 61% of voters recently identified federal inference in November as a “major concern,” according to a UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies poll co-sponsored by The Times.
“We are taking this threat really seriously,” said Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), who helped form a Senate task force to prepare. “Politically, I’m very optimistic about the midterms. But I’m also deeply concerned with the president’s willingness to interfere with them — and the fact that, unlike even in 2020, where there were at least some people around him to try to constrain what he was doing, all those people are gone.”
Much of the work is legal preparation among Democratic state attorneys general and lawyers with leading civic organizations. Nothing is being ruled out after Trump’s supporters, at his goading, violently attacked the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, following his 2020 election loss to Joe Biden.
Other preparation is political, as members of Congress, mayors and other elected officials position themselves to use their bully pulpits and legislative powers to punch back. And grassroots campaigns are also unfolding, as community leaders recruit voters to defend their local elections, including online.
“This is an all-hands-on-deck task,” said Skye Perryman, president of the nonpartisan legal organization Democracy Forward. “We’re anticipating scenarios we haven’t seen before in the United States.”
Trump, who has never accepted his 2020 loss to Biden despite scores of reviews and audits confirming the result, has consistently sought to undermine Americans’ trust in elections, telling the nation in a prime-time speech last month that the voting system was “broken” and claiming that the SAVE America Act, a strict Republican-proposed voter ID and citizenship measure, is necessary to fix it.
The White House said it wouldn’t respond to hypothetical questions about the midterm election, but said anyone who breaks voting laws will be held accountable. Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, blamed “extreme liberal Democrats” for undermining U.S. confidence in elections by blocking the SAVE America Act, which Trump has failed to push through Congress.
Bis claimed voters support such changes, and said “President Trump is absolutely right: We fix this now, or we lose our country.”
Causes for concern
The fears of interference are driven by Trump’s long record of election denial; his recent insistence that the midterms are vulnerable to both domestic fraud and foreign interference; his success installing loyalists and fellow election deniers in powerful positions throughout his government; and his current administration’s many attempts to usurp control over state voting processes, including through executive orders, lawsuits and legislation.
Trump and his allies have sued to compel blue states to turn over voter rolls; seized ballots in Georgia; tried to limit mail voting via new U.S. Postal Service rules; pushed stricter citizenship and voter ID requirements via executive order and in Congress; diminished independent agencies tasking with helping states secure elections; kicked off a nationwide gerrymandering effort to boost Republican chances in the House; and threatened to imprison Democratic leaders who stand in their way.
Some analysts saw Trump’s speech last month as laying the groundwork for greater intervention in November, and he raised further alarm this month by entertaining a suggestion from conservative radio host and election conspiracy theorist Wayne Allyn Root that the president has “the right to declare a national security emergency” to unilaterally enforce new voting restrictions.
“Stranger things have happened,” Trump responded.
The White House has previously downplayed the likelihood of immigration agents being deployed to polling locations, but Trump has refused to rule it out. Legal experts say such a move would probably be swiftly blocked by courts, as would any unlawful deployment of military troops to polls.
Some voting experts said Trump’s efforts shouldn’t be blown out of proportion, particularly given federal courts’ dim view of them to date.
Californians are more concerned about the Trump administration interfering in the state’s midterm elections than they are about voter fraud, noncitizens voting illegally or foreign interference, according to a new poll.
David Becker, executive director of the nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation & Research, noted Trump’s executive orders on elections were blocked, the Justice Department is 0 for 23 in cases demanding state voter rolls, and the primaries have run smoothly with high turnout — showing the president is “having very little effect.”
Kim Alexander, president of the California Voter Foundation, said it is “important that people be aware that there are threats, but to not let those threats be debilitating” or prevent them from voting.
Civic experts are urging regular voters to help debunk misinformation about voting within their communities. Democracy Forward has asked people to take one civic-minded action per day leading up to the election, while Indivisible, a progressive grassroots organization, is training volunteers nationwide to mount public push-back to any interference.
Coordination in Congress
A Senate aide who spoke with The Times on condition of anonymity said members of the Senate task force meet regularly to plan for as many potential forms of interference as possible — and that there is “no bottom” to what they’re considering.
Task force members are studying nuanced local election laws to understand how Congress members should respond to any federal interference in their home states, and working on “coordinated messaging” that all members can use in response to immigration raids or other broad interference, the aide said.
They are also reading “line by line” through recent legal decisions limiting National Guard deployments and other federal actions to identify any “loopholes” the administration might exploit.
They are paying particular attention to districts with competitive congressional races and where past problems have arisen. In California, they’ve studied the recent seizure of ballots by Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco and the criticism of slow ballot counting statewide, the aide said.
Schiff said the scenario he is “most concerned” about is one in which the president or his allies “seed” unrest in big cities to “give the president a pretext, Reichstag fire-like, to call out the military or invoke the Insurrection Act or call out ICE or Border Patrol.”
The Reichstag fire erupted in the German parliament four weeks after Adolf Hitler was sworn in as chancellor in 1933, and was used to justify a sweeping crackdown on political opponents and the suspension of civil liberties — ushering in Nazi rule.
Local elections administrators across California say they have been preparing for once unthinkable threats to the midterms, from their own federal government.
Schiff said lawsuits will be a necessary but “very imperfect remedy” in such a scenario, and Democrats will need to develop a more robust response combining “litigation with mobilization” and legislative oversight.
Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), the ranking Democrat on the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration, which has election oversight, is helping to create an election observer program for hotly contested races, and has warned his colleagues that he will call a vote on any election-related emergency Trump declares, so that they must co-sign or resist it.
Separately in the House, staffers have been building their own “road map” for how to deal with a laundry list of “terrible things that bad-faith actors who seek to subvert the election could do,” with a principal focus on any ways they might disrupt the Jan. 3 swearing in of new Congress members, said a House aide involved in the preparations there, who spoke with The Times on the condition of anonymity.
House staffers are also looking at how court imposed limits on Trump’s emergency powers might be “exploited, weaponized [or] ignored” by the administration, including the Justice Department.
A Justice Department spokesperson said the department is “working diligently” to fulfill the demands of Trump’s election-related executive order purporting to “strengthen the integrity of our elections,” which courts have blocked, and has “statutory authority to enforce our nation’s election laws, including through requesting state voter rolls,” which courts have also blocked.
Assistant Atty. Gen. Harmeet Dhillon, who heads the department’s civil rights division and has threatened local elections officials with legal consequences if they don’t comply with her voter roll demands, said her division “has a statutory mandate to enforce our federal voting rights laws, and ensuring the voting public’s confidence in the integrity of our elections is a top priority of this administration.”
State and local preparations
California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta said attorneys from his office and similar Democratic ones across the country are “hard at work planning, preparing, strategizing, researching, getting ready for all the different ways the Trump administration can break the law.”
That includes any attempts to seize ballots, deploy federal law enforcement or the military, or command the U.S. Postal Service to interfere with mail ballots, he said. “The right to vote is the right from which all other rights flow. It’s fundamental. We need to protect it.”
Dean Logan, registrar-recorder and county clerk for Los Angeles County, said he has a responsibility to ensure that “election operations remain secure and uninterrupted” no matter the threat, and is taking steps to do so, though he declined to address potential acts by Trump. Long Beach Mayor Rex Richardson said big cities are also preparing, including to prevent harassment of voters or election workers.
“Cities are where we host vote centers. It’s where the volunteers come from, where people go with their questions,” Richardson said. “We have to pay attention to national rhetoric. We have to be aware of anxiety that might — tensions that may — arise.”

Extreme weather hits Europe as wildfires, floods and storms force thousands to evacuate

18:59:53 KST

Extreme weather is hitting Europe, with wildfires in Serbia and Bosnia, floods and fires in Spain, and severe storms in Poland. Thousands have been evacuated as firefighters battle fires, floods and power cuts.
Europe continues to struggle with the consequences of extreme weather, with Serbia, Bosnia, Spain, and Poland all facing severe conditions.
In Serbia, the EU has sent helicopters and firefighters to support local crews battling a blaze that has engulfed more than 1,600 hectares of vegetation in the Deliblatska Pescara nature reserve, 60 kilometres east of Belgrade. The effort is also being assisted by a Russian Ilyushin Il-76 water bomber deployed since Thursday, alongside several Serbian army helicopters.
"The situation is extremely difficult," says Ivica Dacic, Serbia's Interior Minister, adding that "more than 400 people are deployed there on a daily basis."
The crisis extends further into the region, where a large fire broke out on Saturday in the border area between Bosnia and Croatia. Bosnian police closed the main highway connecting Trebinje in Bosnia to Dubrovnik in Croatia, forcing thousands of tourists to turn back and alter their holiday plans.
Several villages around the small town of Ivanica were evacuated as the flames approached homes, and local firefighters reported that some livestock was caught in the fire and burnt. Croatian firefighters from nearby Dubrovnik arrived to assist Bosnian crews in battling the forest fire, which is spreading over an area more than 16 kilometres in diameter across narrow, difficult-to-access terrain. Supported by helicopters, emergency teams continue to fight the blaze, but relentless heat and strong winds have pushed the fire further inland. The Trebinje area has not seen rain for months, leaving the parched landscape exceptionally vulnerable during one of the hottest and driest summers in recent history.
Wildfires and floods in Spain
Meanwhile, Spain has faced a weekend of contrasting weather extremes. Torrential rain and flooding in Tarragona left 11 people injured and disrupted road and rail services after more than 145 mm fell in some areas. Further strong thunderstorms are forecast across eastern and northeastern Spain, while an unusually powerful Atlantic low is bringing heavy rain to Galicia.
Elsewhere in the country, firefighters in Spain’s eastern Valencia region continued battling intense wildfires. A blaze broke out in the town of Segorbe late Thursday after a lightning strike and began spreading rapidly Friday afternoon as winds shifted, leading authorities to raise the wildfire emergency to Level 2.
Personnel from Spain’s Military Emergency Unit and local fire departments joined the response, while more than 1,000 residents from the nearby town of Gatova were forced to evacuate over fears for their homes. Supported by aerial resources, crews have since managed to stabilise the fire after it burned around 630 hectares. The events mark a sharp shift from extreme heat earlier in the week, when temperatures reached up to 44°C.
Poland struggled, but the situation is improving
Further north, severe weather has also struck Poland. Since Friday, storms have wreaked havoc across the country, with firefighters responding to more than 6,500 incidents.
The storms hit residents in many areas, forcing the precautionary evacuation of 12 scout camps amid floods and power cuts. Brigadier Karol Kroć from the State Fire Service told the Polish Press Agency that no injuries have been reported so far.
On Sunday, storms are still expected in northern Poland, as the Institute of Meteorology and Water Management has issued yellow weather warnings for two small regions, with a local forecast of heavy rainfall up to 30 litres per square metre and wind gusts of up to 70 kilometres per hour. Hail is also possible in some areas. Ho
However, the general weather in the country on Sunday has improved significantly. Therefore, the weather conditions across the rest of Poland are expected to be much calmer.

"In 1 year alone the robots competing have become twice as fast. This highlights the pace of advancement both in the market, and specifically in Chinese robotics," organisers of the World Humanoid Robot Games said.
Step aside, Usain Bolt, there's a new speed king in town - TienKung the robot.
The Chinese humanoid, manufactured by the Beijing Centre for Humanoid Robotics, ran the 100 metres in 9.39 seconds at the World Humanoid Robot Games on Saturday, beating the Jamaican great's 9.58 world record time - which he set at the Olympiastadion in Berlin in 2009.
"This is a hugely impressive feat," organisers of the Beijing robot games wrote in a post on X, noting that last year's winning time clocked in at 21.50 seconds.
"In 1 year alone the robots competing have become twice as fast. This highlights the pace of advancement both in the market, and specifically in Chinese robotics," they added.
The World Humanoid Robot Games, held in Beijing's "Ice Ribbon" stadium, is bringing together 666 teams and 2,056 robots from 16 countries as they compete across events including athletics, boxing, football, weightlifting, and gymnastics.
Video footage of the robots has been shared widely on social media over the last few days, particularly clips showing the humanoids slamming into large mats and slowly falling backwards at the end of races.
While the rather amusing clips have been entertaining viewers, organisers of the games say people should be impressed.
"It shows a pace of technological advancement that almost beggars belief," they said. "Only a year ago, at the last WHRG, robots were slow, ponderous machines that struggled to complete a track sprint. This year they are expected to obliterate world records. The pace that the Chinese robotics industry is advancing at, much like the robot in the video shows no sign of deceleration".
China has been leaning in hard to the humanoid robot industry, and investors appear to be on board.
Morgan Stanley Research has estimated that the humanoid market is likely to reach $5 trillion by 2050, with more than a billion of the robots potentially in use by then.
According to a report published by the bank last year, China is expected to have around 302.3 million humanoid robots in use by 2050.

Zelenskyy details rift with dismissed defense minister, saying some of his actions were misguided
