Iran has said that not “a single drop of oil” will leave the Persian Gulf and threatened to attack alternative export routes if neighboring states take part in the US economic pressure campaign against Tehran.
The warning comes after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Thursday called on Washington’s allies and other countries to choose sides and stop doing business with Iran, as the US prepares what he touted as “the greatest coordinated economic isolation in the history of the world.”
In an interview with state broadcaster IRIB which aired on Saturday, Mohsen Rezaei, the head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, urged other countries not to participate “in the economic war with America,” saying that otherwise Tehran would treat them as enemies.
“If the countries surrounding Iran join the Americans in the economic war, not a single drop of oil will leave the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, and we will also target other routes through which oil is exported from the Persian Gulf,” he said.
If US President Donald Trump “wants to do something, we will retaliate in a seismic manner,” Rezaei added.
On Thursday, Trump announced what he called the “most crushing economic operation against Iran,” describing it as an “Economic D-Day” and calling on US allies “to stand with the United States of America to isolate and defeat the Iran threat.”
The announcement came after a 60-day window for negotiating a peace agreement with Tehran expired on Monday without a breakthrough, prompting Trump to declare that the talks had ended.
Earlier on Wednesday, the UAE suspended economic ties with Iran after two ballistic missiles were fired at its territory. Tehran denied responsibility, describing the incident as an Israeli “false-flag operation.”
Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, which handles around a quarter of global seaborne oil and LNG trade, shortly after the US and Israel launched their joint bombing campaign against the Islamic Republic on February 28. The US Navy imposed its own blockade on Iranian ports in April and has since been guiding ships along routes that Tehran considers illegal.
Nearly 200 ships navigated the strait last week, up from 150 the previous week and just 40 two weeks earlier, bringing traffic to around 20% of pre-war levels, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations Center.
Kpler data showed that more than 80% of liquid cargo vessels crossing the strait over the past two weeks either used a US-backed route through Omani waters that Iran considers illegal or switched off their tracking systems, likely to use the same corridor. Five vessels were struck by Iranian projectiles during the past week, resulting in two reported casualties. All five ships were reportedly damaged but not lost.

Londoners find ‘horrendous’ cracks in their homes after successive heatwaves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
09:20:00 UTC
18:20:00 KST

Londoners find ‘horrendous’ cracks in their homes after successive heatwaves
LONDON – Londoners are facing historic levels of subsidence risk after five successive heat waves dried out the clay soil on which much of the city is built.
Insurance claims tied to subsidence – a phenomenon associated with bouts of hot, dry weather that shrink the soil and destabilise the foundations on which buildings stand – hit a record last quarter, according to data provided by the Association of British Insurers. On average, households claimed £20,000 (S$34,600) for the risk, more than in any previous quarter and a 15 per cent jump from the same period in 2025, the ABI said.
Laura Hughes, head of general insurance at the ABI, says the upward trend is likely to continue. “We expect to see more subsidence cases because of the hot weather,” she said in an interview.
Londoners have taken to social media to express their dismay. On Reddit, people offered personal accounts telling of “horrendous cracking” in their homes, and “doors sticking” due to subsidence.
One said it was “genuinely scary” to discover that their kitchen had moved as the foundations of the home shifted.
Another Reddit user described the response of a structural engineer they contacted for help. “Before I could finish explaining he laughed and said, ‘You and 20,000 other people in southeast London’,” the person wrote.
“It’s crazy, what’s happening now,” said Otso Lahtinen, chief executive of Geobear, an engineering firm that’s regularly called in to repair damage caused by subsidence. “It’s the new norm, and it seems it will happen more often in the next 20-30 years.”
Data provided by Aviva show that the areas of London that are most at risk are some of the English capital’s most sought after, namely the boroughs of Westminster, as well as Kensington and Chelsea. While subsidence has been affecting homes in the British capital for decades, climate change is making it worse. London clay is especially sensitive to fluctuations in moisture, expanding when wet and contracting when dry.
The threat of subsidence in the UK is concentrated in and around London as well as in parts of the southeast. In the four years through 2025, insurance payouts for subsidence damage soared roughly 90 per cent to reach a record £297 million, according to data provided by the ABI.
The most vulnerable properties are Victorian or Edwardian homes that were built directly onto the upper layers of London clay. By contrast, modern office buildings in the City of London and Canary Wharf have much deeper foundations and are therefore less exposed to such risks.
Subsidence is part of a long list of heat-related challenges to which the UK is now struggling to adapt. Over the past months, extreme heat has forced schools to close, led bus drivers to go on strike, and seen banks relax in-office work requirements to protect staff from unbearably hot commutes. Most of England has been gripped by drought and the country’s hospitals have shown signs of buckling under the strain.
London Mayor Sadiq Khan has warned that the city will need to turn to private investors to help fund the cost of dealing with the impact of rising temperatures. His office estimates that London now faces an annual bill as high as £36 billion into the 2050s in order to prepare the city for what climate change has in store.
“The impact that climate change is having is undeniable,” said Hughes of the ABI.
Subsidence can devalue a property by an average of 20 per cent-25 per cent, according to the Federation of Master Builders. In some cases, homeowners prefer to cover the cost themselves rather than wade through complicated claims processes. The traditional engineering fix for subsidence damage, known as underpinning, can cost anywhere from £20,000 to more than £100,000.
The development represents a particular risk to insurers, with subsidence claims making up an ever larger chunk of the payouts they need to make to customers.
The phenomenon poses “a significant challenge for UK home insurers,” says Cherry Chan, a partner at Deloitte. The consultancy has warned that UK home insurers risk losses in 2026 due in part to the trend.
Along with flash floods and wildfires, subsidence is becoming “an increasingly material climate-related risk,” Chan said. It requires that insurers display “careful consideration in long-term exposure and risk management strategies.”
Extreme weather patterns in 2026 “will not only impact more new claims in this year, but could cause claims deteriorations for unsettled subsidence claims reported in the past,” she added. That includes 2025, which was a so-called surge year for subsidence impacts.
Fresh estimates from the British Geological Survey indicate that under what is known as the RCP 4.5 emissions scenario – reflecting a trajectory that closely aligns with current climate policies – 1.8 million properties, or about 5 per cent of the UK total, are “highly likely or extremely likely” to be susceptible to shrink-swell subsidence by 2070. Under a higher emissions scenario, the figure rises to 4.2 million, or 11 per cent, of British properties. Areas most at risk are densely-populated parts of London, Kent and south-east of England.
The development has the potential to lead to “increased insurance premiums, depressed house prices and, in some cases, engineering works to stabilise land or property, replacement of utility pipeworks and unstable transport infrastructure,” according to the BGS.
Geobear, which tackles subsidence by injecting resin under buildings, says it’s received more homeowner inquiries this summer than ever before. It says insurance clients have confirmed a similar trend, with one telling Geobear it had received 180 claims on a single day, which is significantly more than normal.
“It’s a pretty severe situation,” said Lahtinen, the CEO. “If you’re looking to trade, sell or buy property, this is a trend you can’t ignore.” Bloomberg

Is the US seeing a turning point in obesity rates?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
09:20:00 UTC
18:20:00 KST

Is the US seeing a turning point in obesity rates?
August 23, 2026
The United States has been grappling with an obesity epidemic since the late 1970s, but there is growing evidence that the constantly climbing obesity rates are beginning to drop.
"We're seeing signs that there's going to be a turning point," said Benjamin Rader, an epidemiologist at Boston Children's Hospital and at Harvard Medical School who conducts research into health trends using large datasets. In 2024, he and his colleagues published a study based on data from more than 16 million adults, which suggested there had been a decline in obesity prevalence in 2023 — for the first time in more than 10 years.
The National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey also indicated a slight decline between 2021 and 2023. More recent surveys have also provided evidence of declining figures.
Use of Ozempic, Wegovy and Zepbound skyrockets
This comes as a series of new drugs, which some people are using for weight loss, have come onto the market. The use of the GLP-1 agonist drugs Ozempic, Wegovy and Zepbound has increased rapidly in recent years in the US, with prescriptions more than quadrupling between 2021 and early 2026.
Some of the active ingredients in these drugs were originally developed to treat Type 2 diabetes by mimicking a naturally occurring intestinal hormone to promote a feeling of fullness and to slow down gastric emptying. This has led to many patients losing a significant amount of weight.
For Rader, "it seemed like it [the impact of this medicine] was bound to show up in the data" and that it was possible to be "moderately confident that drugs themselves were having an effect."
'Strong evidence showing significant decline in obesity'
For Peminda Cabandugama, an endocrinologist and spokesperson for The Obesity Society, which provides support to professionals in the obesity field, "there is strong evidence showing that there is a significant decline in obesity."
In a written statement to DW, he said the "general opinion is that GLP-1 medications and their combinations and their increased use as well as the recent attention put on the importance of weight management have played a large and direct role in this reduction in obesity prevalence."
But for Rader there is no definitive proof of a causal relationship. He has no doubt that the drugs have led to weight loss in many people at an individual level, but he told DW that it was too soon to say whether it "will lead to a plateau, […] a decrease […] or a slower decrease in the next 20 years" and what the effect on the general population might be.
Cabandugama thinks the current figures might also have been influenced by lifestyle changes during and after the COVID-19 pandemic, and points out that "these trends are likely a confluence of multiple elements that include the increased use of anti-obesity medications, post-pandemic behavioral changes, increased awareness about the importance of weight management etc."
Is the decline temporary?
Some researchers in the US don't believe obesity rates will decline permanently. A study by the Institute of Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) at the University of Washington in Seattle predicts a rise in rates through 2035 and suggests that the proportion of obese adults could increase from 42.5% in 2022 to 46.9% in 2035.
Though Rader doesn't necessarily consider such predictions to be wrong, he pointed out that many prediction models are based on data from before the boom in GLP-1 drugs and might not take into account their potential effects. In an article for the Journal of the American Medical Association, he warned that the models could overestimate the future burden of obesity.
The authors of the IHME study have not entirely dismissed this criticism, but they did point out that to date only a small proportion of obese people use such drugs and that many patients discontinue treatment within a year. They added that some people gain weight again after initially losing it, and more representative data was needed to assess whether such drugs will have a lasting effect on obesity rates.
Cabandugama has also urged caution, saying that while there are currently strong signs of a decline, "the general consensus is that it is still too early to tell whether this is a true trend reversal."
Consequences of decline in obesity rates would be far-reaching
Though for a long time, obesity was viewed primarily as a result of an individual's lifestyle, it has since become well-known that this complex chronic condition is caused by a combination of biological, genetic, social and psychological factors.
If the US were at a turning point, the consequences would be far-reaching. Weight loss in obese people does not only reduce their risk of related health problems, but also contributes to greater mobility, more independence and a higher quality of life.
For Cabandugama, "the health outcomes to improve first would be betterments in cardiometabolic parameters: blood glucose levels (Type 2 diabetes mellitus), cardiovascular outcomes, fatty liver, obstructive sleep apnea etc.," which in the long term could also reduce pressure on the healthcare system.
Regardless of whether rates are on the decline, Rader said "obesity still remains a huge public health crisis in America that deserves attention, deserves funding, and deserves alternative solutions, especially as we think about how GLP-1s are not accessible to all Americans based on price and other factors."
"A turning point does not mean that we're suddenly in the clear and that we don't have to worry about this thing anymore," he said.
This article was originally written in German.

Pentagon wants new family of maneuverable hypersonic weapons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
09:18:44 UTC
18:18:44 KST

- The Strategic Capabilities Office will hold a classified Industry Day September 14-16, 2026, in Chantilly, Virginia, on a new hypersonic weapons family.
- The briefings will prepare contractors for a solicitation covering multiple Phase 1 Concept Development prototype agreements under 10 U.S.C. § 4022.
The Pentagon is preparing to build a new family of hypersonic weapons designed to maneuver past enemy air defenses, and it wants defense contractors to help design them.
The Department of War’s Strategic Capabilities Office disclosed the effort in a special notice posted August 21 on the primary U.S. federal contracting portal, ahead of a classified Industry Day set for September 14 to September 16, 2026, in Chantilly, Virginia. The notice describes a family of next-generation, maneuverable, and precise hypersonic weapons capable of defeating advanced defensive architectures. Multiple programs will fall under the effort, each using different stand-off ranges, booster sizes, and payload packages to strike a variety of target types.
Hypersonic weapons travel at Mach 5 or faster, more than a mile per second, and can change course during flight. That combination makes them difficult for existing radar and missile defense systems to track and intercept. A ballistic missile arcs high into space along a predictable path. A hypersonic weapon instead flies low enough and fast enough to occupy a gap that neither ground-based air defenses nor space-based interceptors currently cover well. That gap is the core problem the Offensive Fires programs appear built to exploit.
The Industry Day will brief contractors on program specifics in a classified environment, ahead of a future solicitation. SCO plans to award multiple Phase 1 Concept Development Other Transactions for Prototype, a contracting mechanism authorized under 10 U.S.C. § 4022 that lets the Department of War move faster than traditional procurement rules allow. Sessions will run at three classification tiers across the three days, from Secret up to Top Secret with Special Access Required, with separate one-on-one meetings available for companies that request them.
The notice does not disclose funding levels, target production quantities, specific range requirements, or how many distinct weapon programs fall under Offensive Fires. It also does not name the individual systems that will be discussed behind closed doors in Chantilly.
SCO is a Pentagon office built to move fast. Director Jay Dryer has described its mission as identifying, analyzing, and prototyping disruptive uses of new and existing systems, with a goal of fielding capabilities within three to five years rather than the decade or more a standard acquisition program can take. The office sits alongside the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, the Defense Innovation Unit, and several other technology organizations that the Department of War folded into its Research and Engineering directorate this year.
Offensive Fires is not the Pentagon’s only hypersonic push. The Army’s Long Range Hypersonic Weapon, known as Dark Eagle, has moved toward operational fielding in 2026 and took part in the multinational Valiant Shield 2026 exercise. The Air Force is separately funding the Air-Launched Rapid Response Weapon and the Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile, and the Joint Hypersonics Transition Office has awarded research contracts to smaller firms to mature underlying subsystem technology.
It is not clear how the SCO programs relate to those existing service efforts, whether as new systems, follow-on variants, or complementary capabilities. The notice states only that the goal is a flexible family of weapons able to hit a wide variety of targets and defeat defenses built to stop them.
No date has been announced for the resulting solicitation. SCO says the September briefings are meant to prepare contractors for that release, with the office directing further questions to a dedicated Offensive Fires email address rather than a public contracting office.

Ukraine Pounds Russia’s Rear, Destroying Su-24M at Saky Airfield and Drone Relay Stations
Ukraine destroyed a Russian Su-24M combat aircraft and four pieces of airfield equipment at the Saky military airfield in temporarily occupied Crimea, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on August 22.
The Ukrainian President said the attacks are aimed at steadily eroding Russia’s military infrastructure and the economic resources sustaining its war effort.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Ukrainian long-range sanctions continue to limit Russia’s military and economic potential, ensuring the aggressor state feels the impact of the war more directly.”
Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces had also struck the Novokuybyshevsk oil refinery roughly 1,000 kilometers from the front line over the previous 24 hours, along with a logistics facility in Russia’s Samara region and targets in the Black Sea.
“Over the past 24 hours, our forces struck the Novokuybyshevsk refinery—1,000 kilometers from the front line—depriving the Russian war machine of millions of dollars in export revenues. We also hit a logistics hub in the Samara region and targets in the Black Sea.”
He also disclosed confirmed results from earlier Ukrainian operations, including the strike on the Saky airfield and attacks against infrastructure used to support Russian drone operations.
“Previous strikes have yielded confirmed results: at the Saky airfield, a Su-24M aircraft and four pieces of airfield equipment were destroyed, while in the Bryansk region, we took out drone-control relay stations used by the occupiers to guide strike UAVs toward peaceful Ukrainian cities and villages.”
The Su-24M, known to NATO as the Fencer-D, is a Soviet-designed supersonic strike aircraft built for all-weather, low-altitude attack missions. Its most distinctive features are variable-sweep wings and a side-by-side cockpit seating the pilot alongside the navigator-weapons officer.
The upgraded Su-24M variant incorporates the Tigr-N targeting and navigation system, allowing it to employ guided weapons, while an in-flight refueling probe extends its operational range. The aircraft can carry up to roughly 7,000 kilograms of ordnance across eight hardpoints, including guided missiles, bombs, rockets and other air-to-surface weapons.
Powered by two turbojet engines, the Su-24M can reach speeds of around 1,700 kilometers per hour at altitude and approximately 1,400 kilometers per hour closer to the ground.
Despite its Soviet-era origins, the aircraft remains relevant in the current war. Russia continues to operate Su-24-family aircraft for strike missions, while Ukraine has adapted its own Su-24M fleet to carry Western-supplied Storm Shadow and SCALP-EG long-range cruise missiles.
Aircraft of this type remain capable of delivering substantial weapons loads and conducting long-range strike missions.
Zelenskyy also said earlier Ukrainian attacks in Russia’s Bryansk region destroyed relay stations used to control and guide drones involved in attacks against Ukrainian cities and settlements.
The Saky airfield has repeatedly served as an important base for Russian military aviation in occupied Crimea and has been targeted several times during Ukraine’s campaign against Russian aircraft and supporting infrastructure.
Zelenskyy credited Ukrainian forces involved in the long-range operations for continuing to erode what Moscow once considered a secure rear.
“I thank all the warriors of Ukraine’s Defense Forces for their effective work and for depriving Russia of its strategic rear.”
Earlier, reports emerged that a Ukrainian cyber attack may have manipulated Russian air defense into downing its own aircraft, leading to the crash of a Russian Su-57 fighter jet in the Moscow region.

What is the 'political firewall' against Germany's far-right AfD?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
09:15:00 UTC
18:15:00 KST

What is the 'political firewall' against Germany's AfD?
August 23, 2026
A firewall is a wall designed to prevent a fire from spreading from one building to another. In German politics, the term "firewall" serves as a metaphor for a strict boundary drawn against parties regarded as extremist. Just as a firewall is intended to protect buildings from fire, the "political firewall" is intended to safeguard democracy.
Whether the Alternative for Germany (AfD) is in fact a party that is hostile to democracy has not yet been determined by the courts. While Germany's domestic intelligence agency, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution, has classified individual AfD state associations as "confirmed right-wing extremist," the question of whether the party as a whole is acting against the German constitution would have to be decided by the Federal Constitutional Court in proceedings to ban the party.
Calls for an AfD ban have been made repeatedly, but no formal application has been filed to date.
Chancellor Merz is growing tired of the term 'firewall'
The term "political firewall" cannot be clearly attributed to any single originator. However, its widespread use is due in large part to Friedrich Merz.
Upon becoming leader of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in December 2021, for example, he told the German news magazine Der Spiegel: "Under my leadership, there will be a firewall against the AfD."
In 2018, the CDU adopted a so-called "resolution of incompatibility" at its party conference, rejecting "coalitions and similar forms of cooperation" with both the AfD and the socialist Left Party.
This did not apply only to formal agreements and coalitions with the AfD. At times, the CDU also deliberately sought majorities without AfD support, and CDU officeholders declined to be elected to political positions with AfD votes.
January 2025 marked a break from that path: A CDU motion in the Bundestag calling for the rejection of asylum seekers passed with AfD support. At the time, Merz was leader of the CDU and thus of the parliamentary opposition. To this day, critics continue to accuse him of breaching the firewall policy.
Now chancellor, Merz tends to avoid the term and has grown increasingly irritated by questions about it.
The center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) and the ecologist Greens reject any cooperation with the AfD, although without formal resolutions to that effect. Sahra Wagenknecht, founder of the left-wing populist Alliance Sahra Wagenknecht (BSW), takes a different stance. She explicitly opposes excluding the AfD and would even be willing to pave the way for an AfD-led government in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt, where elections will be held on September 6.
No firewall at the municipal level
The reliance on AfD votes by Merz's CDU in January 2025 triggered shock and outrage, but it wasn't the first time a politician who officially supports the firewall doesn't adhere to it in practice. In 2020, Thomas Kemmerich from the neoliberal FDP was elected Premier of Thuringia with AfD votes.
Angela Merkel, who was chancellor at the time, was alarmed and demanded that the election "must be reversed."
Kemmerich resigned just a few days later.
At the local level, however, the firewall is often highly permeable. In city and municipal councils, politicians from other parties have repeatedly voted alongside the AfD. Proponents of this more relaxed attitude often argue that, for example, building a daycare center does not become a bad idea simply because the AfD also supports it.
Critics, however, regularly warn of a gradual process of normalization. In their view, such cooperation makes the AfD socially acceptable, and what begins in local politics could eventually spread to state or even federal politics.
Can 40% of voters be ignored?
The firewall policy does not appear to be harming the AfD. On the contrary, its poll ratings continue to rise, despite, or perhaps even because of, the firewall.
When the AfD is particularly strong, as it is across much of eastern Germany, the other parties represented in state parliaments often have to join forces to prevent an AfD-led state government. This can come at the expense of the credibility of parties whose ideological positions are far apart.
Political scientists also point to a democratic deficit if the political preferences of AfD voters are ignored over the long term.
Sahra Wagenknecht (BSW) recently said of Saxony-Anhalt: "It is simply completely undemocratic to permanently exclude a party supported by around 40% of voters. The firewall has failed."
Some CDU politicians in eastern Germany have questioned the rationale behind the firewall. The Brandenburg branch of the Small and Medium Enterprises and Economic Union, an internal CDU interest group, recently submitted a motion calling on the party "at the federal level to work toward repealing or fundamentally revising the CDU's incompatibility resolution vis-a-vis the AfD."
Following strong criticism from the federal party leadership, the group withdrew the motion.
Saxony's CDU Premier Michael Kretschmer, who leads a minority government in Dresden, recently told the German business daily Handelsblatt: "Anyone still talking about firewalls has failed to recognize the signs of the times. We need to talk to everyone who is willing to talk."
At the federal level, the CDU would prefer to put an end to such debates altogether. Thorsten Frei, the new chair of the Bundestag's conservative parliamentary group, which includes the Christian Social Union (CSU), has made clear that he will not tolerate deviations by individual state branches.
"The ban on cooperation with the AfD is a fundamental party resolution of the CDU. It cannot be interpreted differently from one federal state to another," he told newspapers belonging to the Funke Media Group.
The chancellor, too, is holding firm now. Despite the immense pressure and the challenging political landscape in eastern Germany, and aside from the break in January 2025, he continues to uphold the resolution of incompatibility with both the AfD and the Left Party.
How governing majorities opposed to the AfD can be formed in the future therefore remains an open question.

Where water conflicts pose the biggest threat in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
09:13:23 UTC
18:13:23 KST

Where water conflicts pose the biggest threat in 2026
Water-related conflicts have nearly quadrupled since 2020. As World Water Week begins, Al Jazeera unpacks the data.
The sharp rise in water-related conflicts in recent years is in focus as the World Water Week conference begins on Sunday in Sweden’s capital, Stockholm, and online.
With the theme “Water for People and Progress”, the conference is organised annually by the Stockholm International Water Institute (SIWI) and highlights growing global water-security challenges.
According to the Pacific Institute, a US-based nonprofit water think tank, 420 water-related conflicts were recorded in 2024 – a record high and a 78 percent increase from the 235 conflicts recorded in 2022.
The increase is largely driven by attacks on water infrastructure and disputes over access, particularly in regions affected by prolonged wars.
What are the causes of water-related conflicts?
For more than three decades, the Pacific Institute has tracked global water conflicts through its Water Conflict Chronology, classifying each incident by whether water served as a casualty, trigger, or weapon of war.
- Casualty: Water infrastructure is damaged or destroyed during conflict, either deliberately or as collateral damage. This can include dams, pipelines, wells, treatment plants and power systems needed to maintain water supplies. In 2024, 55 percent of water-related conflicts were driven by casualty events.
- Trigger: Water scarcity, unequal access, or disputes over resources fuel violence, often involving communities, farmers, animal herders, or armed groups. Scarcity and access disputes remain widespread, with 28 percent acting as triggers for water-related conflicts in 2024.
- Weapon: Water is deliberately manipulated to harm or pressure opponents, including by cutting supplies, contaminating sources, flooding areas, or controlling access. Water weaponisation is less frequent but persistent, underscoring the growing links between water stress, climate pressures and conflict, with two percent of incidents in 2024 categorised this way.
Where are water-related conflicts the biggest threat in 2026?
Palestine
In Gaza, 1.9 million of 2.1 million people remain displaced, while about 90 percent of water and sanitation infrastructure has been damaged or destroyed by Israeli attacks, according to UNICEF.
Up to 70 percent cannot collect the minimum six litres of water per person a day for drinking and cooking and 90 percent of households faced moderate-to-high water insecurity.
The medical charity, Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF), also known as Doctors Without Borders, reported that water prices have risen by up to 500 percent. Repeated attacks, restrictions on supplies and damage to water facilities have disrupted distribution, worsening diarrhoeal and skin diseases and increasing risks for children and pregnant women, MSF added.
In the occupied West Bank, settler attacks and Israeli demolitions have damaged and destroyed Palestinian water infrastructure, with repeated raids on the Ein Samiya wells east of Ramallah cutting supply to about 100,000 people.
Sudan
Since April 2023, fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces has displaced about 12 million people and created a humanitarian crisis affecting more than 30 million.
A Geneva Academy report documented attacks on water infrastructure, including reservoirs, treatment plants and distribution networks, particularly in Darfur. The collapse of water and sanitation systems has fuelled cholera outbreaks and worsened food insecurity, with famine risks rising across Darfur, Kordofan and Blue Nile.
Iran
US and Israeli air strikes on Iran since February 28, have further strained a water system already weakened by years of drought, below-average rainfall, depleted groundwater and agricultural demand.
Attacks reportedly damaged desalination plants and reservoirs in Qeshm Island and Hormozgan province, disrupting water supplies to tens of thousands of people. Damage to electricity networks and roads has hindered repairs. The attacks came as Iran’s reserves were critically low, with some reservoirs up to 92 percent depleted. Water levels in reservoirs in Mashhad, Iran’s second-largest city and home to around four million people, dropped below three percent.
Gulf region
The war on Iran has exposed the vulnerability of critical water infrastructure in a region that is among the most water-scarce in the world.
Across the Gulf, water security depends heavily on large desalination plants to convert seawater. They supply about 90 percent of drinking water in Kuwait, 86 percent in Oman and 70 percent in Saudi Arabia. In Bahrain, it is above 90 percent and in Qatar, 99 percent.
Desalination plants were damaged in Bahrain, Kuwait, the UAE and Iran during the war, though the reported impact on water supplies was largely limited.
Ukraine
Ukraine’s water crisis has worsened as the war with Russia damages vital water and energy infrastructure. UNICEF says 4.3 million people received safe-water assistance last year, while 12.7 million need humanitarian support.
Attacks have reduced electricity generation by 70 percent, disrupting water and heating. In Kherson, strikes this month cut supplies to entire neighbourhoods.
The Kakhovka Dam disaster in June 2023 affected more than 100,000 people, while about 10 million now lack reliable access to safe water.

Zelensky: Russia has 600–630 ballistic missiles
President Volodymyr Zelensky said this while speaking with journalists, according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
“I believe Russia may be capable of producing up to 1,300 ballistic missiles a year. They currently have 600–630. We have a rough understanding of the number they could produce from now until the end of winter. They may be able to produce approximately 100 ballistic missiles per month. But they do not have that capacity yet,” he said.
According to the president, Ukraine’s Defense Forces are working to weaken Russia’s defense industry. In particular, they have been tasked with striking military targets and taking other measures to disrupt the production of ballistic missiles.
“I have cited the most alarming figure — we believe it is 1,300 missiles. They would like to have 100 ballistic missiles per month. Because we have started intercepting other missiles quite effectively. Our fighter jets are doing it, and IRIS-T systems have also been added — we have the relevant systems, and missiles for them are arriving to counter Russian cruise missiles. Hawk air defense systems are also being used — we are intercepting cruise missiles with a variety of systems. But ballistic missiles are ballistic missiles. We are now working to ensure there are not 1,300 of them — to reduce that number,” he added.
Zelensky also said that Ukrainian forces are planning operations aimed at preventing Russia from carrying out its planned missile strikes.
“There is another area we are working on. I think you have seen recently that at some point they planned a strike but did not carry it out. This is not a coincidence. In other words, we are working to prevent them from carrying out massive missile attacks. These are separate, complex operations, and we are now beginning to see the first results. They are, of course, not yet sufficient, but this is a certain path, and we are taking our steps,” he said.

- Ukraine suspended elections under martial law, with only 15% supporting voting before the conflict ends.
- Zelensky criticised his former defence minister Fedorov for calling elections and warned against division between society and soldiers.
AI generated
KYIV – President Volodymyr Zelensky said in remarks made public on Aug 23 that it would be too dangerous for Ukraine to hold an election while it fights Russia’s invasion, after a call by his former defence minister to organise a vote.
Ukraine has suspended elections under martial law, a measure still widely supported by the population as the country focuses on fighting off the Russian invasion launched in 2022.
“I believe that in a war like this, elections as such are a huge risk. Elections right now are a tsunami for the country that will split Ukraine,” Zelensky said in the comments.
“If we want to destroy the country, then we can move in the direction of elections during these times of war,” the 48-year-old leader added.
He held a briefing with a group of journalists, including AFP, on Aug 22, the first in months amid several political crises.
The latest upheaval saw thousands take to the streets after Zelensky fired his defence minister, Mykhailo Fedorov.
The ousted Fedorov this week made a surprise call to find a way to organise a vote – but without offering a roadmap – and prompting even some of his supporters to distance themselves from him.
Experts have cited a flurry of obstacles, including how soldiers, millions of Ukrainian refugees and people from occupied territories would vote, as well as disinformation threats from Russia.
The election call also came as Ukraine struggles to fend off daily Russian missile and drone strikes on Kyiv and other cities.
Only 15 per cent of Ukrainians believe elections should be held before the end of hostilities, according to a poll by the Kyiv Institute of Sociology.
Zelensky made numerous jabs at his opponent during the briefing, which came ahead of events to mark the country’s Independence Day on Aug 24, when several international leaders will be present. Allies are also to hold talks on how to bolster Ukraine’s air defences amid the intense Russian strikes.
“I believe he is going himself – or is being pushed – towards wrong things,” Zelensky said of Fedorov.
The former minister was a prominent backer of the drone warfare strategy that has come to dominate the war with Russia, and had pushed for army reforms. But he clashed with the military’s command and its traditionally stiff approach.
The public initially took his side and pushed for the dismissal of commander-in-chief Oleksandr Syrsky.
Zelensky said people had the right to protest but warned against “disrespectful” attitudes to military people.
“Since when has marketing started to outweigh the people who are giving their lives?” he said.
After a political crisis that had weakened him, Zelensky was able to cast himself as a rampart against division.
“I believe that society and soldiers must not be divided,” he said. “We must acknowledge that there is this risk – that there may be movement in that direction, towards dangerous developments.” AFP

Hackers linked to Iran have been blamed for a cyber-attack that caused a British power plant to be temporarily shut down.
The incident involved a small-scale energy generator, according to the UK government, which said that at no point was there a risk to the wider energy system.
However, it marks an apparent escalation in the threat posed by Iran after the UK said it had given permission for the US to launch “defensive” operations against Tehran from British bases.
The power plant was shut down for four days as a result of the attack last month, according to the Sunday Telegraph, which first reported it.
A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “This story refers to an incident impacting a small-scale energy generator, and at no point was there a risk to the wider energy system. The UK has a highly resilient energy system. We work closely with the energy sector to protect infrastructure and ensure the highest security standards.”
The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), which deals with attacks on critical infrastructure, is understood not to have received any reported outages from regulated operators of power stations.
The Conservatives said the incident reflected a “new kind of warfare”, which meant Britain needed to prioritise “cheap, reliable energy”. “The world is getting more dangerous, which is why we need to prioritise our energy security,” said Claire Coutinho, the Conservative spokesperson on energy.
“Leaving ourselves reliant on imports of gas and electricity and failing to build enough reliable gas or nuclear plants for backup at home, all leaves us more vulnerable.”
Hostile states such as Russia, China and Iran are increasingly targeting systems behind the UK’s key services, according to a warning this year from Richard Horne, the NCSC’s chief executive.
The government said last month the UK was “ready to defend itself” after Iran’s military warned any bases being used by the US were “legitimate targets”.
The UK has allowed the US to launch so-called defensive operations from British bases hosting American planes since the start of its war on Iran but has refused to help in offensive operations. That policy has not been altered by the new prime minister, Andy Burnham, who was notified last week that a decision had been made to extend the agreement with the US.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said last month that “any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces”.
Iran has been accused for years of carrying out cyber-attacks on various countries, including in relation to a massive power outage in Turkey in 2015 and several possible breaches of Israeli government websites in 2022.
US government security agencies issued a warning earlier this year of cyber-attacks on critical infrastructure by hackers linked to the IRGC.
The US has alleged that an Iran-affiliated group known as “CyberAv3ngers” carried out a campaign against it in 2023 that compromised at least 75 devices in multiple infrastructure sectors.

U.S. Navy awards nearly $1B contract for global fuel infrastructure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
09:07:26 UTC
18:07:26 KST

- Ten construction firms won a combined $997 million Navy contract to build and repair fuel pipelines and storage tanks worldwide, with work through August 2031.
- The Department of War competitively awarded the contract after receiving 17 offers, obligating a $587,438 seed task order and $10,000 to each company.
Ten construction firms have been awarded a combined $997 million contract to build, maintain, and repair fuel pipelines and storage tanks at U.S. Navy and U.S. Marine Corps installations worldwide.
The award is an indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity, firm-fixed-price, multiple award construction contract. It covers construction, maintenance, repair, and engineering services for pipelines, fuel storage tanks, and related petroleum, oil, and lubricant facilities and equipment.
The 10 companies are Aptim Federal Services LLC of Baton Rouge, Louisiana; Bristol Engineering Services Co. LLC of Anchorage, Alaska; CMS Corp. of Bargersville, Indiana; Dawson Technical Inc. of San Antonio, Texas; Environmental Chemical Corp. of Burlingame, California; Pacific Design Builders LLC of Tamuning, Guam; PCI Bhate JV LLC of Atmore, Alabama; Tepa & Pond Constructors JV of Kansas City, Missouri; Weston Solutions Inc. of West Chester, Pennsylvania; and WSP USA Government Solutions Inc. of New York, New York. Five of the 10 awardees are designated small businesses under the award notice.
Each company holds a separate contract number, running consecutively from N39430-26-D-2001 through N39430-26-D-2010. Under a multiple award construction contract, the Department of War can solicit bids from any of the 10 companies for individual projects. It then selects the company offering the best value for that specific task order.
Work will be split evenly between locations outside the continental United States and locations inside it. Guam, where Pacific Design Builders LLC is based, hosts Andersen Air Force Base and Naval Base Guam, both of which depend on bulk fuel infrastructure that falls under NAVFAC EXWC’s global program. The contract is expected to be complete by August 2031. The maximum combined dollar value across all 10 contracts, including a five-year base ordering period, is $997 million.
At the time of award, the Department of War obligated fiscal 2026 U.S. Navy working capital funds of $10,000 to each of the 10 companies. It also obligated a seed task order worth $587,438 to satisfy the minimum guarantee requirement. The Department of War has not disclosed which company received the seed task order. Those funds expire at the end of the current fiscal year.
The contract was competitively procured through the SAM.gov website. The Department of War received 17 offers. The Naval Facilities Engineering and Expeditionary Warfare Center, based in Port Hueneme, California, is the contracting activity.
The award falls under NAVFAC EXWC’s Global Petroleum, Oil, and Lubricants program, which manages fuel-handling infrastructure at Navy and Marine Corps sites worldwide. The program maintains the bulk fuel systems that supply ships, aircraft, and vehicles, including pipelines, storage tank farms, and pumping stations. NAVFAC EXWC issued a request for proposal for the construction work in March 2025 under solicitation number N3943025R2001. The solicitation set a small business size standard of $45 million under NAICS code 237120, which covers oil and gas pipeline and related structures construction.
The construction contract is separate from a related architect-engineer design services contract NAVFAC EXWC has solicited for the same petroleum, oil, and lubricants program. That design contract carries a 60-month base ordering period and is capped at $145 million across all task orders. It covers mechanical, civil, structural, electrical, fire protection, architectural, waterfront, and environmental design work rather than construction itself.

Shahin Izadyar aims to make his Asian Para Games medal record untouchable
TEHRAN - Iranian para-swimmer Shahin Izadyar, the most decorated Paralympic swimmer in the country’s history, is determined to add to his record haul of 24 Asian Para Games medals at the upcoming Nagoya Games.

“Winning a medal cannot be predicted, especially in swimming, where hundredths of a second can make the difference,” he said. “Nevertheless, I will give everything I have to stand on the podium.”
The veteran para-swimmer now has one clear objective in Nagoya: to return home with more medals and make his record of 24 Asian Para Games medals even harder to surpass.

Saint-Gilles Mayor Jean Spinette told Belga news agency the victim didn’t suffer life-threatening injuries and linked the incident to narcotics-related crime. The shots were fired on a square known as “place des Deux Bancs,” associated with drug trafficking.
The attack comes one day after shooters carrying a heavy weapon targeted a police station in another Brussels municipality, Anderlecht, before fleeing on an e-scooter.
Advertisement
The violence marked “yet another wake-up call” for the Belgian capital, the region’s Minister-President Boris Dilliès reacted on X. “We will not let organized crime take over our city,” he added.
Dilliès said his government was taking measures to address the violence, including by appointing a Brussels commissioner for drugs, who will take on the role from September, and by restricting the use of e-scooters, which he said “unfortunately, are often used by criminals.”
The city’s top prosecutor Julien Moinil said that, given the target of Friday night’s shooting, “there is a clear intent to undermine authority” — but he added that “they will not succeed.” He explained that a lot of shootings are ordered from inside prison, calling for secure zones where phones cannot operate.
A third shooting followed early Sunday morning, when a bullet hit the window of an apartment near Porte de Hal.
Brussels recorded 57 shootings in the first seven months of 2026. Two people were killed and 21 injured, according to VRT.

One Nation MP admits the party's true migration target 'isn't too different' from Labor's
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
09:03:04 UTC
18:03:04 KST

in brief
- Pauline Hanson has rejected claims on immigration made by her own MP.
- David Farley conceded the party's overall intake numbers are not too different from Labor's forecasts.
One Nation's immigration stance is under question after an MP said the party would include an extra 100,000 people annually in its policy — bringing its target total higher than present forecasts under Labor.
Farrer MP David Farley, who clinched Sussan Ley's old seat from the coalition at a by-election, told the ABC Insiders program on Sunday morning that his party had decided to separate a "true NOM", or net overseas migration figure, from certain other categories of migrants.
However, party leader Pauline Hanson was forced to quickly intervene, refuting the claims just hours later on social media. Party policy is to "cut net overseas migration to 130,000".
"One Nation's target is less than half of Labor's current level," she wrote.
This contradicts messaging from Farley, who said One Nation's stated policy of getting net overseas migration down to 130,000 excluded people brought in under a Pacific scheme, aged-care nurses and other in-demand skilled workers.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Adding those groups would amount to an additional 100,000 arrivals, bringing the total to 230,000 — 5,000 more than the budget forecast of 225,000 in the coming four years.
"What we're doing is we're focusing on the NOM in its true form, and then we've got these programs that have been available now for over a decade that drive our economy," Farley told Insiders.
"The raw number is not too different, but the reality is, where do we need them?
"We don't need them in the great urban metroplex — we need them out to be productive, working in agriculture, engineering, mining."
One Nation 'effectively backing' Labor's plan
The comments come as public debate continues around the optimum level of migration to Australia.
Net overseas migration dropped to 306,000 in 2024-25, brought down from a post-pandemic peak of 538,000 under Liberal-National government policy.
Cabinet minister Chris Bowen said net overseas migration could not just be redefined.
"My overwhelming conclusion was he's pretty comfortable with what the government's doing," Bowen told reporters.
"I'm not sure what campaign One Nation's going to run on migration if they're effectively backing in what the Albanese government is doing."
Opposition immigration spokesman Jonno Duniam said voters were owed a clear explanation of what the party's immigration policy actually is.
"These are not semantic distinctions. They have real consequences for housing, infrastructure, essential services, wages, jobs and the economy," he said.
"For a party that has spent years telling Australians it has all the answers on immigration, One Nation is having extraordinary difficulty answering the most basic question of all: how many migrants would actually come to Australia under its policy."
Opinion polls have shown that voters trust One Nation to manage migration better than the two major parties.
Hanson says One Nation's cuts will come from "fewer international students and dependants, a dramatic reduction in temporary graduate visas and their dependants, and a much more targeted skilled migration program focused on the skills Australia genuinely needs".
"Short-term seasonal agricultural workers who do not meet the ABS residency test are not counted in net overseas migration," she wrote.
Individuals must stay in Australia for 12 months in a 16-month period to be included in NOM figures, meaning short-term seasonal workers under the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility scheme are typically not counted.
Long-term workers on the same scheme are counted, as are backpakers and working holiday makers who typically stay in the country for more than a year.
Hanson will test racial discrimination laws in the High Court.
The confusion comes as Hanson declared she would take her racial discrimination challenge with Greens senator Mehreen Faruqi to the High Court.
The senator lost a Federal Court appeal last month against a ruling which found her in breach of racial vilification laws after she told the Greens senator to "piss off back to Pakistan".
Asked if racial discrimination laws should be changed, Farley said he wasn't convinced they should be.
He said his leader's comments "can be taken as an insult" but weren't inciting racial discrimination.
"Hanson's got every right to challenge it," Farley said.
"I think if we went through the pub test, I know which way it would go. It'd go in Pauline's favour."
This is the second time Hanson has had to correct comments made by Farley after he said he would display both the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander flags alongside the Australian flag at his electorate office.
One Nation's policy is to only fly the Australian flag on public buildings. Hanson has described having multiple official flags as "extremely divisive".

North Carolina firm to supply parts for Marine Corps’ NMESIS launcher
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
09:01:35 UTC
18:01:35 KST

- Corvid Technologies received a $33.86 million sole-source IDIQ contract to build a weapon sled assembly for the NMESIS anti-ship missile launcher.
- The Portfolio Acquisition Executive Marine Corps issued the award under FAR 6.302-1, with no funds obligated until individual task orders are placed through August 2034.
Corvid Technologies LLC has been awarded a $33.86 million contract to build a weapon sled assembly for the Navy/Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System, the U.S. Marine Corps’ land-based anti-ship missile launcher.
The award is an indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contract combining firm-fixed-price, cost-plus-fixed-fee, and cost reimbursement terms. Work will be performed at Corvid’s facilities in Mooresville, North Carolina, where the company is headquartered. The contract’s ordering period runs through August 2034, giving the Department of War nearly nine years to place orders against it.
No funds were obligated at the time of award, meaning the Department of War has not yet committed any money against the $33.86 million ceiling. The Department of War will issue individual task orders and delivery orders as the work is scheduled, and money will be committed against those orders rather than the base contract.
The Portfolio Acquisition Executive Marine Corps, based at Quantico, Virginia, is the contracting activity, and the award carries the contract number M67854-26-D-1008.
The contract was not competitively bid, meaning the Department of War did not solicit offers from other companies before making the award. It was issued under Federal Acquisition Regulation 6.302-1, which allows agencies to sole-source a requirement when only one company can reasonably meet it.
NMESIS pairs the Naval Strike Missile with the ROGUE Fires carrier, an unmanned launch vehicle that Oshkosh Defense builds on the Joint Light Tactical Vehicle chassis. Raytheon, an RTX business, produces the Naval Strike Missile in partnership with Norway’s Kongsberg Defence & Aerospace. The missile has a stated range of roughly 185 km (115 miles). It is designed to fly low over the sea to avoid radar detection before striking a ship near the waterline.
A weapon sled assembly is a structural component of a missile launcher. It supports and positions a missile canister on the launch platform before firing. The Department of War announcement does not specify further design details, integration requirements, or which portion of the NMESIS system the assembly will serve.
NMESIS entered low-rate initial production in 2024, after the Department of War awarded Raytheon a contract worth nearly $50 million to begin building launcher units, with deliveries due by August 2027. The U.S. Marine Corps fielded its first six NMESIS systems to the 3rd Marine Littoral Regiment at Marine Corps Base Hawaii in November 2024. Marine Corps Systems Command has said the service ultimately plans to field 48 NMESIS launchers.
Marines took NMESIS to the Philippines for Exercise Balikatan in April and May 2025, staging a launcher on Batan Island in the Luzon Strait. In June 2026, the 12th Marine Littoral Regiment on Okinawa, Japan, received its own NMESIS launchers, giving the unit land-based anti-ship missiles along the first island chain.
NMESIS is organized under Medium-Range Missile batteries within Marine Littoral Regiments, formations built for Expeditionary Advanced Base Operations. Naval News reported, citing a Marine Corps release, that each battery is structured into six sections of three launchers, for a total of 18 anti-ship missile systems per battery. A separate system, the Marine Air Defense Integrated System, provides close-in protection for NMESIS batteries against drones and aircraft.
Corvid Technologies is a small, employee-owned defense contractor founded in 2004 and based in Mooresville. The company employs more than 200 engineers and scientists. It specializes in computational physics modeling and uses an in-house supercomputer to simulate high-rate physical events such as blast and ballistic impacts. Corvid holds an 8(a) small business designation and has previously worked with the Missile Defense Agency and the U.S. Navy.
The company’s existing Navy work includes a contract for short and medium range sub-orbital target vehicles used in missile defense testing, awarded in 2025 and valued at up to $268.4 million, and a potential 10-year, $385 million contract to support Missile Defense Agency test instrumentation. Corvid has also served as a subcontractor to Kratos Defense on Department of War hypersonic flight test work.

People’s Daily defends China’s economic resilience, says annual targets will be met

‘The line’s running half-empty’: Llanwern steelworks feels the heat from cheap steel imports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
09:00:28 UTC
18:00:28 KST

At Tata Steel’s factory in Llanwern, south Wales, production lines that should be running full-time are now falling quiet for parts of the day, with workers being put on to maintenance and cleaning work while machines sit idle.
There aren’t enough orders to keep them running all the time, the company says, because of a surge of cheap steel coming from Asian countries that is threatening the viability of several UK sites that make similar products, and risk hundreds of jobs.
“The line has been left running half empty, and the result of that is it won’t last very long unless we can find a solution here,” said one insider.
New 50% import tariffs introduced by the government in July were designed to protect against cheap steel from countries including China and India from undercutting UK producers such as Tata.
But for some types of product, such as the galvanised steel made at Llanwern, near Newport, the situation has worsened, after the government increased the tariff-free quotas – the amount of steel that can be brought in without paying the levy – for some countries.
India’s allowance of galvanised steel rose from 98,000 to 125,000 tonnes, while Vietnam’s more than tripled, from 51,000 to 174,000 tonnes. South Korea was given an increased quota of 100,000 tonnes.
The larger quota for India is understood to have been a last-minute move to help get a trade deal with the country over the line, which was first reported by the Financial Times. World Trade Organization rules require comparable exporters are. reated equally, forcing the increase in quotas to Vietnam and South Korea.
Earlier this summer the Tata UK boss, Rajesh Nair, said he was “very concerned” about the new arrangement.
Now, nearly two months later, Llanwern is struggling to compete on price and running at about half capacity as a result. The factory produces about 600,000 tonnes of galvanised steel a year, nearly half the UK’s total demand.
Galvanised steel is a type of steel that has been dipped in molten zinc, giving it a protective layer that can last for decades and stop it corroding. It is widely used in items such as bridges, outdoor signs and car bodywork.
The company is understood to have met Blair McDougall, the minister for industry, two weeks ago, and laid out the scale of the problem facing Llanwern.
Russell Codling, the commercial director of Tata Steel, said: “Our world-class Zodiac galvanising line in Llanwern, south Wales, is already being significantly impacted by the new quotas, and that situation just isn’t sustainable.
“The quotas have the power to turn this around and make us a truly sustainable business.”
Tata is in the process of switching from its old blast furnaces in Port Talbot, south Wales, to a 3m tonne electric arc furnace. The move will reduce its carbon emissions but it cost 2,000 jobs in the region when the blast furnace was closed down in 2024.
The process involves £1.25bn in investment, about £500m of which has come from a government grant. But a steel industry source said prolonged tariff pressure could even endanger that switch.
The person said: “If there is a prolonged impact across a number of Tata Steel’s core sectors that affects the outputs of its downstream processing sites, that in itself could have a knock-on effect on the ability of its electric arc furnace and green steel making to transform the future of the business as they were hoping.”
Alasdair McDiarmid, the assistant general secretary at the Community union, said: “There is no doubt that the increase in duty-free steel imports from China and Vietnam poses a threat to our domestic steel industry, and at Llanwern our members are already feeling the impact.
“We will continue to call on the government to adopt a more robust approach to ensure that the long-term sustainability of Llanwern steelworks is not jeopardised.
“Llanwern is a crucial strategic site for the Welsh and UK steel sectors, supplying top-quality galvanised steel to the automotive and construction sectors. It is vital that the plant and its dedicated workforce have security for the future.”
The government has previously said it will review the quota system before it changes again in July 2027.
A government spokesperson said: “Our steel measure aims to strike the right balance between protecting domestic production and maintaining a secure supply, and final quotas were shaped by extensive engagement with industry.
“While category 4 imports are currently below the quota levels that have been set, we will continue to take industry feedback into account, monitor the impact closely and review the measure after 12 months.”

When I first moved to Glasgow from India, I felt welcomed and included. Now I just feel scrutinised | Sanghmitra Singh
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
09:00:28 UTC
18:00:28 KST

Scottish people have always been known for their friendliness. “We’re not like the south of us,” they say, referring to England. The official slogan of Scotland’s largest city, “People make Glasgow”, appears everywhere – on T-shirts, buildings, bus stops and mugs. And when I first moved to Scotland from India in 2018, I was immediately welcomed by kind strangers and helpful neighbours. People showed curiosity, rather than intrusiveness. They respected queues; told me I fit right in. Music, art and cultural events were considered inclusive spaces in the city, with calls for diversity, creativity, inclusion – all the good things.
As an outsider, this was a dream come true: to be myself, to be alone, to have brotherhood and a community. It was life-changing. I could do whatever I wanted, wear whatever I wanted, walk by myself at night, even. That is a luxury, especially for a woman. But something has changed, particularly after Covid, a global recession and years of austerity. Now, I watch the steady rise of far-right, fringe violence and I feel a special scrutiny upon me.
In June, we saw disorder and racists assaults in Glasgow as hundreds of masked protesters marched through the streets. Asian business owners were harassed and people were attacked – according to the police – “because of the colour of their skin”. Later that month, a man was charged with attempted murder after allegedly attacking men leaving a mosque in Edinburgh. A video appeared to show him shouting that he was “protecting the country”. In July, a delivery driver was assaulted after anti-immigration protesters, many of them masked, some shouting racist abuse, once again “rampaged” through Glasgow. We have seen mosques defaced with “hate graffiti” – one is attacked in Britain every five days, according to new data. We’ve heard a speaker at a protest outside an asylum hotel in Falkirk calling for a crowd to “keep Britain white”. There have been activists outside the Scottish parliament staging fascist-style demonstrations. It goes to show top-down propaganda funnels to real-life incidents.
I feel this increasing hostility personally, too. Strangers point-blank question me about my nationality, accent, religion or clothes. A stranger once told me that my accent was weird. An acquaintance said immigrants were taking away jobs from locals, after I told them I was struggling to find work despite being qualified. People jump queues and are quickly confrontational. The “outsiders” that Glasgow loved and accepted have seemingly become the subject of derision and suspicion.
I find people staring at me, head to toe, for an uncomfortably long time. A customer in a Govan pub casually remarked aloud that immigrants are criminals and that we “need to go back”. An old lady on a bus interrupted me and my very white, very British husband to tell us to stop talking the way we were talking. Was it because we’re clearly an interracial couple? Is it because we categorically don’t sound like the locals? I’ll never know, but it’s gnawing now at the back of my mind when it never would have a few short years ago.
Colleagues who have been here since the 1980s and earlier tell me that racist violence has happened in Scotland before, but this time it feels different. We’re afraid to step out now. There’s a clear, marked shift in our levels of nervousness. It is certainly more imminent, more immediate – closer to home.
I blame a combination of factors for this unsettling change: the high cost of living, the worsening climate crisis and the rightwing agenda of some of the mainstream media have all increased resentment and suspicion of one’s neighbours. Then, during the Covid-19 pandemic, many people felt that they had been left alone. That the state wasn’t taking care of them as a democracy is supposed to do.
Even a global health emergency, it seemed, couldn’t make for a better world. Instead of a fairer, more equal or accessible society, we have extreme wealth inequality that is persistent and increasing. And it doesn’t help that inflammatory posts are favoured by social-media algorithms. All of this creates a tinderbox in which people of colour understandably feel afraid.
Many places, including Leith and Glasgow, held anti-racist, pro-immigrant, pro-humanity rallies days after the racist incidents occurred. People carried signs reading: “Racism is weird, have you tried hobbies?”; “Migrants make the NHS”; “Hate has no home”. They made passionate speeches about standing up to bigotry. But is that enough? While it was heartwarming to see thousands of people come out, uniting for diversity, inclusion and multiculturalism, it won’t stop a growing hatred and fear of people like me. And so every time I’m out in public now, my stress levels go up. Am I safe alone? What is my exit strategy? Can I even afford to be angry? Others feel it, too.
I understand why many British people feel overlooked and badly done by – it’s true that Britain is unequal and unfair. But I wish that the media would not validate people’s inherent biases and misconceptions, nor politicians legitimise their worst sentiments by calling for reactions like “pure, cold rage”. It is easy to whip up hatred between neighbours, but systematic hatred and divisiveness can take decades to undo. The only individuals who benefit from scapegoating are the powerful.
We have to say “no” to this normalisation of bigotry, violence and othering. We have to focus on the living conditions and inequality we all share. We need to remember we have more in common with each other than with any billionaire. We must remember that the real blame lies with the system that wants us divided. Talk to real people who look and sound different from you. You’ll realise we’re all humans. We can do better than this.
- 
  Sanghmitra Singh is a human rights lawyer and a writer

Is Expensive Bottled Water Actually Better for You?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Water is supposed to be the simplest thing we consume. The premium bottled water industry has transformed it into something that requires a backstory.
Supermarket shelves now distinguish between glacial, iceberg, volcanic, spring, mineral, and alkaline water. Restaurants are introducing water menus, while trained water sommeliers assess bottles by their mineral composition, mouthfeel and provenance. At the extreme end of the category, Svalbarði Polar Iceberg Water sells Arctic water for as much as €100 (around $116) a bottle.
The category’s growth rests on a mixture of verifiable differences and carefully constructed associations. Water can contain different minerals. Those minerals can change how it tastes. But claims about purity, alkaline pH, and remote natural sources can also create the impression that expensive water must be healthier.
According to Michael Mascha, who founded the platform FineWaters in 2002 to train water sommeliers and drag premium bottled products out of the commodity aisle, prices often reflect remote sourcing and difficult transport rather than superior health benefits. Luxury water, he argues, is better understood as a dining experience than as a more effective source of hydration.
Does Expensive Water Hydrate You Better?
There is no established evidence that luxury water hydrates an otherwise healthy person better simply because it is more expensive or comes from a celebrated source.
“Fundamentally, true hydration is about consuming enough water throughout the day to replace daily losses rather than brand status or origin,” says Lucy Semerjian, associate professor of environmental science and technology at the University of Sharjah in the United Arab Emirates.
What matters most is drinking enough safe water to replace the fluid the body loses. Its chemical and microbial composition must also remain within safe limits.
Are the Minerals in Bottled Water Better for You?
Minerals are responsible for some of the genuine differences between waters. As water travels through soil and rock, it can absorb calcium, magnesium, bicarbonate, sodium, and other dissolved substances. Their type and concentration depend partly on the geology surrounding the source.
These minerals are already dissolved into ionized forms, meaning the gastrointestinal tract can absorb them. Mineral water can therefore contribute to a person’s calcium or magnesium intake, although its nutritional significance depends on the concentration, the quantity consumed, and the rest of that person’s diet.
The word “mineral,” however, does not tell consumers how much of any particular nutrient is present.
“People see terms like rich in minerals, high TDS numbers, or alkaline pH on a premium label and assume those are automatically markers of superior quality,” says Maria Abi Hanna, cofounder and CEO of nutrition intelligence software Food Label Maker, “when in reality none of those numbers tell you anything on their own.”
Total dissolved solids, or TDS, measures the combined concentration of dissolved substances in water. A higher number does not function as a score for safety, purity, or health. It mainly describes the water’s mineral load.
The same problem applies to alkaline water. Its higher pH is frequently positioned as a wellness advantage, but pH alone does not establish that a bottle is healthier. The stomach is already highly acidic, and the body tightly regulates the pH of the blood.
Consumers should instead look at which minerals appear on the label and in what concentrations. People limiting their sodium intake, for example, may have different priorities from someone specifically looking for a water containing calcium or magnesium.
Does Mineral Content Change How Water Tastes?
Minerals may not transform hydration, but they can transform taste.
“Some waters taste very light because they have very low mineral content,” Mascha says.
Rainwater that has had little contact with the ground may contain very few dissolved minerals. Iceberg and some glacial waters can also fall towards the low end of the TDS scale, producing a relatively light or neutral taste.
At the other end, water containing upwards of 2,000mg of mineral content can have a noticeably heavier mouthfeel and a stronger flavor. Individual minerals can introduce salty, bitter, chalky, or slightly sweet characteristics.
The differences are real. The leap from “tastes different” to “is healthier,” however, is usually where the marketing begins to outrun the evidence. Luxury water makes the most sense when treated as a taste category: something selected for a particular mineral profile, dining experience, or personal preference. The price is not a reliable shorthand for its nutritional value.
Is Glass-Bottled Water Safer Than Plastic?
The most consequential thing about a bottle of water, though, may not be the water itself.
Premium brands often use glass packaging, reinforcing the perception that the water is both luxurious and protected from the concerns surrounding plastic.
“Plastic bottles are sensitive to thermal stress, UV radiation, or extended storage times,” says Nidia Rodriguez-Sanchez, senior lecturer in physiology and nutrition at Scotland’s University of Stirling.
This is particularly relevant in hot climates. Leaving bottled water inside a vehicle or storing it for prolonged periods at high temperatures can increase the migration of substances from PET into the water. Studies have found that heat can increase the release of antimony, a substance used during PET manufacturing, although the concentrations vary by bottle, temperature, and storage time.
Glass is not an entirely plastic-free solution. A 2025 study led by France’s Agency for Food, Environmental and Occupational Health and Safety, or ANSES, found microplastics in beverages packaged in glass.
The glass itself was not identified as the main source. Researchers traced many of the particles to the painted coating on metal bottle caps, which could become scratched as the caps rubbed together during storage.
The results also varied by beverage. Soft drinks and beer in glass bottles contained considerably more particles than the same drinks in other packaging. Water contained far fewer particles overall, although glass-bottled water averaged slightly more than water packaged in plastic or cartons.
The study does not prove that glass packaging is more dangerous than plastic. It demonstrates that changing the bottle material does not eliminate every other potential source of plastic exposure.
Mascha’s response to all this is that the anxiety is selectively applied. “Everyone talks about microplastics in water. There’s also microplastics in wine, in beer, and in Coke,” he says.

U.S. Unveils AIM-424 Malice: Ultra-Long-Range Missile With Range of Over 463 km
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
08:59:34 UTC
17:59:34 KST

The U.S. Navy’s Naval Aviation branch has unveiled a new ultra-long-range air-to-air missile, the AIM-424 Malice, with a stated range of more than 463 km.
The relevant photographs were published by DVIDS, the official media platform of the U.S. Department of Defense.
The missile was shown on two types of carrier-based fighter aircraft: the F-35C Lightning II and the F/A-18E Super Hornet.
The missile was developed and manufactured by the U.S. company Raytheon. It is powered by a solid-propellant rocket motor.
The missile is 4.11 meters long, has a diameter of 0.34 meters, and a wingspan of 0.67 meters. Its launch mass is 680.4 kg. The missile has a stated range of more than 463 km and is equipped with a high-explosive fragmentation warhead.
Although photographs of the AIM-424 Malice were not released until August 22, 2026, available information indicates that testing of the missile began as early as the winter of 2026.
There is currently no detailed information regarding the completion of the missile’s integration with its carrier aircraft. However, the released photographs demonstrate that the F/A-18E Super Hornet can accommodate at least four AIM-424 Malice missiles.
The carrier-based F-35C can carry these missiles in its internal weapons bays, allowing the aircraft to maintain a low observable signature while conducting combat missions.
It is currently unknown what specific role the AIM-424 Malice will play in the U.S. Navy’s weapons inventory. The U.S. Air Force and U.S. Navy have traditionally developed their own air-launched missiles in parallel. Naval aviation already employs the AIM-120, while the U.S. Navy recently unveiled and test-fired the long-range AIM-174 during an exercise.
The AIM-424 Malice could potentially complement the AIM-174 or partially replace it.
In terms of design, the new missile more closely resembles conventional air-to-air missiles, whereas the AIM-174 was developed from the ship-launched SM-6 surface-to-air missile. The latter is also capable of intercepting ballistic targets, making it an important component in countering Chinese anti-ship ballistic missiles.
Meanwhile, the U.S. Air Force is developing its own long-range AIM-260 missile. It is likewise intended to engage targets at extended ranges. However, no official data on its range or other key performance characteristics have been released to date.
