New travel guide traces Ian Fleming's footsteps in Switzerland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
08:59:15 UTC
17:59:15 KST

New travel guide traces Ian Fleming’s footsteps in Switzerland
Even before James Bond was created, Ian Fleming had a passionate romance in Switzerland with a young woman from the canton of Vaud. A new travel guide now traces the writer’s connections to French-speaking Switzerland and Lake Geneva.
In the Footsteps of Ian Fleming in Switzerland, published in English and French by Editions romandes 180°, invites readers to follow in the footsteps of the man who would later become the creator of James Bond during his time in the 1930s. The itinerary includes Geneva, where Fleming undertook an internship at what was then the League of Nations, as well as Coppet and Vich, where his love story with Monique Panchaud de Bottens unfolded.
A relationship as the central theme
This relationship forms the central theme of the book. It led the two young people to become engaged before they went their separate ways. “When he met her, she was very avant-garde for her time,” travel guide author Cornelius Schregle told Keystone-SDA news agency. He highlighted her love of skiing, the high mountains and driving – activities that were still unusual for a young woman from her social circle at the time.
More
James Bond: half-Swiss, totally profitable
According to the author, this story may also have left its mark on the James Bond universe. “The women who populate the Bond universe have something of Monique about them: free-spirited women who take their fate into their own hands,” said Schregle.
At the Beau-Rivage Palace in Lausanne
Fleming discovered Switzerland at a very early age. Among other places, his family stayed at the Beau-Rivage Palace in Lausanne. Later, the landscapes and locations of French-speaking Switzerland reappeared in his work, while certain scenes from the James Bond films, in turn, turned Switzerland into a mythical backdrop.
The travel guide brings together historical and contemporary photographs, maps, archive documents and extracts from the novels. The majority of the places mentioned in the guide can therefore still be visited today, allowing the reader to turn reading into a journey.
With this journey through Switzerland, Cornelius Schregle sought not so much to write a new biography of Fleming as to shed light on a little-known phase of his life. “I wanted something lighter, something more entertaining,” with the aim of enabling everyone to discover these places “at their own leisure”.
Nevertheless, the work is the result of several years of research and encounters, in particular with members of the Fleming and Monique Panchaud families, as well as with the British biographers Nicolas Shakespeare and Andrew Lycett.
It builds on Cornelius Schregle’s work on the links between Switzerland and the cinema, which began with the book Backdrop Switzerland, published in 2016. The latter focuses on films that were shot in Switzerland or used Switzerland as a backdrop.

Zelenskyy rejects wartime elections citing "huge risk" and "split" for Ukraine
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy rejected the idea of holding elections during the war with Russia, four days after the former defense minister publicly called for them.
"I believe that in a war like this, elections as such are a huge risk. Elections right now are a tsunami for the country that will split Ukraine," Zelenskyy said in remarks made public Sunday.
Ukraine's former defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who was fired last month, posted a video Tuesday where he called for the country to be given a chance to go to the polls.
In the video, Fedorov said "democracy cannot be held hostage by Russia," and called for a "legal, safe and realistic mechanism that will allow Ukraine to restore a full democratic process even amidst a prolonged war."
"We are fighting precisely because we want to remain a free European state," he added.
The move was widely seen as the largest challenge to Zelenskyy's power since the start of the conflict, but the ousted minister did not reveal whether he had any political ambitions for himself. The president imposed martial law, which prohibits elections from being held, when Russian forces invaded the country in February 2022.
In an interviewed aired Sunday by the BBC, which is CBS News' international partner, Fedorov said the Ukrainian president had "questions to answer" about alleged corruption in his government, citing a money laundering investigation announced last week. He also told the BBC Ukrainians should not be afraid of discussing the idea of holding elections during the war.
"If I cannot share my ideas and be open about them with my own society, then what are we fighting for," Fedorov told the BBC.
Zelenskyy fired Fedorov in mid-July, citing an unsolvable feud between him and Zelenskyy's top general, Oleksandr Syrskyi. The move sparked weeks of protests from thousands of people across the country, criticizing the removal of the widely respected minister.
Fedorov was credited with turning the tide of the war in Ukraine's favor, increasing Ukraine's strikes deep into Russia tenfold and bolstering its domestic arsenal.

Hungary Paks nuclear plant could operate at full capacity by Wednesday, PM Magyar says
BUDAPEST, Aug 23 - Hungary's Paks nuclear plant restarted its reactor 3 late on Saturday and the facility could be operating at full capacity by Wednesday, a day or two sooner than expected, Prime Minister Peter Magyar said on Sunday.
The 2-gigawatt plant, which produces nearly half of Hungary's electricity, was forced to cut output to just over 10% earlier this month, barely escaping a full shutdown due to a historic drought and record-low water levels on the Danube.
• The nuclear plant currently produces about 800 megawatts of electricity, based on data from its operator.
• "Four turbines out of eight are producing electricity already at Paks. Full restart is underway, the nuclear plant could be producing 2,000 megawatts again by Wednesday," Prime Minister Peter Magyar said on Facebook on Sunday.
• Rising water levels on the Danube, the facility's main coolant source, as well as engineering work done at the river near the plant helped avoid a full shutdown.
• Hungary last week began to construct a riverbed sill, a crosswise dam-like structure at the river bottom, to regulate water flow.
• As a short-term solution, the government sank two barges near Paks to raise the water levels enough so that the plant's two turbines could be kept working while the riverbed sill was under construction. REUTERS

Taiwan’s National Security Council expands role in countering Chinese pressure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
08:55:46 UTC
17:55:46 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s National Security Council (NSC) has taken on a broader role in countering Chinese coercion, according to Nikkei Asia.
Nikkei Asia cited multiple sources as saying the council is driving military and civil defense reforms aimed at bolstering asymmetric warfare capabilities and whole-of-society resilience. The sources said the council is also coordinating with other government ministries and conducting diplomatic outreach to garner international support for Taiwan.
Referring to the military’s focus on drones, Tristan Tang, a nonresident fellow at the National Bureau of Asian Research, said, “The NSC is important because it helps the president develop and coordinate that policy, track how the defense ministry is implementing it, and identify problems that may require intervention,” per Nikkei Asia.
“Militaries are naturally conservative institutions, so political authority from NSC can be important in pushing major defense reforms forward,” Tang said.
Over the past 10 years, the NSC has taken on a broader role because the boundaries among security, foreign policy, and domestic policy have become less clear, a former senior NSC official told Nikkei Asia.
Issues such as international trade policy and technology restrictions are now more closely linked to Taiwan’s foreign affairs and national security decisions rather than being treated separately.
“The NSC has emerged as the core executive power of security and intelligence and policymaking,” the former official said.
An official from a G7 government, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the NSC has played an important role in improving Taiwan’s maritime security, Nikkei Asia reported. The official also praised NSC Deputy Secretary-General Lin Fei-fan (林飛帆) for “truly impressive” work on urban resilience.
“I’m not sure other countries could pull together such an ambitious agenda, at all levels of government, this fast,” the official added.
However, a Western official warned that the NSC and the government must accelerate reforms in asymmetric warfare and civil defense, according to Nikkei Asia.
“The urgency is implementing the changes in the armed forces, not think-tank style discussions,” the official said.
British lawmaker Tom Tugendhat said Taiwan is already facing online and offline attacks, as well as maritime intimidation. Without better coordination, he warned, Taiwan could be “divided and overwhelmed by Beijing before it can mount any meaningful response.”
Britain and Japan have recently moved to establish new intelligence bodies. Philip Shetler-Jones, an Indo-Pacific security expert at the UK’s Royal United Services Institute, said there was room for cooperation between the NSC and these agencies.
Given Japan’s acknowledgment that a Taiwan emergency is also a Japanese one, “it is natural that the new intelligence services would benefit from a link with Taiwan’s NSC as a source of information to complete assessments on a potential crisis,” Shetler-Jones said.
Earlier this month, NSC Secretary-General Joseph Wu (吳釗燮) told Nikkei Asia that the council had not changed its mission but had expanded its priorities.
“In the old days, defense of Taiwan was a responsibility of the (Ministry of National Defense),” Wu said. “But nowadays, thinking about the resilience of Taiwan’s government or Taiwan society as a whole, we need to coordinate among government agencies so that when a crisis comes, whether it’s a natural or man-made disaster, society can understand how they can survive, how they can help themselves, and how they can help others.”

Kazakhstan parliamentary vote to cement president's power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
08:54:00 UTC
17:54:00 KST

Kazakhstan parliamentary vote cements president's power
Published August 23, 2026last updated August 23, 2026
Kazakhstan's ruling party comforably won an election for the country's new, single-chamber parliament on Sunday, according to exit polls.
State television shared three exit polls giving the Adilet party between 70% and 72% of the vote.
The vote comes after a new constitution approved in March did away with the Senate to create a new unicameral Kurultai — a reference to the medieval councils of the region's nomadic past.
Backers of the new body say it will give parliament more say in decision making, critics argue it will only cement the power of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev.
The 73-year-old took the reins from authoritarian Nursultan Nazarbayev — who himself ruled the country for 30 years after the collapse of the Soviet Union — in 2019.
The pro-presidential Adilet party was expected to win an overwhelming majority in Sunday's vote, while exit polls showed four smaller parties loyal to Tokayev also won seats in the new parliament.
Seven state-approved parties have been allowed to field candidates for the 145-seat parliament while genuine opposition parties have been banned.
The election took place amid soaring inflation (which is hovering around 10.2%) and rising taxes, fueling concerns for the government — and particularly Tokayev — of a repeat of January 2022 cost of living unrest that left 238 protesters and police dead.
Press crackdown and financial strain color Kazakhstan's election
Beyond financial strain, Sunday's vote also took place against the background of crackdowns on press freedom, with numerous reporters under house arrest and official criminal cases being brought against 10 independent journalists and bloggers.
Tokayev, a former Soviet official and Kazakh diplomat who worked at the UN, touted his reforms and justified the many changes he has initiated — including the introduction of the new constitution — as necessary in a fast-changing world.
"Without a doubt, these elections will be remembered as perhaps the most interesting in our country's history," said Tokayev on Friday.
"Amid unprecedented geopolitical tensions and mounting global challenges, we must firmly and consistently implement our strategy to transform Kazakhstan into a truly developed state," he added.
Tokayev has sought to maintain a delicate balance between Moscow — with their shared Soviet ties — and the West since sanctions were imposed on Russia over its invasion of Ukraine. Resource-rich and strategically located Kazakhstan also has ties to China and the European Union.
Although Tokayev has said that he has no plans of staying in power beyond his current term, the constitutional reform that 87% of voters backed this March effectively reset term limits for the office — making him eligible to run for another seven-year stint in 2029 should he change his mind.

Russian attacks kill 5, injure 44 across Ukraine over past day, as jet-powered drone hits passenger train in Odesa Oblast
Russian attacks killed at least 5 people and injured at least 44 across Ukraine over the past day, as its forces attacked a passenger train in Odesa Oblast, local authorities said on Aug. 22-23.
In Odesa Oblast, a Russian jet-powered attack drone hit a passenger train that was traveling from Zhytomyr to Odesa, Ukrainian Railways CEO Oleksandr Pertsovskyi said in a post on Facebook on Aug. 23.
There were 593 passengers on board, including 15 children, but no casualties were reported as an evacuation was ordered in time and the train was brought to an emergency halt on the track, Pertsovskyi said.
Alongside the attack on Odesa Oblast, Russian forces launched 127 drones across Ukraine overnight on Aug. 23, the Air Force said.
Ukrainian air defense downed 97 drones over the north, south, and east of the country. Twenty-seven drones made it through and struck 22 locations, and the debris of downed drones was found at three locations, the report read.
In southeastern Zaporizhzhia Oblast, three people were killed, and 20 were injured by Russian attacks, regional governor Ivan Fedorov said on Aug. 23. Russian forces carried out 559 attacks on 40 settlements in Zaporizhzhia Oblast over the past day, Fedorov said.
He later added at around 10 a.m. local time that Russia attacked the area around a shopping center in the city of Zaporizhzhia. A 49-year-old man was injured as a result of the attack.
In eastern Donetsk Oblast, two people were killed and five injured in Russian strikes in the region over the past day, governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In southern Kherson Oblast, Russian attacks in the region injured 11 people, regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin said.
In northeastern Kharkiv Oblast, over the past day, three people were injured, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
Ukraine's State Emergency Service reported on Aug. 23 that overnight Russia launched a drone attack on a post office in the town of Lozova, Kharkiv Oblast, and a fire broke out covering an area of 350 square meters.
Russian attacks on Dnipropetrovsk Oblast injured two people over the past day, Governor Oleksandr Hanzha reported, according to the reports published on Aug. 22 and Aug. 23.
July of 2026 saw the most civilians killed or injured in Ukraine since March 2022, according to the U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine (HRMMU).
At least 437 civilians in Ukraine were killed and 2,610 injured in July alone, the monitoring group said on Aug. 13. This represents a 30% increase from June, which previously held the record for the deadliest month since April 2022.
Ukrainian civilian casualties in July 2026 were 70% higher than July the previous year, while casualties among children also rose to their highest level since April 2022, with 17 children killed and 166 injured.

Prime minister in Kyiv: Russia shouldn't count on us tiring of Ukraine support
Ukraine must receive everything it needs to defend itself, Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform) said as he arrived in Kyiv for an NB8 summit with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Michal is in the Ukrainian capital on Sunday and will co-chair a summit of Nordic-Baltic (NB8) and Ukrainian leaders with Zelenskyy, and will take part in events marking Ukraine's National Flag Day.
Estonia holds the NB8 presidency this year, and Michal's visit comes at a time of intensified attacks by Russia on Kyiv and Ukraine and stalled diplomatic efforts.
The visit also closely follows the 35th anniversary of the restoration of Estonian independence. "This year marks 35 years since Estonia restored its independence and Ukraine declared its independence. Both our countries secured the right to decide their own future. Today, Ukraine is defending that right on the battlefield while standing up for the freedom and security of all Europe," Michal said.
The Nordic and Baltic countries have stood with Ukraine since the first day of Russia's full-scale war of aggression, now in its fifth year. "Ukraine must receive everything it needs to defend itself and resist Russian aggression," the prime minister went on, via a press release.
He noted that "everything Ukraine needs" primarily means more air defense, more ammunition and greater investment in Ukraine's defense industry. "At the same time, we must increase pressure on Russia, strengthen sanctions and close the loopholes Russia uses to evade them," Michal added.
"We are helping Ukraine prepare for winter and protect and restore critical energy infrastructure, which remains under threat because of Russia's brutality," the head of government went on.
While in Kyiv, Michal will meet his Ukrainian counterpart, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi, to discuss bilateral relations and preparations for the Ukraine Recovery Conference to be held in Tallinn in January next year.
Michal's visit also coincides with Ukraine's National Flag Day, which is marked annually on August 23.
The NB8 format brings together the Nordic countries — Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden — and the Baltic states — Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania — for regular dialogue on security and regional issues. Following the summit, a joint press conference is expected to outline outcomes and new commitments, as Estonia's NB8 presidency has placed regional security and support for Ukraine at the top of the agenda.
Estonia has been one of Ukraine's strongest supporters since the full-scale invasion began in February 2022, providing military aid, humanitarian assistance and political backing, while consistently calling for increased international pressure on Russia. The Reconstruction Conference in Tallinn next January will bring together international partners to coordinate Ukraine's long-term recovery, and Michal's visit continues a pattern of high-level engagement between the two countries.
Michal's visit is scheduled to last one day, with the prime minister returning to Estonia later Sunday.
The summit comes as diplomatic efforts to end the war remain stalled, with Russia insisting any deal must reflect "realities on the ground" — a reference to its control of around one-fifth of Ukrainian territory. On the battlefield, fighting has intensified, while Russia continues its long-range strikes on Ukrainian cities . Ukraine has expanded its own deep strikes inside Russia.

Pollard later said the only way to prevent another October 7 was to place people he trusted in positions of responsibility.
“The only way to prevent another October 7 is to put people like you in positions of responsibility, because I know where your heart is,” he told Haskel. “You fought for me without boasting about it. You were quiet, loyal and effective. And that is what we need in the new Knesset.”
Pollard, 72, is an American-born Jew who spied for Israel while working as a civilian intelligence analyst for the U.S. Navy in Washington. He was arrested by the FBI in 1985 and pleaded guilty to providing classified information to Israel. He was sentenced to life in prison in 1987.
He was released on parole in 2015, and after restrictions on his movement expired, he moved to Israel in 2020.
Pollard has previously weighed into Israeli election campaigns. In 2022, ahead of the previous election, he announced his support for former interior minister Ayelet Shaked, only to withdraw the endorsement later the same day following pressure from figures on the Israeli right.
Haskel welcomed Pollard’s support, describing it as a significant boost for her party.
“Israel First is receiving meaningful support from an Israeli hero who paid an extremely heavy personal price for his commitment to Israel and the Jewish people,” she said. “To hear from him that he places his trust in me is a great privilege and a great responsibility.”

Ukraine continues talks on using Starlink in Russia for long-range drones – Zelensky
President Volodymyr Zelensky said this while speaking with journalists, according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
“In the first half of this year, I received a request from the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine to find a way to reach an agreement with President Trump on using Starlink in the Russian Federation for our defense purposes. “Today, it is all in the hands of the President of the United States, and they are having their own internal discussions. I did what I was asked to do. I did it during two meetings,” Zelensky said.
The president also noted that he had involved other world leaders in promoting the idea.
Earlier, media outlets reported that Trump had not supported Ukraine’s request for his assistance in obtaining Musk’s permission to use Starlink for Ukrainian long-range drones in Russia.

Expert outlines three pillars of counter-drone strategy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
08:43:00 UTC
17:43:00 KST

News of the story 
        
                "On Point"
        
    
                                                              
            
                                                                              
            
                                    MINSK, 23 August (BelTA) - To successfully counter drones, it is necessary to develop air defense and electronic warfare systems that can neutralize the threat posed by unmanned aerial vehicles, military observer with the Russian newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda, Colonel (retired) Viktor Baranets said in the latest episode of BelTA’s V Teme [On Point] project.
Speaking about improving counter-drone systems, Viktor Baranets noted that Russia is actively working on interceptor drones - unmanned aerial vehicles designed to destroy enemy UAVs. “Unique systems have already emerged, but we are still in the acceleration phase. It will take some time to produce such drones on an industrial scale,” the military observer said.
 
Another area in counter-drone efforts, he noted, is the improvement of air defense systems. “We are thinking about how to make them more effective. There has never been, is not, and will not be for a long time an air defense system in the world that destroys 100% of enemy threats. We can only improve the effectiveness of neutralizing this menace. For Russia, there is no more global or important task than minimizing drone attacks, which are growing in number and penetrating deeper into Russian territory,” the military observer said.
 
Equally important is the development of electronic warfare systems, Viktor Baranets added. Advanced EW systems can “burn out the brains” of drones, neutralizing the threat they pose. “We are also in search mode in this area. Although the groundwork we already have is quite substantial. But we need to keep moving forward,” he added.

Reaffirming the Unbroken Canon in Ukraine’s 35 Years of Modern Independent Statehood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
08:42:00 UTC
17:42:00 KST

As Ukraine marks the 35th anniversary of its restored independence, its foundational documents affirm that modern Ukrainian statehood is not a Soviet residue or a post-Cold War accident, but the fulfillment of a long constitutional and political trajectory.
Nowhere is this continuity clearer than in a side-by-side reading of Ukraine’s two modern declarations of independence: the Fourth Universal of the Ukrainian Central Rada (Ukraine’s de facto parliament at the time) proclaimed on Jan. 22, 1918, and the Act of Declaration of Independence of Ukraine, adopted on Aug. 24, 1991, by the republic’s parliament, the Verkhovna Rada.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Separated by 73 years of Soviet suppression, forced famine, and totalitarian violence, these two texts read like sequential chapters of a single constitutional manifesto: crises engineered from Moscow, an unbroken lineage of Ukrainian state-building, a rejection of imperial rule in favor of uncompromised sovereignty, legitimacy grounded in the democratic will of the people.
But between them is silence that tells us as much about the fragility of independence as the declarations themselves do about its legitimacy.
                                                                                                                                                                         
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul Arrives in Kyiv
Ukraine’s modern declarations of independence compared
Recall the atmosphere in Kyiv during the winter of 1917-18. The Russian Empire had collapsed into revolution, and the Ukrainian Central Rada led by the historian Mykhailo Hrushevsky, had initially sought autonomy within a reformed, democratic Russian federation. But as Vladimir Lenin’s Bolshevik regime launched a military invasion against the fledgling Ukrainian state, federalist illusions evaporated.
The Fourth Universal opens not with abstract theory but with the plain language of emergency, describing four years of war, economic collapse, and encroaching famine, before naming the immediate catalyst: Russian troops advancing on Kyiv to crush Ukraine’s young democracy.
Then comes the constitutional turn: “From this day forth, the Ukrainian People’s Republic becomes an independent, subjection-to-no-one, free, sovereign state of the Ukrainian people.”
Seventy-three years later, history repeated its cadence. On Aug. 24, 1991, in the immediate aftermath of the failed hardline coup in Moscow, Ukraine’s parliament convened in Kyiv.
Drafted by the democratic minority that included former political prisoners, the Act of Declaration of Independence was short, urgent, and historically decisive. Like its 1918 predecessor, it opens by invoking crisis: “In view of the mortal danger that hung over Ukraine in connection with the coup d’état in the USSR...”
It places the decision on three pillars – a thousand-year tradition of Ukrainian state development, the right to self-determination under the UN Charter, and the execution of the 1990 Declaration of State Sovereignty. With those words, the Soviet empire was legally dissolved on Ukrainian soil.
Ukraine’s Act of Declaration of Independence
Set beside each other, the two documents reveal the enduring mechanics of Ukrainian statehood. Independence in both cases was a matter of self-defense, not aggressive nationalism – a bulwark against instability and imperial manipulation, not a quest for territory or glory.
Each marks the exact moment Ukrainian leaders recognized that coexistence within a Russian-dominated federation was impossible – in 1917 the Rada sought autonomy and got war; in 1991 Ukraine was being pressured into settling for a reformed union treaty but got a coup aiming to preserve Moscow-rule over the crumbling Soviet empire.
Sovereignty, in each text, belongs to the people themselves rather than to a monarch or a party elite: the 1918 Universal vests power exclusively in the people of Ukraine, the 1991 Act invokes universal democratic principles and international law.
The aspiration behind these declarations reaches further back than either 1918 or 1991. The 1991 Act’s reference to a “thousand-year tradition” gestures toward the medieval statehood of Kyivan Rus, the democratic customs of the Cossack Hetmanate, and Pylyp Orlyk’s 1710 Constitution – one of Europe’s earliest attempts to limit executive power by written law.
Early modern maps labeled the region Ukraine, terra Cossacorum – “Ukraine, land of the Cossack” – while Orlyk’s own defiant phrase, Ucraina, quae libera semper fuit, “Ukraine, which was always free,” captured a belief that self-governance was inherent, not granted by a tsar. The great Voltaire conveyed this sentiment when he wrote in 1731 “Ukraine has always aspired to be free.”
In the 19th century, the poet Taras Shevchenko carried that conviction through generations of imperial suppression, turning the memory of Cossack freedom into a modern political awakening. Long before 1918, in other words, Ukrainians had already insisted – in law, in cartography, in verse – that they governed, or sought to govern, themselves.
How and why Ukraine’s first modern declaration of independence has been ignored
And yet, for all it shares with its 1918 predecessor, the 1991 Act withheld something crucial: any mention of 1918 itself. It does not name the Fourth Universal, does not acknowledge that Ukraine had proclaimed – and briefly held and fought for – modern independence once before.
That silence is not a minor omission. It reveals how deeply Soviet historical consciousness had penetrated even the moment of its own undoing.
The parliament that voted for independence in 1991 still held a Communist majority, inherited from the very system it was leaving. To acknowledge 1918 openly meant admitting that Ukrainian independence had a pre-Soviet history – that the Ukrainian SSR was not Ukraine’s original or natural form but the product of conquest and forced incorporation.
It meant recasting 1991 as restoration rather than creation: a renewal of sovereignty violently interrupted, not a first arrival at it. Whatever calculus individual deputies made, the effect was to let Ukraine’s newest independence appear unprecedented, experimental, uncertain – Soviet in origin even as it broke from Soviet rule.
The consequences were not merely symbolic. By declining to fasten itself to 1918, Ukraine’s new state missed a chance to root itself in a deeper constitutional memory – to insist that it was not a novice learning self-rule for the first time, but a nation reclaiming a sovereignty it had already, however briefly, exercised and lost.
Instead, the country inherited a subtler version of the narrative it was trying to escape: that Ukrainian statehood began with Soviet power and that anything before it was prelude, irrelevant, or illegitimate.
The perpetuation of a damaging myth
The importance of what had occurred on Jan. 22, 1918, was further obscured under President Leonid Kuchma in early 2001 by his focusing on what had happened exactly a year after the Fourth Universal.
On Jan. 22, 1919, the union of central and western Ukraine was proclaimed by the representatives of their respective independent republics even as they were fighting the Russians in the east and the Poles in the west. Of course, this too is an important historic date. But the seemingly calculated celebration on Jan. 22 only of the “Day of Unity” had the effect of removing the Ukraine’s first modern declaration of independence from national memory.
It is worth recalling that this occurred when the “patriotic” Viktor Yushchenko was already Kuchma’s prime minister. The same president went on to publish a book named “Ukraine is not Russia,” and when Yushchenko was himself elected president he did not set the record straight about the significance of Jan. 22, 1918.
This half-completed reckoning helps explain why decommunization proceeded so haltingly through the 1990s, why Soviet-era elites slid so easily into post-Soviet institutions, and why Ukraine struggled for years to articulate a national identity distinct from both Soviet and Russian frameworks.
Even in 2018, on the centenary of Ukraine’s declaration of independence, the then also “patriotic” president, Petro Poroshenko, observed Jan. 22 in the presence of foreign diplomats as simply the Day of Unity. President Zelensky also seems to be neglecting to emphasize that independence was declared in early 1918 and the attempt to unite western and central Ukraine in one sovereign state followed logically a year later.
Lessons for today
In 1991 the formal empire had fallen; the revolution in consciousness took much longer – and in some respects is still underway.
That unfinished work of memory is not an academic footnote to the present war – it is one of its stakes. Russia’s invasion is not a contemporary border dispute; it is the latest iteration of a centuries-old imperial campaign to deny that Ukraine has ever governed itself or ever had the right to.
Just as Lenin’s forces invaded Ukraine in 1918 under the language of “brotherly assistance,” Putin’s forces invaded in 2022 claiming to rescue a country from an identity it does not, in Moscow’s telling, own. The argument has not changed in a century. Only the weapons have.
The failure to hold the state won in 1918 offers a sober lesson that Ukrainians have not forgotten: internal fragmentation and insufficient outside support allowed the Bolsheviks to conquer a fledgling republic, and the price was seven decades of totalitarian rule, the engineered starvation of millions in the Holodomor, and the attempted erasure of a people’s memory of itself and their very identity.
Ukraine’s 1991 declaration should have said, plainly, that it had happened before, had been crushed, and was now being restored. It did not say so.
But 35 years on, during a protracted war fought explicitly over the question of whether Ukraine has the right to exist as a sovereign state, Ukrainians are saying yes and still reclaiming a thousand years that no empire’s manipulation or internal foes can undo.
Ukraine was not created by bureaucratic fiat, and it was not created by the collapse of an empire it happened to be trapped inside of. It was built on an ancient inheritance of self-rule, reasserted at moments of mortal danger, and is now being defended by a generation that understands, with total clarity, what earlier generations sometimes could not yet say aloud: without a sovereign state, there is no liberty, no democracy, and no peace worth the name.
As Ukraine celebrates its 35th anniversary of modern independent statehood, it is time Ukraine’s current government set the record straight and finally acknowledge unambivalently that Aug. 24, 1991 was an affirmation of what had already occurred on Jan. 22, 1918, and what the patriots of the day were also fighting for.
There are no more excuses for forgetting or pretending that it was otherwise.
The author is completing a book examining Ukraine’s first 35 years of modern independent statehood, provisionally titled “Indomitable Ukraine 1991-2026: The Reemergence of a European Nation.”
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.

The judiciary said Majid Adineh had been convicted of "operational action in favour of hostile groups" in nationwide rallies that broke out late last year.
Adineh is one of a string of people put to death over the protests, which were sparked by economic hardships in Iran.
He was accused of "deliberate arson, gathering and collusion with the intention of committing crimes against the country's internal security", the judiciary's Mizan Online website said in a report Sunday.
"Based on numerous documents and evidence in the case and the defendant's statements, the Karaj Revolutionary Court sentenced him to death and confiscation of all his property."
An appeal by Adineh was unsuccessful and the Supreme Court upheld the verdict, with his execution carried out Sunday morning, Mizan said.
Iran warns countries joining US sanctions considered 'enemy'
Iran on Saturday warned countries against participating in the United States' economic war against the Islamic Republic, saying they would be considered enemies.
Washington has pushed its allies to back its new campaign to isolate the Iranian economy, as the President Trump's unpopular war drags toward the six-month mark.
"We declare to all countries... do not join the economic war waged by the United States," said Mohsen Rezaei, the head of Iran's supreme national security council, on state television.
"Any country participating in the imposition of economic restrictions against us is considered an enemy," he added.
If the countries concerned refused to "distance themselves" from the United States, Iran would "harm" their interests, he added.
Rezaei also said that the Islamic Republic had more cards to play in the war, claiming that "we have not yet attacked any American economic interests".
"So far, we have only targeted military bases, but if they want to impose economic sanctions on us, the United States has oil and economic companies around Iran and elsewhere, and we will strike them," he said.
Should Trump "take action, our confrontation will be like an earthquake", he added.

Congress MP Deepender Hooda (File photo)
NEW DELHI: Congress MP Deepender Hooda on Sunday denied calling Sajjan Kumar a “role model” following the ex-Congress leader’s death on August 20.Kumar was serving two life sentences in connection with the 1984 anti-Sikh riots and died at the age of 80.When reporters asked Hooda if he had called Kumar a "role model," he replied, “I did not use the words, nor did I harbour any such sentiment. These words are being put in my mouth by those who wish to play politics by undermining the spirit of brotherhood.”“As for the Sikh community, people know that we have always stood by them and supported them in every way. We share a centuries-old bond of brotherhood with Sikhs; our family has been connected with them through both joys and sorrows, and we have stood by them in every struggle," he added.Hooda, son of former Haryana chief minister Bhupinder Singh Hooda, described the anti-Sikh riots as a “grave injustice” and demanded strict punishment for the guilty.“A grave injustice took place; the guilty must face strict punishment; the Sikh community deserves justice — this has been our consistent stance. We stand fully with the Sikh community,” he said.Condoling Kumar's demise, Hooda had termed it a “loss to the country’s political landscape”, and praised the former Lok Sabha MP for his “connect with people and contribution to Delhi’s development”.
The comments drew sharp reactions, particularly in poll-bound Punjab, where the SAD, BJP and AAP hit out at the Congress over its “anti-Sikh mindset”. Leaders from his own party also condemned the remarks.Congress leader and former Punjab chief minister Charanjit Singh Channi described Kumar as a “murderer of Sikhs” and a “traitor”.“He conspired to have Sikhs killed... Far from being a role model, even uttering his name is a sin. If such people become role models, the country will be destroyed,” Channi said.Punjab Congress president Amrinder Singh Raja Warring also sought to distance the state unit from Hooda's statement, saying it may have reflected the Rohtak MP's “personal view”.
AAP MLA from Punjab Kuldeep Singh Dhaliwal stated that the wounds of the 1984 anti-Sikh massacre were still alive in the hearts of Sikhs, calling Kumar’s remarks deeply hurtful to the community.“If a senior Congress leader calls Sajjan Kumar his role model, it raises serious questions about the mindset and politics of the party,” Dhaliwal remarked.Punjab BJP president Kewal Singh Dhillon also said the wounds of the victim families remained unhealed.“At such a sensitive time, describing a key convict in the 1984 anti-Sikh riots as a role model was a condemnable attempt to rub salt on the wounds of the victim families and reopen their painful memories,” Dhillon said.(With PTI inputs)

Syria expects to resume negotiations with Israel, aiming for IDF withdrawal, foreign minister says

17:32:34 KST

Syria expects negotiations to resume soon with Israel over a security deal it hopes will lead to Israel's withdrawal from Syrian land, a top Syrian minister said, urging Israel to seize a "historic opportunity" as the door for diplomacy is open.
In a Reuters interview in Damascus on Saturday, days after Israel bombed a Syrian airbase, Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani also stressed that Damascus' priority is to halt Israeli attacks, saying confidence-building steps were needed in this direction.
Washington has been seeking to forge a security deal between Israel and the government of Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, a new US ally in the Middle East, for over a year. But it has proven elusive as Israel has sent troops into Syrian territory and attacked government assets, citing threats to its security.
Shaibani said negotiations over the security agreement had been frozen since the start of the Iran war, but he expected them to restart. Contact between Syria and Israel was cut after the airbase strike, he said.
"We believe there should be contact, especially with a party that constantly threatens the security of Syria. But if this contact doesn’t bring results, then we don’t need it," Shaibani said. "We do not trust Israel currently."
The Israeli prime minister's office did not respond to a request for comment.
Sharaa has said Syria poses no threat to other countries, with Damascus focused on rebuilding from 14 years of war.
Israeli officials have talked about a range of potential dangers in Syria since Bashar al-Assad was toppled, with some describing the new rulers as barely disguised jihadists last year, even as Sharaa forged close US ties.
In the days after Assad fell in 2024, Israel seized territory in southwest Syria, citing the need to safeguard its citizens against attack, and bombed scores of Syrian military sites.
US pressuring Israel to return to dialogue with Syria, Shaibani claims
"Israel has tried to maintain its security through brute force, and it hasn’t succeeded" anywhere, Shaibani said. "I believe negotiations will resume soon."
No date has been set.
"The US is trying continuously to put pressure on Israel to return to the dialogue table," he added.
Asked how optimistic he was, Shaibani said: "It’s very hard to bet on Israel." But Syria had "very great hope" of building stable relationships with its neighbors.
"Syria is extending its hand for understandings, for peace, for diplomacy" and regional stability.
Tensions over Syria were brought into focus on Tuesday when Israel bombed the Abu al-Duhur airbase, saying Damascus was about to allow Turkish forces to deploy there. Syria and Turkey denied the claim.
Shaibani said Syria respected Israel's security concerns but that Israel must respect those of Syria, including Israel's use of its airspace, Israeli raids, and arrests in the south.
He said that around the beginning of the year, the sides had "agreed on paper to almost everything" regarding a security deal that would require Israel to stop attacking Syria and was tied to its withdrawal from territory seized after Assad fell.
The deal would include several security zones in Syrian territory near the Israeli border, including a buffer zone where only the United Nations would be present, and others where Syrian forces would deploy in varying degrees of force.
But he said Israel had sought to evade implementation, adding: "We did not see they had the real will to reach an agreement."
Syria and Israel have technically been in a state of war since 1948. Israel seized the Golan Heights from Syria in a 1967 war.
The priority now is to "stop Israeli aggression even before reaching a security agreement", Shaibani said. "Then perhaps we can open the topics of peace and the Golan."
Washington working on conflict-prevention mechanism for Israel, Turkey, Syria
US special envoy for Syria Tom Barrack said on Tuesday that Washington was working to establish a mechanism to prevent conflict among Israel, Turkey, and Syria.
Shaibani said there was no agreement yet on the mechanism, which he said must stop attacks and pave the way for the security deal rather than "entrenching... Israeli occupation."
The US State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Shaibani said Israel had bombed Abu al-Duhur even after Syria conveyed a message that it would not be a Turkish base.
Syria draws on Turkish support in military training and cooperation, he said, noting that this was also the case with Jordan, Saudi Arabia, and others.
Damascus was thankful for Turkey’s support in rebuilding its military “and we won’t forgo support," he said.

Cole Robert Worthy, 17, Theo Rae, 17, Makai Saddington, 18, and 23-year-olds Michael Robert Cahill and Jacob Matusiak died when their Volkswagen Passat, believed to be using cloned plates, collided with a marked armed response vehicle early on Saturday near Middlesbrough.
Blades, 37, and Clough, 38, of Cleveland police, who were also killed in the collision, had been driving in the correct direction. Tributes have been paid to the officers, with their chief constable, Victoria Fuller, describing them as “brave officers protecting our communities”.
Clough’s family described him as “our hero with a fantastic sense of humour” and someone who “jumped into action whenever needed, and [was] willing to help anyone for any reason”.
In a statement issued via Cleveland police, the family said Clough had “proudly fought for his country to make the world a better place. Always on public duty throughout his short life.
“We as a family and Tom’s partner would like to express our sincere gratitude for the overwhelming support and condolences from friends, colleagues and the wider community.”
Blades’ wife said the pain of losing him is “beyond words” and the family’s lives “will never be the same”.
In a statement issued through the force, she said: “No words will ever feel like the right words to honour our Matt – my beloved husband, my best friend, and the most devoted father to our two young boys.
“He was an adored son and brother, a perfect son-in-law, and the most fun uncle. He was loved beyond words by all his family and friends, and his loss has left a space that can never be filled.

“The pain of losing him is beyond words, and our lives will never be the same. Neither will the love he gave us ever fade.

“He may have left this world committed to the duty he believed in, but his greatest legacy will always be the love he gave to his family.”
Blades’ wife, who has not been named, also expressed “deepest gratitude and heartfelt thanks” to the police and emergency services and concluded: “Forever loved. Forever missed. Forever our superhero.”
A local football club, Seaton Carew FC, said Blades had recently joined as coach and was preparing for the season with the new under-sevens Seahawks team. “He was looking forward to being part of the team and, most importantly, to coaching his own son, who is going to be playing for the Seahawks this season,” the club said on social media.
“Matty and his oldest son are much-loved members of our club and our U10 Lions football family. Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with Matty’s wife, his two boys, and all of his family and friends at this incredibly difficult and heartbreaking time.”

At that point the pursuit was aborted, the IOPC said. “Approximately 10 seconds later, the Passat collided with another police vehicle which was not involved in the pursuit but in the area to assist in a search for the Passat believed to be using cloned plates that had activated an ANPR camera.”

“I do want to place on record my tribute to PC Blades and PC Clough. The bravery that we see from our police officers every day, every night is incredible. No one should not come home to their families at the end of their shift.”

Security camera footage from local houses appeared to show the police pursuit moments before the fatal crash on the A66.

Thank you to the emergency services responding in incredibly difficult circumstances. I would urge people to avoid speculation at this time.”

The young men in the car were named by Cleveland police on Sunday afternoon. The force said family liaison officers were working with the families.

Asia is reaching for the open road that Chinese AI offers

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23

Asia is reaching for the open road that Chinese AI offers
Countries seeking sovereign AI want to control their own AI capabilities rather than rent them from a foreign platform
At a recent Apec digital technology and AI forum in Chengdu, ministers across the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum issued a statement in support of open-source artificial intelligence models – a rare point of agreement in a debate often framed as a zero-sum US-China contest.
Across the region, countries are entering that order along three distinct roads: the flagship national model built directly on a Chinese base, the government pilot that puts Chinese systems into public services, and the private start-up that ships on whatever is most open. China’s rising influence flows from aligning with those goals rather than from any strategy that has outpaced Washington’s.
The economics leave little room for hesitation. Building a frontier model costs billions of dollars and demands rare talent, leaving just China and the United States still training at the frontier. For everyone else, an open Chinese model removes the barrier: the weights are free, they run on local servers without sending data abroad, and they cost 60 to 90 per cent less to operate than the leading American systems while trailing by only months.

Dying with dignity, living with freedom: Denis Côté on ‘Nobody’s Violence’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
08:30:00 UTC
17:30:00 KST

Dying with dignity, living with freedom: Denis Côté on ‘Nobody’s Violence’
In his latest film, premiered in Locarno, Canadian filmmaker Denis Côté follows a woman who delivers assisted death to strangers. But beneath the film’s meditation on mortality lies a deeply personal story of illness, survival and artistic renewal.
Though Switzerland has historically been home to some of the highest rates of assisted suicide in the world, a new player has joined the global leaderboard: Quebec, the home province of Canadian filmmaker Denis Côté, where reports indicate that medical assistance in dying (the Canadian term, with the acronym MAID) now accounts for roughly 8% of all deaths annually.
Côté, a longtime regular at the Locarno Film Festival, where he’s collected more than a few awards since his debut in 2005, insists that his latest film, Nobody’s Violence (Violence du corps de l’autre in the original French), is not intended as a political statement on assisted suicide.
“Obviously I’m going to get some questions about that with my film,” Côté told Swissinfo. “But it’s not a documentary. It’s not a comment on the subject.”
Perhaps viewers ought to be the judge: Nobody’s Violence stars frequent Côté collaborator Larissa Corriveau as Mira, a young woman who says little and about whom we know even less, only that her job seems to consist of providing a fatal poison to people that have requested it.
Life and death à la canadienne
MAID – only legal in Canada since 2016, some 70 years after it was legalised in Switzerland – has been a hot-button issue in Côté’s home country. Plans to make individuals who suffer from mental health issues eligible for assisted suicide have been delayed until 2027, a postponement being challenged in court and in the pages of The New York TimesExternal link. It’s an uncomfortable national conversation and one that, willingly or not, Coté’s latest quasi-experimental fiction film participates in.
In Côté’s lengthy filmography (he says he tries to produce a film a year), Nobody’s Violence harkens most closely back to Ghost Town Anthology (2019), his first collaboration with Corriveau, also shot on Super 16mm film, and also set in rural Quebec. The earlier film was Côté’s attempt, in his way, at a horror film. In a tiny Quebecois town, the closure of a local mine prompts existential questions for the population’s continued viability, questions that are exacerbated when the recently deceased begin to appear walking the town’s empty streets.
Côté stages a strange interplay of life and death in these two films, speaking of mortality as a practical reality for his characters to deal with. In Ghost Town Anthology, civic leaders convene at a town hall to discuss the living dead. “You will probably continue to see these apparitions,” one public official says. “Our advice is to stay calm, and try to live your lives as usual.”
More
How film and literature have influenced the acceptance of assisted suicide
Looking at death up close
If removing death from its discursive pedestal and dealing with it in pragmatic terms is the mandate of MAID advocates, it was also a matter of necessity for Côté when he was writing Nobody’s Violence. In 2007 he was diagnosed with kidney insufficiency, a condition that worsened significantly over the years. He wrote Nobody’s Violence at his lowest point: kidneys functioning at 15%, wondering if he would soon be able to function at all without dialysis.
“Ghost Town was connected with my degenerative situation,” Côté said of this dark time in his life. “Then it got worse and worse. You start having this concrete, unconscious dialogue with death at all times. Since I didn’t want to make an autobiographical film about my condition, for Nobody’s Violence I created this character of Mira.”
Corriveau portrays Mira as a kind of alienated angel of death. In the film’s first section, she arrives demurely at various locales – a car park, a suburban home, a metalhead’s basement – and provides individuals, young and old, with a fatal dose of poison, to be taken with water.
Cinematographer Vincent Biron’s camera admits a certain warmth through its numerous light leaks, but Côté’s film observes a strict formal discipline in these early scenes: when the person has taken the poison, the frame will hold only on Mira. The semantic difference between helping people to kill themselves and killing them oneself is placed under significant pressure in these moments. Watching Mira, the viewer observes as she tries her hardest to maintain a distance from the crucial act: this is nobody’s violence, her face seems to impart, not hers.
Staring at life, reborn
Côté saw something of himself in Mira, with one foot in this world and one, through her work, in the next. “She’s in between worlds,” he mused.
But in August 2023, after Nobody’s Violence was written but before it was shot, Côté’s world changed: he received a long-awaited kidney transplant. His vitality regained, the director started to look at his morose script with fresh eyes. If death had led the dance in previous films, he wanted to give life a turn.
“I just had more energy on set,” he said. “I was ready for everything, and I wanted to insert a lot more liberty into the way we were shooting the film. I was totally open to improvisation and longer days of shooting, which I was too tired for, before. I was open to new ideas.”
The most controversial scene in Nobody’s Violence has nothing to do with MAID. For the middle section of Côté’s film, the taut structure of the opening episodes gives way to an extended improvisatory dinner sequence. Mira self-exiles to the sidelines, and the viewer slowly pieces together that the assembled merrymakers form the shady company for which she works, a black-market MAID alternative.
Côté, to his credit, clarifies nothing, leaving the viewer to languish in mystery for as long as possible – a vibes-based interlude either “flaccid and aimless”, per one review, or exhilarating, depending on taste.
Lost in creation
“I’m a bit like the audience,” Côté said. “I like to be lost in front of my own creation. When you control everything, you’re just executing something. But when you’re in front of that long dinner scene, you don’t know how to put the pieces together. It’s active. It’s fun.”
Fun isn’t a word one might think to apply to Nobody’s Violence at a script level, but the film’s fascinating production history, intertwined with the ups and downs of Côté’s health, introduces a tension in every shot. The script’s fixation on death and mortality vies with the film’s renewed obsession with life, in all its mysteries, light leaks, and flights of fancy. A project about dying with dignity finds inspiration in living with dignity, too.
“I want to continue making these free films,” Côté says at the end of the interview. “I want to try stuff, instead of growing old, growing bourgeois, with these very clean and organised scripts. If I can go on, I want to go on with a very loose cinema.”

Iran official says support for new sanctions would be an ‘act of war,’ and other Middle East news
The new head of Iran’s top security body warned Sunday that Tehran will see any country’s support for new U.S. economic measures against the Islamic Republic as an “act of war,” while Iran’s president defended a memorandum of understanding with the United States as the best way out of the stalled conflict.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday is expected to announce the new measures after the U.S. vowed to impose an “unprecedented” level of economic warfare and isolation on a country that has lived for decades under sanctions. Also Monday, Pakistan’s army chief is expected to visit Iran as mediators try to revive talks.
Meanwhile, attacks calmed on the Strait of Hormuz but posturing did not, as a recently created Iranian authority listed dozens of vessels it said will face restrictions on future transits.
Here’s a look at the latest developments in the Iran war and the wider Middle East on Sunday. Full coverage can be found here.
Iran’s security chief sharpens warning to neighbors
The hard-line leader of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, issued his latest warning on X, with the comments quickly shared by Iranian state media.
It came a day after Rezaei’s most extensive public comments since being named to the post this month.
“If (Trump) wants to do something, we will retaliate in a seismic manner,” he had told the state broadcaster in an interview that aired late Saturday. He said Iran would target other oil-shipping routes from the Persian Gulf — alternatives to the Strait of Hormuz.
Rezaei, a former Revolutionary Guard commander and military adviser to Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, was part of senior appointments widely seen as hardening Tehran’s political and military stance.
Iranian president wants to move past ‘neither war nor peace’
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian earlier Sunday said the memorandum of understanding signed in mid-June was the best way to move beyond a situation of “neither war nor peace,” adding that Tehran can’t attract investment nearly six months after the war began.
“There is not a single provision in this agreement that amounts to capitulation,” Pezeshkian said in a speech published by state-run IRNA. “The supreme leader sets the policies, and we will follow that path.”
The interim deal opened a 60-day period for talks aimed at ending the war and reaching an accord on Iran’s nuclear program. That period ended last week with no signs of compromise or extension.
No attacks confirmed on the strait, but new restrictions
There were no confirmed attacks in the Strait of Hormuz over the past 48 hours, a multinational coalition overseen by the U.S. Navy said Sunday, with shipping traffic still at reduced levels. The U.S. military said its blockade of Iranian ports had redirected 70 commercial ships and disabled three as of Sunday.
Iran’s recently created Persian Gulf Strait Authority, sanctioned by the U.S., published a list of dozens of ships it said had violated arrangements for transiting the strait and would face future restrictions like fines or seizures. The strait had been considered an international waterway before the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28.
Iran and Oman, on the strait’s other side, are now discussing management of it, which likely will include ships paying fees.
Pakistan’s army chief will visit Tehran
Pakistani Field Marshal Asim Munir will lead a delegation to Tehran on Monday, Iranian state television reported, citing Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei.
Two regional officials said the visit was part of Islamabad’s efforts to de-escalate tensions between the United States and Iran and urge them to return to the negotiating table. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the matter publicly.
— By Munir Ahmed in Islamabad
Iran executes man arrested during January protests
The Iranian judiciary’s Mizan news agency reported the latest execution connected to nationwide protests early this year, saying Majid Adineh was arrested Jan. 9 in Mohammadshahr, west of Tehran.
The judiciary said forensic examinations indicated the handgun found on him had been fired on Jan. 8 and 9. Mizan said Adineh had joined the unrest following calls by groups opposed to Iran’s government and alleged that he had received training from groups outside the country. He was convicted under Iran’s law imposing harsher penalties for espionage and cooperation with hostile states.
Israeli settler arrested in beating of Palestinian amputee
Police arrested a 16-year-old boy from the Israeli settlement of Avigayil in the beating of a 61-year-old Palestinian, Saeed Muhammad Ibrahim Rabah, outside his home in the occupied West Bank, a year after he lost a leg after being shot by a settler.
Rabah told The Associated Press that the violence at his home in Khirbet al-Rakeez on Saturday was an effort to make families leave, but “we will remain, no matter what happens.”
Separately, the West Bank Health Ministry said a 14-year-old in the Askar refugee camp in Nablus was shot dead by Israeli forces, who did not immediately comment. The uncle of Islam Maher Ajouri, Nehad Ajouri, called the shooting indiscriminate.
And Israel’s military said it detained a suspect in a stabbing attack that wounded a 24-year-old Israeli man in the area of al-Auja in the West Bank. Israel’s emergency services said the man was in moderate condition.
Airstrike in Gaza kills a 4-year-old child
Four-year-old Mohammed Taha died after an Israeli airstrike hit a central Gaza house on Sunday and wounded at least five others, according to the Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital, which received the casualties.
Israel’s military later said it struck and killed a Hamas commander in central Gaza. The hospital confirmed that the man named, Ismail Abu Ful, was killed.
An Israeli strike in southern Gaza wounded at least seven people, including three children, according to health officials at Nasser Hospital. The military did not immediately comment.
And Defense Minister Israel Katz in a statement said he instructed the military to “act immediately and forcefully” to prevent launches of balloons, kites or drones from Gaza toward nearby Israeli communities.
Before the Oct. 7, 2023, attack by Hamas-led militants on Israel — when 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage — burning kites and balloons were sent from Gaza into southern Israel, causing fires and other damage.
Hamas in a statement Sunday accused Israel of “using children’s toys as a pretext” for attacks and further displacement of Gaza residents.

Syria expects negotiations to resume soon with Israel over a security deal it hopes will lead to Israel's withdrawal from Syrian land, Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani said, urging Israel to seize a "historic opportunity" as the door for diplomacy is open.
In a Reuters interview in Damascus on Saturday, days after Israel bombed a Syrian airbase, al-Shaibani also stressed that Damascus' priority is to halt Israeli attacks, saying confidence-building steps were needed in this direction.
Washington has been seeking to forge a security deal between Israel and the government of Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, a new U.S. ally in the Middle East, for over a year. But it has proven elusive as Israel has sent troops into Syrian territory and attacked government assets, citing threats to its security.

"We believe there should be contact, especially with a party that constantly threatens the security of Syria. But if this contact doesn't bring results, then we don't need it," Shaibani said. "We do not trust Israel currently." The Israeli prime minister's office did not respond to a request for comment.
"Israel has tried to maintain its security through brute force and it hasn't succeeded" anywhere, Shaibani said. "I believe negotiations will resume soon." No date has been set. "The U.S. is trying continuously to put pressure on Israel to return to the dialogue table," he added.
Asked how optimistic he was, Shaibani said: "It's very hard to bet on Israel." But Syria had "very great hope" of building stable relationships with its neighbours. "Syria is extending its hand for understandings, for peace, for diplomacy" and regional stability.

Akhmat Kadyrov's name to be forever inscribed in history of Russia — Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
08:20:25 UTC
17:20:25 KST

MOSCOW, August 23. /TASS/. The name of the first president of the Republic of Chechnya, Akhmat Kadyrov, is forever inscribed in the history of Russia, President Vladimir Putin said in a video message on the occasion of the 75th anniversary of the birth of Akhmat-Khadzhi Kadyrov.
"Today, August 23, would have marked the 75th anniversary of the birth of Akhmat Kadyrov - the first president of the Chechen Republic and a Hero of Russia," the president stated.
"His name has been enshrined forever in the country’s history, and for us he will remain a person whose strength of spirit and unconditional love for his people could overcome evil and make a step to returning peace to the ancient Chechen land," Putin emphasized.
According to him "It was the faith in his people and its future that determined the path in Akhmat Kadyrov’s life, helped him make the most important, very conscious decisions during the dramatic and hard period that Chechnya was going through in the 1990s."
"At the most difficult juncture, when the society was split and divided and the republic was virtually in ruins, Akhmat-Khadzhi took on a tremendous responsibility. His position based on his deep conviction was clear-cut: Chechnya’ destiny is inseparable from that of Russia, and his main objective was not only to stop the fratricidal conflict, but also to put an end to it forever, to revive Chechnya, preserve the entire North Caucasus and to put up a reliable barrier to the aggression of international terrorism supported from abroad by the enemies of Russia’s multiethnic people."
The Russian president pointed out that "Akhmat-Khadzhi was a courageous man, who understood very well how hard the burden was and what risks he was going to take on."
"Being a truly spiritual leader, he managed to lead the people and do everything to bring back peace to the long-suffering Chechnya and confidence about the future to its residents," according to Putin.
"His word and influence rescued many people from the traps set by radicals and false preachers whereas his consistent position delivered a crushing blow to the pseudo religious propaganda and attempts to impose extremist ideology in Chechnya alien to the republic and turn religion into an instrument of statehood destruction," the Russian president noted.
"I remember our meetings and conversations. I remember how he explained to me why he had decided to head Chechnya. ‘Today, he said, we need people ready to sacrifice everything, and if necessary, their lives for the sake of their people’."
"Regretfully, these words were prophetic. He did not manage to accomplish much of what he had planned, and there can be neither forgiveness nor oblivion for that crime, committed despicably and cynically on Victory Day which is sacred to our country," Putin said.
"Akhmat-Khadzhi always believed that Chechnya would be thriving and prosperous. I am confident that he would have been proud of the present-day republic, its transformation and dynamic progress. He would have been proud of how worthy his course is continued by his adherents, above all by his son," the Russian president added.
Akhmat Kadyrov became president of the Chechen Republic in October 2003. On May 9, 2004, he was killed in a bomb blast at a stadium in Chechnya’s capital Grozny during the World War II memorial victory parade.

Powerful storm sweeps across Baltic states, killing 2
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
16:19:47 CST
17:19:47 KST

This photo taken on Aug. 23, 2026 shows the aftermath of a powerful storm in Riga, Latvia. A powerful cyclone swept northward across the three Baltic states on Saturday, killing two as strong winds, torrential rain and thunderstorms ravaged Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia. Meteorological data showed Saturday's storm was the most destructive to hit Latvia since January 2005. (Photo by Edijs Palens/Xinhua)
RIGA, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- A powerful cyclone swept northward across the three Baltic states on Saturday, killing two as strong winds, torrential rain and thunderstorms ravaged Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia.
Meteorological data showed Saturday's storm was the most destructive to hit Latvia since January 2005.
Latvia's State Fire and Rescue Service said one person was killed and two others injured when part of a building collapsed in Jelgava. By Saturday night, emergency services had received more than 1,000 calls related to wind damage.
Transport was also disrupted, with fallen trees blocking railway lines and halting some train services. RIX Riga Airport warned of flight delays and diversions.
In Lithuania, a man was killed by a falling tree in the Anyksciai district, while a woman was injured in a separate incident. Firefighters received more than 1,200 storm-related calls during the day.
In Estonia, heavy rain and strong winds continued into Sunday morning. The Estonian Environment Agency forecast 50-70 millimeters of rainfall over 24 hours, with up to 90 millimeters in some areas, while coastal wind gusts could reach 22 meters per second on Sunday as the storm moved northeast.
The storm caused extensive damage to power networks across the three countries, disrupting power supplies for about 254,000 people in Latvia, while leaving about 256,000 people without power in Lithuania and more than 3,400 households in Estonia. ■

Xinhua Headlines: Chinese teenagers flock to tech frontline to touch the future amid AI study-tour boom
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
16:19:47 CST
17:19:47 KST

*To help children prepare for an AI-driven future, China unveiled an "AI Plus Education" initiative earlier this year, encouraging schools to take AI learning beyond the classroom through after-school programs and hands-on activities.
*Moving beyond textbooks, students are flocking to tech giants, university labs and science centers, eager to get hands-on experience with cutting-edge AI technologies and see firsthand how the future is taking shape.
*AI study camps are opening a new window onto how the technology is reshaping the world around them and how they can use it to make a difference.
BEIJING, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- On a summer day, cheers erupted as clusters of children watched robots race across a soccer pitch, battling it out in playful matches, at a science center in Jiaxing, east China's Zhejiang Province.
At a nearby workbench, nine-year-old Zhang Qihang was busy assembling a robot of his own. "Building robots is awesome! I can let my imagination run wild," he said, beaming with excitement.
This was the scene at an artificial intelligence (AI) summer camp -- part of a new wave of study tours gaining traction across China. Moving beyond textbooks, students are flocking to tech giants, university labs and science centers, eager to get hands-on experience with cutting-edge AI technologies and see firsthand how the future is taking shape.
AI STUDY-TOUR BOOM
During this summer vacation, AI-themed study tours have begun to gain ground, with bookings surging 370 percent year on year, according to online travel platform Ctrip.
To tap into the growing demand for AI-focused tech tourism, a travel agency based in Nanjing, east China's Jiangsu Province, began adding visits to technology companies to its trip programs last summer. "On our Shanghai-Hangzhou independent study tours, AI-related activities now account for more than 80 percent of the itinerary," founder Zhu Ping said.
The boom is unfolding against the backdrop of China's broader AI boom, powered by a wave of homegrown models and applications. For a growing number of Chinese teenagers, AI tools such as DeepSeek, Kimi and Doubao are becoming familiar companions in their everyday lives.
The number of AI enterprises in China had surpassed 6,000 last year, and the output value of the core AI industry was projected to exceed 1.2 trillion yuan (about 177 billion U.S. dollars) during the same period, representing a year-on-year increase of nearly 30 percent.
Moreover, China was home to more than 140 humanoid robot developers in 2025, with shipments reaching 14,400 units -- accounting for 84.7 percent of the global market, according to an industry research report.
To help children prepare for an AI-driven future, China unveiled an "AI Plus Education" initiative earlier this year, encouraging schools to take AI learning beyond the classroom through after-school programs and hands-on activities. The goal is to help students understand and use AI properly, while sparking curiosity, nurturing creativity and honing their critical-thinking and problem-solving skills.
Today, the AI study-tour wave is sweeping through China's schools, as primary and secondary schools incorporate it into their educational programs. Parents are taking their children into the heart of the tech industry to see how AI transforms the real world.
China's tech-tourism boom is also drawing international visitors keen to get a close-up look at the innovation behind "Made in China."
Since opening in Shanghai in May, Unitree Robotics's first embodied intelligence experience store in Asia has attracted many foreign visitors.
Victoria, from Denmark, visited the store last month. "I've seen some of the dancing videos, but it's really cool to see them in real life," she said, viewing the development of AI and robotics in China as "revolutionary, new and exciting."
FROM AI USERS TO AI CREATORS
Today's children are growing up as AI natives, already fluent in AI tools. But AI study camps are opening a new window onto how the technology is reshaping the world around them and how they can use it to make a difference.
For Liang Yiduo, a Beijing middle school student, an AI summer camp run by internet giant NetEase offered a fresh perspective on the AI technology he thought he already knew.
"I realized that large language models aren't just chatbots or simple tools," he said. "They can be assistants that work alongside you and help you create things tailored to your needs, like 'claws.'"
"The goal of the study camp is to help children move from simply using AI to understanding it, creating with it and even building their own AI agents," said Wang Lijin, director and founder of Beijing Venus Future Education Consulting Center, which assists NetEase in running its study camps.
Some study tour organizers design programs around students' interests and abilities, aiming to spark curiosity and encourage deeper thinking.
Shanghai Qingbao Robot Co., Ltd., for example, offers students who enjoy building things the chance to assemble robotic arms and explore the mechanics of shoulder and neck structures. It also gives students a comparative look at the robotics and AI industries in China, the US, Europe and Japan, helping them gain a more balanced understanding of China's strengths and shortcomings.
Wang Lei, the company's chairman, believes that study tours can greatly broaden students' horizons in science and innovation. "Through immersive study tours, students start thinking for themselves about how robotics can be applied to everyday life, from unmanned retail to automated pharmacies," he said.
Some students are taking it a step further, learning to spot real-world problems and use AI to develop solutions.
In the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, a group of students spent six days in a camp turning ideas into an AI-powered product.
"I've realized that learning AI isn't about showing off what I can do with it, but about using it to solve real problems for others," said one team member. "I want to keep learning AI so I can help more people in the future." ■
